20019-lectures-on-landscape-delivered-at:
John Ruskin delivered his Lectures on Landscape at Oxford in Lent term 1871. He compares two Turner paintings by their harmony of color. One is a harmony of cool color, the other of hot. Both are exquisitely designed in ornamental lines, he grants. But they were not painted for those qualities, he insists. One scene is full of delight to men; the other, of pain and danger. Turner's object is the human meaning of landscape.

Ruskin was Oxford's first Slade Professor of Fine Art. His lectures drew crowds and set Victorian taste. Landscape here means truth to nature, morally read. These talks teach students how to see before judging. Turner stands as prophet of that seeing throughout. The lectures remain a gateway into Ruskin's mind.
20765-diary-of-anna-green-winslow-a-bost:
Alice Morse Earle edited the diary of Anna Green Winslow, a Boston schoolgirl of 1771. Anna was sent from Nova Scotia to Boston, her parents' birthplace, to be finished at good schools. She wrote with care, both for her parents' joy and for practice in fine handwriting.

Daily life in colonial Boston fills the small pages: lessons, calls, dress, and church. A girl's eye catches what grand histories miss. The diary shows the prim, narrow round of a town on the edge of revolt. Few sources let young readers hear the past in a voice so close to their own age.
arxiv-2512-00071:
Prime numbers follow patterns that are simple to state and hard to prove. Yung-Hua Chen studies correlations between primes separated by a fixed shift, in a 2025 study. The sequence involved has no multiplicative structure and no Euler product, which blocks many standard analytic tools.

Chen builds a framework based on Mellin-Laplace kernels to expose structural obstructions in these correlations. Work at this level is theoretical, aimed at showing what cannot happen as much as what can. It contributes to analytic number theory, where prime pair patterns remain among the deepest open questions. Such results clarify where analytic methods reach their natural edge and map terrain for later work.
arxiv-2512-00371:
In open-source games, players submit computer programs instead of choosing actions directly. Swadesh Sistla and Max Kleiman-Weiner evaluate large language models in that setting in 2025. Submitted programs are interpretable, transparent to other agents, and formally verifiable.

Programs also enable program equilibria, outcomes that exploit the transparency of code and are unreachable in ordinary game settings. Testing models as program-writers probes both their coding skill and their strategic reasoning. The setting offers a clean laboratory for studying how AI agents compete and cooperate when everyone can read everyone else's strategy. Open-source games are a public arena, so model strategies can be inspected by anyone. That openness is the feature the whole setting is built to exploit.
arxiv-2512-00471:
Quantum chaos is often measured by correlators that deliberately scramble the order of operations in time. Andrew Hunt studies out-of-time-order correlation functions in single-body systems in 2025. These correlators quantify how fast quantum information spreads and becomes inaccessible.

Maldacena and co-authors conjectured a universal, temperature-dependent bound on that scrambling rate. Single-body systems are the simplest arena in which to test such claims, free of many-body complications. Hunt's analysis helps clarify whether the bound reflects deep principles or artifacts of the complicated systems where it was first proposed. Single-body systems strip quantum chaos down to its simplest possible stage. If the bound fails there, its claimed universality needs rethinking.
arxiv-2512-00671:
Four physicists, J Altmann, L Bernardinis, P Skands, and V Zaccolo, tackle a puzzle from the Large Hadron Collider in 2025. When protons collide, the share of strange hadrons grows as more charged particles are made. A hadron is a particle built from quarks, and strange ones carry a strange quark.

The widely used Pythia event generator, with its default Monash tune, predicts no such growth. The authors test a possible fix called string closepacking. In that picture, overlapping strings from the collision form a background field, mostly along the beam line. Checking this idea may help event models match what detectors see.
arxiv-2512-00871:
Na Wang and five coauthors search for rhythmic flickers in blazars in a 2025 astronomy paper. Blazars are galaxies whose jets point almost straight at Earth, making them look bright and variable. A quasi-periodic oscillation is a rough rhythm in that flickering, which hints at regular motion near the galaxy's black hole.

Using data from the Zwicky Transient Facility, the team picked ten blazars as their sample. Four of them showed possible signs of such rhythmic modulation. The authors name each candidate and treat the signals as indications, not proof. Firmer rhythms, if confirmed, could clock the inner workings of blazar jets.
arxiv-2512-00971:
Yunfeng Lin and six coauthors present H-Zero in a 2025 robotics paper on humanoid walking. Humanoid robots need controllers that keep them stable and efficient as they move. Most existing controllers are built for one robot design, so each new body demands fresh tuning of rewards, physical parameters, and training settings.

H-Zero pretrains locomotion across humanoid bodies, learning shared walking skills that are not tied to one design. The authors show that this cross-humanoid pretraining enables few-shot transfer to new embodiments. A robot maker could adapt the controller to a fresh design with little extra training, speeding up development across product lines.
arxiv-2512-01271:
Pratik Chattopadhyay works on rules for very soft light in an expanding universe. In quantum theory, soft photons are light parts with very low energy. Known rules link them to how charged parts scatter. Past work dealt with heavy charged parts in de Sitter space, a model of fast growth.

The light-mass case was left unclear in that past work. Taking the mass to zero gave a muddy result. Chattopadhyay works out the fix for that case step by step. Clear rules for soft light help check that quantum sums in curved space stay sound.
arxiv-2512-01471:
Luis Reis, Mario Baldiotti, and Orfeu Bertolami study gas falling onto coupled black holes. Some black holes may gain mass from the cosmos itself as space expands. Dark fluids drive that expansion. The team asks how such a fluid falls onto those holes.

They focus on a fluid called generalized Chaplygin gas. To keep the fluid's global traits, they use the McVittie metric. That metric blends a black hole with an expanding cosmos. The study shows how inflow shifts with coupling. Results feed the debate on whether black holes can grow with the universe.
arxiv-2512-01671:
Aurelien Drezet and Bernard Nabet link Maxwell theory to the de Broglie-Bohm view in a tiny cavity. In an optical microcavity, a photon acts like a massive particle. Its energy law comes from Maxwell's equations. The Bohm view tracks a probability fluid for that particle.

The pair show the two conservation laws match in form. That formal match ties wave energy flow to Bohm trajectories. Such links help interpret quantum optics tests. They also clarify what Bohm paths mean for light in confined spaces. Two-dimensional cavities keep the match exact, giving a clean case where looser analogies in higher dimensions can be judged against truth.
arxiv-2512-01771:
Ahsan Raza Siyal and co-authors register medical images with learnable edge kernels. Registration aligns images from distinct scans, times, or subjects. Diagnosis and treatment plans rest on that alignment. Classic methods strain with contrast gaps, warps, and modality traits.

Their method learns edge kernels that guide the match. Edges stay more stable across modalities than raw brightness. The approach covers both rigid and non-rigid alignment. Steadier alignment helps doctors compare scans over a treatment course without hand fixes at each visit. Edge kernels are learned per task, so the same frame adapts to brain, lung, or joint scans without hand-set filter banks.
arxiv-2512-01871:
Stein spaces are a central setting in complex geometry, and mathematicians have long wanted an equally clean version in non-archimedean geometry, where distance works differently. Tom Biesbrouck's 2025 paper builds that version algebraically, starting from a new class of Banach algebras he calls Liu algebras.

He defines non-archimedean Stein algebras as inverse limits of these locally affinoid algebras, then shows the spaces match the algebras in a complete, functorial way through their Berkovich spectra. In doing so, the paper settles a conjecture posed by Michael Temkin. The result gives non-archimedean geometers a firm dictionary between spaces and their algebras.
arxiv-2512-02171:
The brightest objects in the universe, quasars, X-ray binaries, and gamma-ray bursts, pour out energy drawn from gravity or spin. Elisabete Dal Pino's 2025 paper reviews how such high-energy sources work when the central object has no event horizon, the point of no return that defines a black hole.

Converting gravitational or rotational energy into radiation, jets, and relativistic outflows is the engine in all these sources. If the central body is a horizonless compact object rather than a black hole, the extraction mechanisms and their signatures change. Understanding those differences gives observers a way to test what really sits at the heart of these cosmic powerhouses.
arxiv-2512-02371:
Tensor accelerators, the specialized circuits behind modern AI chips, are powerful but notoriously hard to program beyond matrix multiplication. Yihong Zhang and three co-authors present in 2025 a user-schedulable language that lets developers direct these accelerators at a wider range of workloads themselves.

Today most programmers must use vendor kernel libraries, which confine tensor hardware to traditional machine learning and scientific computing shapes. A schedulable language hands scheduling decisions to the user instead of the library. Opening tensor accelerators to general computation could reclaim a large and growing share of the world's computing capacity for new tasks.
arxiv-2512-02571:
Kobe Grobben, Phablo F. S. Moura, and Hande Yaman study approximation schemes for hard covering and packing problems. Such mixed integer programs include multidimensional knapsack, facility location, and supplier selection. Exact solutions grow too slow on large inputs, so near optimal answers with guarantees are prized.

The authors first study the vertices of the linked polytope, the shape that encodes the problem. They then split problems into knapsack cover cases with one continuous variable per dimension. Structure aware splitting is a classic route to schemes that run in reasonable time while staying provably close to optimal. The split turns one hard nut into many small ones, each of which a fast code can crack with care.
arxiv-2512-02971:
A. D. Lindsay, S. Rhebergen, and B. S. Southworth speed up fluid flow simulation at high Reynolds number. Their solver uses a hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin method on the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Fast, turbulent like flows make such systems hard to solve iteratively without a good preconditioner.

Their preconditioner rests on an augmented Lagrangian form of the full discretization. Unlike standard grad div augmentation, theirs builds on divergence conformity. Better solvers shorten design cycles for aircraft, ships, and turbines, where high Reynolds flow decides performance and fuel use. Fast solves mean more shapes can be tried per day. More shapes tried is how a wing or a hull gets good in the end, not by one big guess.
arxiv-2512-03071:
Mixed data, with both numbers and labels, are hard to group. Loup-Noé Levy, Guillaume Guerard, Sonia Djebali, and Soufian Ben Amor offer a new tool in this 2025 work. Their method, called PretopoMD, rests on pretopology, a flexible way to define closeness.

The tool builds groups in layers without first shrinking the data down. It uses plain logic rules that users can set to fit their own needs. Users can also tune settings to shape the groups they get. Such control helps when data sets differ a lot from one field to the next. For data teams, the appeal lies in rules they can adjust without rebuilding the whole method from scratch each time.
arxiv-2512-03271:
Muslims pray toward the Kaaba in Mecca, a direction called the Qibla. Duaa Abdullah reviews ways to find that direction in this 2025 work. Muslim scholars and astronomers have worked on the problem for centuries with great care.

Old methods use tools like the astrolabe and compass. Newer methods use spherical trigonometry to compute the Qibla angle from any place on Earth. Abdullah compares astronomical and geometrical approaches. The study joins history of science with a live religious need for accurate prayer direction. Trigonometric methods give a precise azimuth for any site, once its coordinates are known.
arxiv-2512-03371:
Partial processes need a math frame that respects their limits. Marcello Lanfranchi and Jean-Simon Pacaud Lemay set out such a frame in this 2025 work. Older frames for partial work exist, but the authors seek new ones that fit more cases.

They present three new frames: local, partial, and inclusion types. In the local type, objects are resources that can be reached in part, and maps are processes that link them. Such frames help model work that may fail or lack full data. They may serve the study of code, data banks, and systems where some inputs are missing by design.
arxiv-2601-06771:
Shihui Feng wrote a 2026 arXiv paper with Baiyue He, Dragan Gasevic, and Alec Kirkley. The paper sets out a new way to map how learning takes place. It calls the way Heterogeneous Interaction Network Analysis, or HINA for short. The name points to links of more than one kind.

Most older work treats learning as a chain of acts by one learner. It can also treat each link as if it were much like the next link. The authors say that view misses how acts spread out in real class settings. HINA works at more than one level at once. It tracks hard learning steps as they move across people and tools. For teams who study how people learn, the paper gives a clear plan to use and test.
arxiv-2601-07271:
Research by Mohan Raj Chanthran and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with Document-Level Zero-Shot relation extraction with entity side information. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Document-Level Zero-Shot Relation Extraction (DocZSRE) aims to predict unseen relation labels in text documents without prior training on specific relations.

Existing approaches rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate synthetic data for unseen labels, which poses challenges for low-resource languages like Malaysian English. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07871:
Minh H. N. Le and colleagues argue that heart disease data should be analyzed together, not in separate pipelines. Cardiovascular disease arises from inherited risk, molecular programs, and tissue remodeling. Clinicians see that remodeling through imaging. Health systems now gather cardiac MRI, CT, and echocardiography alongside bulk, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomics. Yet these data types are still usually analyzed apart. Their 2026 preprint reviews imaging-anchored multiomics.

Anchoring molecular data to images ties gene activity to visible tissue change. That link can reveal which molecular programs drive the patterns doctors see. Integration is hard because the data differ in scale, format, and noise. The authors survey how the field is meeting that challenge. The paper serves cardiology and genomics scholars. It makes the case for joint analysis as the default, not the exception.
arxiv-2601-08271: Angshul Majumdar formalizes sparse control for tool-using language model agents. The 2026 arXiv paper describes a regime learning theory has largely ignored. Agents choose in sequence from a massive discrete set of tools, APIs, and documents. Only a small, unknown subset matters for any fixed task distribution. Majumdar names this setting sparse agentic control and gives policies block-sparse representations. The paper argues sparsity is necessary for polynomial-time stability in such systems. The result guides theory for agents whose action menus keep growing.
arxiv-2601-08371: Anastasios Tsalakopoulos and co-authors present Geo-NVS-w for novel view synthesis from wild photo collections. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets unstructured images taken under varied real-world conditions. Existing in-the-wild methods already produce strong novel views. Yet they often lack geometric grounding on complex surfaces and can yield inconsistent results. Geo-NVS-w adds geometry awareness with an SDF renderer, which models surfaces as signed distance fields. The aim is high-fidelity views that stay consistent in shape, useful for tourism photos, heritage scans, and scene reconstruction.
arxiv-2601-08571: S. R. Luwang and co-authors discover market regimes and study returns inside each regime. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that financial markets alternate between tranquil periods and episodes of stress. Return dynamics can change substantially across those regimes, so one global model may mislead. The team studies developed and developing equity indices. Their pipeline uses Hilbert-Huang-based regime identification and profiling, then variable-length Markov modeling of categorized returns. Regime-aware models could improve risk forecasts that now assume calm and crisis behave alike.
arxiv-2601-08871:
Junhua Huang, Chao Huang, and Chenliang Xu work on how sound is mixed for a film scene. A scene mix must weigh speech, song, and sound effects so the tale stays clear. That mix is now done by hand, and it takes long hours of skilled work. New tools can rebalance sound with help from the image, but we know little of which image cues help most.

The team tests which sight cues guide a good sound boost. A face in close view may call for clear speech. A wide street view may call for more street sound. A reader who makes film or games gets a map of cues that count. It can steer auto mix tools to choices a human mixer would trust.
arxiv-2601-09371:
Ángel López-Oriona and Ying Sun build new tests for dependence in functional time series. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks whether curve-valued data, observed over time, behave like pure white noise. The tests rest on functional quantile autocorrelation, a quantile-based way to track dependence.

Older tests lean on the classical autocovariance kernel, which outliers and nonlinear patterns can fool. The new approach uses quantile excursion sets to catch dependence in a more robust way. It is built for infinite-dimensional data, where each observation is a whole curve. Such tools help analysts check models for data like daily pollution or yield curves.
arxiv-2601-09671:
Frederick J. Vrba and a large team report distances and motions for the coldest known classes of star-like bodies. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers 173 L and T dwarfs observed by the US Naval Observatory's infrared astrometry program. Parallaxes and proper motions were measured with the ASTROCAM imager on the 1.55-meter telescope at Flagstaff Station.

The sample holds 74 L dwarfs and 99 T dwarfs, some single and some in binary systems. Each object was observed at a median of 62 epochs over about five years. Near-infrared photometry comes with the positions. Distances turn faint smudges into a mapped population of the solar neighborhood's coldest residents.
arxiv-2601-09871:
Andrea Ferrario, Alessandro Facchini, and Juan M. Durán argue that epistemology can rescue a key idea about human-AI teamwork. Their 2026 arXiv paper concerns human-AI complementarity: a human with AI support beating either one alone. The claim has spread through the human-AI interaction literature.

Complementarity generalizes the older reliance paradigm and offers a more practical frame than the contested idea of trust in AI. The authors ask what epistemology, the study of knowledge, adds. Grounding the claim in how knowledge works could tell designers when teamwork truly helps. It also clarifies what evidence would prove complementarity real.
arxiv-2601-10371:
Malte Hellmann and Jürgen Gauss extend a symmetry trick to harder point groups. Coupled cluster math is a top tool for molecule states. Symmetry can cut its cost by a vast share. A direct product split sorts terms by their symmetry kind. That works well for plain groups.

Non Abelian groups are less plain. Their kinds mix in rich ways. The team show the split for one such group, named C3v. They sort pair terms and cluster terms into blocks. Each block comes from a split of kinds. The work opens the trick to more molecule shapes.
arxiv-2601-10571:
C. Richard and co authors fix bias in a beam width test used in photo injectors. Such rigs make the first burst of grains for a light source. Beam width sets how well the full rig can do. A slit profiler reads that width by a mask with a thin cut.

Such reads can hold set flaws. A flaw can shift the width that is read. The team name those flaws and give fixes for them. The fixes rest on the form of the test rig. A true width read is key. It tells a lab if its source is fit to run.
arxiv-2601-11071:
The LHAASO collaboration reports observations of the pulsar wind nebula DA 495. A pulsar wind nebula is a bubble of particles blown by a spinning neutron star. DA 495 has been watched from radio to TeV gamma rays. LHAASO, a high-altitude air shower observatory, adds fresh eyes at the highest energies.

The new data reveal an energy-dependent morphology: the source's shape changes with photon energy. The water Cherenkov detector array measures an extended source of a stated angular size. Shape changes with energy trace how particles cool as they drift from the pulsar. The work helps map how a dead star keeps lighting its surroundings for tens of thousands of years.
arxiv-2601-11271:
Martin Ortiz recasts part of Serre's conjecture in geometric form in this work. His 2026 preprint deals with the weight part of that conjecture. Serre's conjecture links modular forms to Galois groups. The weight part asks which weights can arise for a given form.

Ortiz uses de Rham cohomology of special fibers for the task. Special fibers come from Shimura varieties, key spaces in number theory. He conjectures his form matches the classic one. The classic form uses Serre weights and etale cohomology. The work also builds generalized mod p BGG decompositions. Those splits break big cohomology groups into graded pieces. A geometric form could give new tools for old questions.
arxiv-2601-11371:
Stephanie Roden and five coauthors trace how hot electrons settle in metals. Their 2026 preprint deals with Fermi systems hit by light. A fast flash of light knocks electrons out of balance. The energy spread then shows a step shape from Pauli blocking.

On a femtosecond scale, electrons hit each other and share energy. Those collisions drive the spread toward a hot Fermi form. The team derives the full collision term for that process. It is the electron-electron Boltzmann collision integral. The derivation uses the random-k approximation for the math. A full term lets simulations track thermalization with more care. That matters for ultrafast optics and laser-cut metals.
arxiv-2601-11471:
James O'Neill, Robert Clancy, Mariia Matskevichus, and Fergal Reid shrink transformer memory. Their 2026 preprint gives Low-Rank Key Value attention, or LRKV. Transformers store keys and values for all past tokens. That KV cache is a primary bottleneck on memory.

The team exploits redundancy across attention heads to cut it. Each layer shares one full-rank KV projection for all heads. Low-rank, head-specific residuals then restore each head's flavor. The design gives a smooth dial between two extremes. One end shares all, the other keeps heads fully apart. Compute stays efficient while memory drops in their design. Longer contexts on the same hardware are the prize.
arxiv-2601-11771:
Tong Mao, Jinchao Xu, and Xiaofeng Xu solve hard maths problems that span many variables. Such problems, called PDEs, rule heat, flow, and fields. A new route fixes the inner part of a shallow net and trains just the last layer. That turns training into a plain least squares task.

These nets sit in the random feature method and in extreme learning machines. They have shown strong results of late. The team study how to use this linear form well in high dimensions. Fast PDE tools aid design in planes, chips, and more.
arxiv-2601-12371: Nishant Rathee and Manoj K. Yadav work in algebra on skew left braces. They study extensions of these structures and their second cohomology groups. Their route goes through groups built as natural semi direct products. A skew brace extension can be written as a short exact sequence, and that form guides the work.
arxiv-2601-12571:
Benjamin Grant and Zhongyang Li study self avoiding walks on cubic graphs. A self avoiding walk never visits the same vertex twice. Cubic graphs give each vertex degree three, and the graphs here are infinite and quasi transitive. The team apply local transformations that swap each vertex for a small gadget. Each gadget is finite, symmetric, and has three ports.

To each gadget they attach a two port generating function. That function counts walks that enter and exit the gadget through set ports. Generating functions turn counting problems into algebra that can be solved. Local swaps of this kind let one graph be reshaped into another. The work asks which walk counts survive such reshaping, a core question in combinatorics.
arxiv-2601-12671:
Thamara Leandra de Deus Melo and three co authors, at Brazilian universities, classify brain tumors in MRI scans. Early tumor diagnosis is crucial for good treatment outcomes. Diagnosis is hard because lesions vary a lot and images are complex. The team evaluate convolutional neural networks in a federated learning setting, so data can stay at each hospital.

They compare models trained on original scans against preprocessed ones. Preprocessing includes resizing, grayscale conversion, normalization, filtering, and histogram equalization. They also exploit test time augmentation, a trick that averages views of a scan at test time. The study asks which pipeline choices pay off under federation. Answers guide clinics that cannot pool patient images.
arxiv-2601-13671:
Apoorva Adimulam, Rajesh Gupta, and Sumit Kumar map how teams of AI agents can be run as one system in 2026. In such setups, many autonomous agents talk and coordinate to reach shared goals. Firms now test these systems for real work, not just in labs. Loose coordination can bring chaos, cost, and risk.

The team gathers the parts of orchestration into one clear frame. Planning, policy rules, state tracking, and quality checks all sit in one layer. That layer steers the agents as a group. A shared frame could help firms adopt agent teams with more trust and control.
arxiv-2601-14271:
Denise M. Case states and proves a theorem about shared data systems in this 2026 paper. Modern systems must support accountability, even when users hold clashing legal, political, and analytic views for good. That need sets strict rules for any ontology meant to serve as a shared base layer. An ontology is a formal map of terms and their links.

Case proves an impossibility result for ontological neutrality. In her terms, neutrality means the base layer takes no side and stays stable when clashing views extend it. She shows that such a base cannot also hold causal or normative claims at its root. Her title draws the upshot: neutral substrates must be pre-causal and pre-normative.
arxiv-2601-14371:
Small asteroids and large meteoroids hit Earth often, yet their physical traits stay poorly known. When such bodies burn as fireballs in the atmosphere, their ablation and fragmentation behavior can reveal those traits. This 2026 paper, the second in its series, works on decameter-sized Earth impactors. A 2022 release of once-classified United States Government satellite sensor data changed the field. It gave hundreds of new fireball light curves for detailed study.

The authors built a Bayesian inference approach to meteoroid ablation modeling. Bayesian methods weigh how well each model fits the data against prior knowledge. Readers should note the evidence pack lists no authors for this entry. The paper's value lies in a firmer way to read fireball curves.
arxiv-2601-14471:
A. Kumar and a large team trace carbon in a fusion device in this 2026 paper. The device is the DIII-D tokamak. A helicon antenna injects radio waves to heat and drive the plasma. During high-power helicon discharge, carbon appears in the plasma. The team asks where that carbon comes from and how it travels.

Their focus is the helicon antenna surfaces themselves as a source. Carbon sputtered or released there can enter the plasma and affect its state. The study follows both sourcing and transport from those surfaces. Readers get a fuller account of impurity flow in a working tokamak, a detail that matters for clean, steady fusion runs.
arxiv-2601-14571:
Yan Meng, Kainan Chang, and Luxia Wang study energy transfer in a hybrid nanomaterial in this 2026 paper. The system pairs an organic molecule with an inorganic nanoflake. The molecule is para-sexiphenyl, known as 6P. It sits adsorbed on a finite-sized MoS2 nanoflake, a transition metal dichalcogenide. The team investigates excitation energy transfer between the two parts in theory.

They describe the electronic structure of the MoS2 nanoflake with an 11-band tight-binding model. Edge states are passivated with hydrogen atoms to restore a well-defined bandgap. The work is done in math and code. No lab test is used, but the model can be checked by lab work later. Readers get a model of how energy moves in a nanohybrid, a design used in light-harvesting and optoelectronic devices.
arxiv-2601-14771:
Puneet Sharma and four co-authors work on colon capsule endoscopy in this 2026 paper. A colon capsule is a swallowed camera that films the colon. Identifying unique polyps across its images is a critical yet challenging task for medical personnel. The volume of images is large. The cognitive load on clinicians is heavy. Labeling specific frames is also ambiguous, since one polyp appears in many frames.

The team uses multi-instance learning to identify unique polyps. In that method, a model learns from bags of frames with loose labels, rather than exact frame tags. Readers get a tool to count each polyp once, so follow-up care rests on the true count.
arxiv-2601-15571:
Tristan Simas studies how hard it is to judge sufficiency in decisions in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is a formal decision problem. An action set, a state space, and a utility function define it. The state space is a product of coordinates. A set of coordinates is sufficient when it pins down the optimal action. If two states agree on those coordinates, they share the same best action.

Simas characterizes the computational complexity of that judgment. In plain terms, he asks how costly it is to test whether a coordinate set suffices. The answer guides anyone who wants to trim inputs to a decision rule. Fewer needed coordinates mean simpler, cheaper decisions. Complexity bounds tell us when that trimming is feasible and when it is hopeless.
arxiv-2601-16071:
Giacomo Graziani studies the shape of neural layers built from maths maps. His 2026 preprint looks at layers made by a fixed power map. He tracks a count known as the Euclidean Distance degree. That count tells how many best close fits a plain point has. The fits are made with a plain choice of length rule.

Graziani asks when that count stays firm as terms shift. Firm counts help teams know what a layer can and can not do. The study uses the shape maths of these layer sets. It links deep learning form to pure maths of curves and sets. The result gives a firm base for later work on layer shape.
arxiv-2601-16371:
Jiwon Jang and coauthors test a trade scope set for sky views. Their 2026 preprint sets out the PIXIS 1300BX cam and its mate scope parts. Trade sets must be checked as a whole ere use in night work. The team runs the set through lab and sky tests. Tests span sharp grade, noise and true light counts.

A full trait map tells users what the set can and can not do. It also gives a base line for later wear checks. Trade sets at low cost serve schools and small teams well. Firm trait maps help those teams plan night work. The work is a tool note for sky users.
arxiv-2601-16771:
Jiahao Li, Yunpeng Bai, Yongkang Dai, Hao Guo, Hongping Gan, and Yilei Shi build a new way to make 3D parts by machine. Parts in design files are stored as B-reps. A B-rep lists the faces, edges, and links of a solid. Past AI tools split shape and links into two tracks. That split blocked the use of text-style AI models.

Their 2026 preprint packs the whole B-rep in one token chain. Text-style models can then learn and make parts in one flow. The chain keeps both shape and links in full. This could let firms draft parts from prompts. It could also speed search in vast part stores.
arxiv-2601-17071:
Jisui Huang, Andreas Alpers, Ke Chen, and Na Lei split shots in the face of harsh light gaps. Some shots mix bright and dim zones in stark ways. Plain splits fail where light shifts that hard. Their 2026 preprint takes a two-step path. First, pixels group in small tiles called superpixels. A lean least-squares step does that group work fast.

Next, tiles merge in whole zones by a spread gauge. That gauge is the squared 2-Wasserstein gap. It weighs tile trait spreads, not just means. Clean splits feed car, scan, and scope tools. The path runs fast for big shot sets.
arxiv-2601-17171:
Yehya Cheryala, Mokhtar Z. Alaya, and Salim Bouzebda work on a hard math problem in optimal transport. The field asks how to compare and align several chance distributions at once. It is used in machine learning and statistics, where such joint matching comes up often.

The authors present one full Kantorovich duality theory for this multi-way case. The theory holds on general Polish product spaces. It needs only a bounded, continuous cost function. A clear duality result helps users check solutions and build methods on firm ground. Readers in math and data work gain a single frame where older split results now fit together.
arxiv-2601-17371:
Shuning Zhang and seven co-authors present Collab, a web plugin to help users flag deepfake videos. Deepfakes shift in space and time in subtle ways. One viewer can miss signs that a group would catch. Platforms also lack tools that scale human review. Collab lets users mark and share notes on videos as a team.

Joint annotation pools many eyes on one clip. Notes build a record that moderators can use. The tool aims at social media, where fakes spread fast. It treats viewers as partners, not just targets. That shift could raise the quality of public checks. It also gives platforms richer proof than a lone flag.
arxiv-2601-17871:
Huy Trinh, Sebastian Ratto, Elliot Creager, and George Shaker build a bridge between radar simulation and the real world. Their 2026 preprint is about FMCW radar, a type that sweeps its tone to sense range. Training radar models on real data is costly. It needs controlled tests, repeated setup, and long hours of labeling. Many teams cannot pay that price.

The team uses a digital twin shaped by physics to stand in for real rooms. Their light frame trains models in the twin for tasks like spotting people in a room and counting them. The goal is that the models still work when moved to real radar. Less time in the lab means faster progress for sensing tools.
arxiv-2601-17971:
Junior Cedric Tonga, Chen Cecilia Liu, Iryna Gurevych, and Fajri Koto turn language models into sources of cultural knowledge. Their 2026 preprint starts from a simple fact. Models soak up cultural know-how from vast and varied web text. That know-how is rich, but it sits inside the model in a loose, hidden form. Hidden knowledge is hard to check, share, or build on.

The team draws the knowledge out into a graph of cultural commonsense. Nodes and links state what people in a culture take for granted. An iterative process pulls the facts out step by step. A structured graph can serve search, teaching, and cross-cultural tools. It also lets scholars inspect what the model has absorbed.
arxiv-2601-18571:
Maël Dumas and Aliaume Lopez study when a set of graphs can be sorted by a kind of well rule. A well rule here means no chain of graphs in the set drops for ever, and no set of graphs in it all fail to hold each other. The graphs in view have a cap on how wide their tree-like form can be. Their points can bear tags.

The pair show that one can tell, from a finite plan of the set, if the set is well ruled in this sense. That is a strong claim: a finite check can settle a trait of a set with no end. Such checks sit at the base of proofs that some searches must end. They also serve the maths of graphs with caps, a field that feeds code checks and chip design.
arxiv-2601-18671:
N. Balabanova, H. Duong, and C. Hilbe study a game of give and take in which the two sides move in turns, not at once. The base game is a famed one: each side can help or cheat, and joint help pays best for both in the long run. In the turn form, one side gives first and the next side then picks its move with that gift in view. That break of step fits real trades, such as gift chains.

Each side can hold a long mind of past moves. The team ask which ways of play grow strong as groups of such players change over time. Long minds let a side tell a slip from a cheat. That skill can keep joint help alive when a same-time game would kill it. The work adds to the maths of how trust grows.
arxiv-2601-18771:
Yanming Liu and nine colleagues build Dep-Search, a way for language models to reason through hard asks with the help of search. Such models can call on out-side facts as they work, step by step. The field has grown past plain fetch-and-read plans, in which facts are pulled once and the reply is wrote at once. New plans search in rounds, with each round set by what the last round found.

Those rounds lean on each other: a late search rests on the facts and picks of the rounds ahead of it. If those links are lost, the chain can drift or loop. Dep-Search learns traces that keep the links in view as it goes. It also keeps a store that lasts across rounds, so past finds stay in hand. A chain that minds its own links should reach sounder ends.
arxiv-2601-18871:
Zoe Le Conte and nine colleagues find a small disc of stars at the heart of a far galaxy, from a time when space was young. Such discs are built by bars: long lines of stars that sweep gas to the core. The gas then forms new stars in a tight ring or disc. To find a disc of that kind at such a young age is to find that bars did their work far back in time.

Past work had shown bars in place a few years of space time past the start. This disc shows the next step: a bar that has had time to build a core disc. That means bars can shape a galaxy from its youth, not just in its old age. The find rests on sharp shots of a galaxy at what the field calls cosmic noon.
arxiv-2601-19171:
Seokhyeon Park and six co-authors study the gaps between what users want and what AI interface builders give. Generative tools can now draw polished interfaces from text prompts. Yet users often cannot state their design intent in words, and they struggle to judge or refine what comes back.

The team names these the gulfs of execution and evaluation, and offers semantic guidance to bridge them. Guidance in terms of meaning, not pixels, helps users steer by intent. The work speaks to a broad design problem: tools that generate well still fail if people cannot direct them.
arxiv-2601-19571:
Antonio Lei and Katharina Müller bring a deep number theory method to the study of graphs. Iwasawa theory tracks how algebraic objects grow across towers of number fields. Here the tower is made of directed graphs, stacked in layers with a regular symmetry. Two groups are watched as the tower climbs: the Picard group and the Bowen-Franks group of each graph.

The authors formulate and prove main conjectures for these groups in this graph setting. A main conjecture links an analytic object to an algebraic one, and proving it is a strong check on the theory. Their towers are indexed by prime powers in several directions at once. The work shows that ideas born in number theory can govern combinatorics too.
arxiv-2601-19771:
Deeksha Arun, Kevin W. Bowyer, and Patrick Flynn work on identifying people by their ears. Ear shape is stable and distinctive, making it a useful biometric. Vision transformers are strong recognisers, but they cut images into rectangular tokens. For an ear, those rectangles pull in background and hair, which pollutes the signal.

Their method, PaW-ViT, warps the ear image before recognition. The warping is rooted in anatomical knowledge of how ears are shaped. Normalising the image this way makes the transformer's job cleaner. The team tests the approach on ear verification, deciding whether two images show the same ear. Preprocessing guided by anatomy could lift other biometric systems too.
arxiv-2601-20171:
Kazuma Yamasaki and five colleagues ask who writes project documentation now that AI agents contribute code. As software work moves toward what they call SE 3.0, agents carry out more tasks and open pull requests of their own. The authors compare documentation pull requests written by agents with those written by humans.

Their study looks at how much agents contribute and how human reviewers step in. That pattern shows where trust in agent work is high and where people still check closely. The results matter for teams setting rules on agent use, since docs shape how well a project can be maintained.
arxiv-2601-20371:
Kenta Fujisawa and seven colleagues monitor a methanol maser in the star-forming region G33.641-0.228. Masers are bright, narrow radio signals from gas clouds. This one, at a frequency used to trace young massive stars, shows burst-like flashes for unknown reasons. The team watches its flux and circular polarization at high cadence.

They observe with left and right circular polarizations at the same time. The polarization pattern can reveal magnetic fields and the geometry of the bursting gas. Pinning down why these masers flare would sharpen a tool astronomers use to study how massive stars are born.
arxiv-2601-20571:
Anna van Elst, Igor Colin, and Stephan Clémençon study robust distributed learning on resource-constrained edge devices. Algorithms there must be communication-efficient, robust to corrupted data, and light in memory. Gossip-based methods meet the first need, but robustness is harder to achieve.

The authors turn to asynchronous decentralized ADMM methods for estimating quantiles, starting from the median, which resists corruption better than the mean. Edge networks, from sensors to phones, must learn without a central server and despite bad actors. Robust quantile estimation gives such networks a trustworthy summary of their data.
arxiv-2601-20871:
Rylan Malarchick measures how much trust survives each step of quantum circuit optimization. The 2026 paper spans the full compilation stack. It runs from high-level gate optimization down to pulse-level control. A modular framework links a C++ circuit optimizer with pulse simulation. The pulse model uses Lindblad dynamics, which account for noise and decay. Hardware parameters come from the IQM Garnet quantum processor.

Four optimization passes come under the lens. They are gate cancellation, commutation, rotation merging, and identity elimination. Each pass simplifies a circuit, but each can also cost fidelity. The study evaluates that cost in a systematic way. End-to-end numbers show where simplification helps and where it hurts. The work guides compiler writers who must trade neat circuits against true accuracy.
arxiv-2601-20971:
The Spherical-Rindler Framework is built in this 2026 paper as a new view of flat spacetime. It starts with Rindler-type pictures of Minkowski space. The standard hyperbolic map is shown to be one of an infinite family. Each member is a new coordinate map of the same flat space. The authors add cyclic coordinates to this family. Unlike the usual Rindler wedge, these mark out a compact region.

From that start, the frame reaches toward curved settings. Its subtitle promises a path to black hole and cosmology solutions. Compact regions of flat space give a controlled test bed. Lessons learned there can guide work on horizons and expanding worlds. The paper is a theory build, dense with geometry. It serves relativists who craft new coordinate tools.
arxiv-2601-21171:
Kamal Berahmand and four co-authors hunt abnormal nodes in networks with very few labels. Their 2026 paper presents AC2L-GAD, a method for graph anomaly detection. The task is to spot abnormal patterns in networks. Label scarcity and extreme class imbalance make it hard. Anomalies are rare almost by definition. Graph contrastive learning offers a strong unsupervised route. Old versions of it suffer two key flaws.

Random changes can break meaning in positive pairs. Naive negative sampling yields trivial, useless contrasts. The method's name answers both: active counterfactual contrastive learning. Counterfactual cases are crafted to inform, not to randomize. Active selection spends effort where the model is unsure. The work targets fraud, intrusion, and fault detection in network data.
arxiv-2601-21271:
Tram Thi Minh Tran and eight co-authors ask what augmented reality built on sound, not sight, could do in daily life. Smart glasses with speakers are already on the market. Hearing is a main way people sense context, sense change coming, and move through social space.

Yet sound-based augmentation is still little studied next to visual overlays. The authors map out uses, needs, and open design questions for everyday settings. Sound can guide without blocking the view or drawing stares. The work lays ground for tools that help people notice and navigate the world through their ears.
arxiv-2601-21371:
Sifat Chowdhury, Yihsu Chen, and Yu Zhang plan power grid upgrades that hold up against more than one hazard. Extreme weather is growing more common and knocks out power for long stretches. Some defenses help against one threat but hurt under another, such as floods versus high winds.

The authors build a two-stage plan that adapts as conditions unfold. Early choices set up the grid, and later choices respond to the hazard that arrives. Weighing clashing threats together avoids defenses that backfire. The approach gives utilities a way to spend hardening money where it protects against the widest range of storms.
arxiv-2601-21471:
Ruicheng Ao, Hongyu Chen, Siyang Gao, Hanwei Li, and David Simchi-Levi study how to find the best option when judges are cheap but biased. A language model can grade many samples at low cost. True labels from human audits are accurate but expensive, so they can only be bought for a few samples.

Unlike classic setups, the cheap judge is biased in ways that depend on the option and the context. Ground truth also arrives only where the team chooses to look. The authors design a method with firm guarantees for this setting. It fits modern evaluation, where AI judges do the bulk grading.
arxiv-2601-21571:
Neil Rathi and Alec Radford shape what a language model can do by filtering its training data before training starts. Most attempts to remove unwanted skills happen after training and can be bypassed. Filtering the data itself attacks the skill at its root.

On a test task of removing medical skills, simple filtering proved highly effective. It also held up against attempts to undo it and cost little at large scale. The result suggests data curation is a strong safety lever. Builders could decide early which skills a model should never gain, rather than patching them out later.
arxiv-2601-21671:
Divya D. Joshi, Trupti R. Sharma, and Prashant M. Gade study pattern formation in a two-dimensional grid of excitable neuron-like units. Each unit follows the Chialvo map, a simple model of a neuron that can fire. Neighbors are linked by nearest-neighbor coupling, in two different styles.

One coupling style grows ring-like patterns, and the rings widen as coupling strengthens. The other style grows spirals, which break into turbulence and fade at strong coupling. The contrast shows how the wiring rule alone can flip a system's whole behavior. Such maps help explain waves seen in brain tissue, heart muscle, and other excitable media.
arxiv-2601-21771:
Hadi Banaee and Stephanie Lowry model abstract concepts as regions in a geometric space, using chess strategy as the test case. Concepts like attack or sacrifice unfold over time and resist crisp definitions. In their framework, each concept is a region across interpretable quality dimensions.

A game becomes a trajectory moving through that space. When the path heads toward a region, the intended strategy can be recognized. The chess study is a proof of concept for the wider idea. If it generalizes, the same geometry could track strategy in teaching, sport, or negotiation, where plans are real but hard to name.
arxiv-2601-21971:
Lorenzo Mazza and co-authors teach robots to imitate surgeons. Imitation learning works well for ordinary robotic manipulation, but surgery is harder. Data are scarce, workspaces are tight, and the needed safety and predictability are exceptional. A small error at an operating table is not like a dropped cup.

The team presents a supervised mixture-of-experts architecture built for surgical tasks that unfold in phases. Specialized expert networks handle different phases of a procedure, under supervision that keeps behavior structured. Their 2026 preprint aims at policies that are both capable and predictable. Surgical robots that learn from expert surgeons could extend specialist skill to hospitals that have none on staff.
arxiv-2601-22071:
Pranav Nagarajan and co-authors debunk a sensational claim about the star BE Lyncis. BE Lyn is a well-studied pulsating star of the delta Scuti type, with large brightness swings. A recent analysis of decades of its peak-light timings claimed it is an extremely eccentric binary hosting the nearest known black hole.

The team's 2026 preprint uses astrometry from Gaia and Hipparcos, precise measurements of the star's position and motion, to test that claim. Their conclusion stands in the title: BE Lyn is not a black hole binary. The paper is also a lesson in method, showing how a timing pattern alone can mislead. And how independent data can settle an extraordinary claim before it hardens into fact.
arxiv-2601-22171:
Jort de Groot extends a framework from quantum geometry to a new setting. Spectral triples are the core objects of noncommutative geometry. Each triple has three parts. They are an algebra, a Hilbert space, and a Dirac operator. Together they encode a space and its geometry. De Groot works with the group SU(1,1), a non-compact group central to relativity and representation theory.

Using harmonic analysis on that group, he shows that a triple built from Kostant's cubic Dirac operator forms a pseudo-Riemannian spectral triple. His 2026 preprint adapts the machinery, which was designed for Riemannian cases, to the indefinite metric of pseudo-Riemannian geometry. That widens noncommutative geometry toward the spacetime-like settings where it may eventually meet physics.
arxiv-2601-22571:
Zhipeng Chen and a large team built PerfGuard, an agent that watches the true limits of its tools. Their 2026 preprint notes that most agent frames assume each tool call works, and judge tools by text blurbs alone. Real tools for visual content have sharp performance edges that blurbs hide.

PerfGuard tracks what each tool can really do, and plans with those bounds in view. That should cut failed runs and poor picks in image and video tasks. The work is a dose of realism for agent design. It treats tool skill as data, not faith.
arxiv-2601-22871:
Alexander Loth, Martin Kappes, and Marc-Oliver Pahl study how easily people fall for false content made by AI. As large models write with near-human fluency, telling real from synthetic text gets harder. Their work uses two tools, JudgeGPT and RogueGPT, to probe that weakness.

The framework splits two questions: does a text feel authentic, and who or what made it? Keeping those apart shows where human judgment fails first. The findings matter for news, schools, and platforms fighting large-scale deception. Separating authenticity from attribution also helps platforms decide whether to label, limit, or remove suspect content at scale.
arxiv-2601-23071:
Massimo Bocus and Louis Vanduyfhuys present ThermoLIB, a Python library for free energy surfaces. Such surfaces summarize how likely each state of a molecule is, and what barriers separate them. The library builds these surfaces from of molecules model run output.

It can also convert surfaces between different collective variables and pull out thermodynamic and kinetic properties. The package is free on GitHub, with docs and many guides. A shared, tested tool saves labs from rewriting the same analysis code for every project. Tutorials and extended docs ship with the library, lowering the barrier for groups new to free energy methods.
arxiv-2601-23171:
Anthony Almudevar revisits the lost submarine problem as a test case for statistical inference. The example, highlighted by Morey and co-authors in 2016, targets blind faith in confidence intervals. It asks where a lost submarine likely lies, given limited sonar-style information.

A decision-theoretic treatment weighs actions by their costs and risks, not by interval habits alone. The case shows how a tidy interval can mislead when the real question is what to do. It remains a sharp teaching example for applied statisticians. The submarine story's role is diagnostic: it exposes where confidence interval practice breaks as a formal inference statement.

Augustine of Hippo wrote The City of God in Latin in the years after Rome fell. Marcus Dods gave the work English dress in 1871. Book one of this set holds Books One to Thirteen of the work. Augustine wrote to meet pagans who blamed Christ's faith for Rome's fall.

aurelius-victor-historia-romana-1871:
Sextus Aurelius Victor wrote his short history of the emperors around 361 CE, when brief handbooks of the Roman past were in wide demand. His De Caesaribus runs from Augustus to Constantius II. The text here is the Tauchnitz edition of 1871, a Latin school printing from Leipzig. No English version in the public domain exists.

The volume joins the lives of Victor with three short works that traveled with them through the ages. These are the Origo Gentis Romanae on the first kings, the De Viris Illustribus on famous men, and the Epitome de Caesaribus. Together they form the handbook line of late Roman history writing.
baldwin-ancient-america-1871:
John Baldwin asked who built the great mounds of the Ohio and Mississippi valleys, and answered with a lost race. Ancient America, printed in 1871, surveys the ruins and earthworks of the old New World. Baldwin's book was the most read case of its kind in its century.

He walks readers through mounds, forts, and carved stones, arguing a civilized people raised them and then vanished. The claim fed the era's deep hunger for a grand American past. Later dig science gave the mounds back to the ancestors of living Native peoples. Baldwin's survey still shows the debate at its fullest stretch.

cooley-constitutional-limitations-1871:
Thomas Cooley, a Michigan judge and professor, published his Constitutional Limitations in 1868, with the second edition of 1871 here. Its full title names its subject: the limits on the lawmaking power of the states. The book became the leading treatise of its kind.

Cooley sets out due process, vested rights, and the police power with care. He defends courts striking down laws that cross constitutional lines, while granting legislatures wide room. His work supplied the legal charter of laissez-faire constitutionalism in America. Judges cited it constantly in the age of railroad and labor battles. Modern scholars still study Cooley to understand that era.
dialectical-society-report-1871:
