Its band sat with seers, heard scores of guests, and ran tests in homes of their own. Most came in as doubts. Their report stuns: much of it backs the claims as real and past fraud.

That split from the scorn of the press made the book a flag for fans. Foes cried the band was soft. The report is the first great board weigh of the theme. Its words still get quoted.
doe-osti-3006952-energy-improvements-of-: Fire Station 71 got energy-improved, and this DOE text covers the upgrades. The pages detail the findings. The building folks get their case study. The station was 71. The study was building. The upgrades were energy. The study was case. The station was fire.
eliot-george-middlemarch-1871:
George Eliot published Middlemarch in 1871 to 1872, her supreme achievement of Victorian realism, subtitled a study of provincial life. Dorothea Brooke and the interwoven lives of a Midlands town fill a canvas. Eliot wrote it in parts, and its web of marriages, money, and reform is the English novel's widest net.

Dorothea, ardent and idealistic, weds the dry scholar Casaubon and finds a living tomb in his Lowick library and jealous will. Dr. Lydgate, ambitious for medical reform, is trapped by his pretty wife Rosamond and debts in the town's petty economy. Bulstrode's buried past, Fred Vincy's growth, and the 1832 Reform Bill bind private fates to a nation's slow change in England. Eliot's narrator, wise and pitying, weighs every soul with a fairness no character quite earns or escapes. Many judges rank it the greatest novel in the English language.
europmc-pmc10354071:
Cords and colleagues sorted support cells found in breast tumours into clear types in 2023. These cells are called cancer-associated fibroblasts, or CAFs for short. They live around a tumour and can help or hinder its growth. The team read gene activity in over 16,000 such cells from 14 patients.

Nine CAF types emerged, plus one class of vessel wall cells. Cords gave each type a name based on its gene pattern and likely job. The scheme held up in four other cancer types. A scan of protein markers in matched tumours then confirmed the types. It also showed where each type sits inside a tumour, which may guide new treatments.
europmc-pmc10487271:
Najjar reviewed in 2023 how AI is reshaping radiology, the use of scans in medicine. The field began with the discovery of X-rays and now runs on rich digital images. Machine learning and deep learning can read those images at scale. Najjar traces that arc and asks what it means for care.

AI now helps split an image into parts, flag disease, and predict risk. Case reports from many fields show gains in speed and in spotting illness early. Care plans can also be tuned to one patient from scan data. Blocks remain: patchy data, opaque AI logic, high setup costs, and ethics. Najjar backs joint work between scan doctors and AI builders.
europmc-pmc10567571:
Eldjarn and co-authors compared two big blood protein platforms in 2023 through gene and disease links. The platforms, Olink and SomaScan, each read thousands of proteins in blood plasma. The team used Olink data from over 50,000 UK Biobank members. A past SomaScan study of 36,000 Icelanders gave the match point.

Agreement between the two tools was modest, Eldjarn reports. Both found gene links for a like count of tests, near 2,100 each. A higher share of Olink tests had such backing, 72% versus 43%. Some proteins gave gene links that split by platform. Mixed ancestry in the UK set also surfaced new links and sharpened gene maps.
europmc-pmc10748771:
Koliaki, Dalamaga, and Liatis asked in 2023 whether the world obesity surge has begun to flatten. Obesity rates rose fast for decades and strain health systems world-wide. Some data hint at a plateau in rich nations after 2010. The review tests that hope against the full proof.

In rich nations, adult rates look stable in recent years, Koliaki reports. Rates in children and teens have also levelled since 2000 in most such nations. Better food habits and more activity may play a part. In poor nations, though, rates climb with no break. Severe obesity grows fast in rich and middle nations alike. Its share may reach 20% by 2035, twice the level seen in 2020.
europmc-pmc10777171:
Zhang and colleagues review how AI could sharpen a network-based way of studying herbal medicine in this 2023 paper. Traditional Chinese medicine treats the body as one linked system. Network pharmacology, a method that maps how drugs, targets, and diseases connect, fits that whole-body view well. Huge gene and protein datasets now make those maps hard to read by hand.

The review sorts AI tools for this field into three jobs. Some tools mine links in a network, some pinpoint likely drug targets, and some guide the search toward new targets. The authors show how these tools were used to probe cold and hot syndromes, a classic pair of illness patterns. They frame the work as a step toward care matched to each patient.
europmc-pmc10791971:
Li and colleagues review what lives in our lungs and why it matters in this 2024 paper. Lungs were long thought to hold no microbes at all, meaning no tiny living things. Better tests showed a small, shifting community does live there. It comes mostly from the mouth and throat, and it is kept sparse by coughing, immune cells, and the sweep of tiny hairs in the airways.

The review links this lung community to the gut and to the immune system. It then walks through roles in asthma, chronic lung disease, scarring, pneumonia, COVID-19, and lung cancer. The authors note that fungi and viruses in the lung are still poorly studied. They suggest that learning to steer this community could one day aid treatment, but much basic work remains.
europmc-pmc10853571:
Cui and colleagues review what may cause severe depression and how it might be treated in this 2024 paper. Major depressive disorder is a lasting low mood that harms work and daily life. Cases rise each year worldwide, adding social and economic strain. No single theory fully explains the illness, the authors note.

The review walks through leading ideas about its causes. These cover brain signal chemicals, stress hormones, immune signals, and the brain's power to rewire itself. It also stresses links between organs as a newer clue. New drug targets and drugs are surveyed, and some have already won approval for clinic use. Light therapy and acupuncture are noted as options that eased symptoms in some studies. The authors back multi-target plans over single fixes.
europmc-pmc10855871:
Seyhan surveys the promise and the setbacks of tiny RNA drugs in this 2024 review. MicroRNAs are short RNA pieces that tune how genes are used. Faults in them are linked to many diseases, above all cancers. That link drew heavy spending on drugs built from them. The success of COVID mRNA vaccines then revived wider interest in RNA drugs.

Progress in the lab has been strong, the review says, but the clinic tells a harder story. Few microRNA drugs have reached human trials, and none has passed late-stage trials or won US approval. Some trials were halted over harmful side effects. Seyhan argues that better chemistry and better delivery into cells are the keys. Until those gaps close, broad use in patients will stay out of reach.
europmc-pmc1088971:
Cirz and colleagues found a way to stop bacteria from evolving drug resistance in this 2005 study. Drug-proof bacteria are a grave threat to health. With some drugs, germs gain resistance fast through gene mutations during treatment. The team focused on the SOS response, a cell alarm that raises mutation rates when DNA is damaged.

Blocking a protein called LexA kept the alarm off, they showed. Gut bacteria in infected animals then failed to evolve resistance to two key drugs. Lab tests showed the damage repair path switches on error-prone copying enzymes that create the mutations. The authors propose blocking mutation itself as a new drug strategy. Such a blocker, paired with a standard drug, could keep treatments working longer.
europmc-pmc10937371:
All of Us Research Program Genomics Investigators describe a huge US gene dataset in this 2024 paper. The All of Us program is a long-term study aiming to enrol at least one million varied volunteers. Its goal is to speed research and improve health for all groups. Many past gene studies drew mostly on people of European ancestry.

The release holds 245,388 full genome readouts of clinical grade, the team reports. Most volunteers come from groups long left out of such research. The data hold over a billion gene variants, more than 275 million of them never reported before. Checks against health records confirmed most known disease links in both European and African ancestry groups. Approved researchers can reach the data through a workbench, often within about a day.
europmc-pmc11045871:
Fleishman and Kumar reframe bile acids as powerful body signals in this 2024 review. Bile acids were once seen as mere soaps that help digest fat. They are now known to steer how the body handles fats, sugars, and proteins and to tune inflammation. When their signalling goes wrong, heart, metabolic, and cancer risks rise.

The authors build their account from the ground up, covering bile acid chemistry and their receptors, both classic and newly found. They argue that ceramide synthesis, a fat-building path, may be a shared driver of heart and metabolic disease. Existing drugs that tune bile acid receptors are reviewed, with their flaws named. One leading candidate was lately rejected by the US drug agency. The paper proposes fixes and fresh targets rather than abandoning the field.
europmc-pmc11306271:
Sweatt, Garvey, and Martins weigh the strengths and limits of body mass index for diagnosing obesity in this 2024 review. Body mass index, or BMI, divides weight by height squared. Diagnosing obesity requires measuring adiposity, meaning body fat. BMI alone cannot prove that a high value reflects excess fat rather than muscle.

In clinic, BMI should be confirmed as excess fat and paired with a fat distribution measure, the authors advise. Waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio are the standard options, and the ratio is favoured. Digital body scanning and bioelectric impedance, which passes a small current through the body, can estimate fat distribution feasibly. Diagnosis should also weigh weight-related complications and their severity. The review asks what path forward best serves patients.
europmc-pmc1166571:
Licastro and colleagues argue that lifelong low-grade swelling is a key driver of age-related disease in this 2005 review. Swelling, called inflammation, is the immune system's answer to invasion by viruses or bacteria. It is not harmful in itself. Human immunity evolved to run for 40 or 50 years, but it must now stay active far longer.

That long activity breeds a chronic state that slowly damages organs, the authors say. Alzheimer disease, atherosclerosis, diabetes, muscle wasting, and cancer all have an important inflammatory part. People with pro-inflammatory genotypes, gene variants that fan swelling, age less successfully. Keeping swelling in check tracks with longer life. The review frames innate immunity, the body's first-line defence, as the key to understanding these diseases.
europmc-pmc11961771:
Cai and colleagues reviewed light-based cancer treatment in 2025. Light therapy harms tumors while sparing much healthy tissue. It can be aimed with great precision. Three main forms use light in distinct ways.

One form makes toxic oxygen species inside tumors. A second heats tumor tissue, and a third wakes immune attack. Weak output, poor targeting, and low oxygen still limit results. Deep tumors are hard for agents to reach. Cai surveys fixes now in study, from better agents to smart carriers. It appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy.
europmc-pmc1475771:
Fast DNA tests usually need costly machines that heat and cool samples. Piepenburg and co-authors presented a simpler method in 2006, called recombinase polymerase amplification. It uses proteins that guide DNA copying at one steady, low warmth. No pre-treatment of the sample is needed.

The method proved keen and exact in tests. It found fewer than ten copies of DNA from MRSA, a drug-proof staph germ. A simple strip test could read the result with no instruments. Piepenburg argues the mix of speed, ease, and low gear needs could bring DNA testing to clinics and field sites that lack full labs.
europmc-pmc1599771:
Fruit fly DNA carries the marks of migration and lucky mutations. Li and Stephan read those marks in 2006, using variation at over 250 gene spots on the X chromosome. They compared flies from Africa, the ancestral home, and Europe.

Their model dates an African population expansion to about 60,000 years ago. The European line split off about 15,800 years ago and shrank hard on the way. Since the expansion, about 160 helpful mutations were fixed in Africa. About 60 more were fixed in Europe, with stronger effects. Li's method infers past numbers and recent selection at once.
europmc-pmc1783671:
Kornmann and colleagues engineered mice in 2007 to ask what really drives daily gene rhythms in the liver. Mammals keep a master clock in the brain and similar small clocks in most body cells. Liver gene rhythms could come from its own clock or from daily signals sent by the whole body.

The team built mice whose liver clock could be switched off with the drug doxycycline, by blocking the core clock gene Bmal1. Genome-wide measures showed most rhythmic liver genes stopped cycling when the local clock was halted. Yet 31 genes kept their rhythm, including the core clock gene mPer2. In liver tissue grown in a dish, mPer2 cycled only when the local clock worked. So body-wide signals can drive some genes, while most need the local clock.
europmc-pmc1784071:
Horii, Zhang and co-authors designed in 2007 tiny fiber scaffolds to help bone-forming cells grow. The scaffolds self-assemble from short peptides, the small chains that also build proteins. Such materials can fill tissue defects and give cells a three-dimensional home that mimics real tissue.

The team attached short active signals to a base peptide called RADA16-I. The signals came from proteins that guide bone growth and cell sticking, including an osteopontin motif and an RGD binding sequence. Mouse pre-bone cells grown on the designer scaffolds multiplied faster than on the plain scaffold. Two markers of bone maturation, alkaline phosphatase activity and osteocalcin output, also rose sharply. One design, named PRG, drew cells deep into the scaffold, a promising sign for bone repair.
europmc-pmc1892571:
Xu, Gordon and co-authors sequenced in 2007 two bacteria that live in the human gut, to watch evolution at work in that habitat. The adult intestine holds trillions of bacteria from hundreds of species, dominated by the Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes groups. Which pressures shape their genomes was largely unknown.

The new genomes came from Bacteroides vulgatus and Bacteroides distasonis, both normal residents of the lower gut. Comparing them with gut and non-gut relatives showed three forces at work: genes gained sideways from other microbes, mobile DNA elements, and gene copying. Those forces let the bacteria vary their surface coat, sense what surrounds them, and harvest the nutrients that reach the far gut. The authors frame human evolution itself as partly a story of our microbes.
europmc-pmc1914371:
Shalgi, Pilpel and co-authors mapped in 2007 the joint control network of microRNAs and transcription factors in mammals. Transcription factors switch genes on at the DNA level, while microRNAs tune protein output afterward. Together they were expected to govern thousands of genes, but the network's architecture was unexplored.

Using conserved binding sites, the team built two networks. The first linked microRNA pairs that share many targets, arranged in a hierarchy where a few microRNAs partner with many others. It exposed hundreds of target hub genes, each potentially controlled by dozens of microRNAs, and many hubs were themselves developmental regulators. The second network linked microRNA and factor pairs that co-control large target sets. It was built from recurring motifs, often where the factor also controls the microRNA itself.
europmc-pmc2000971:
Gutenkunst and colleagues argued in 2007 that biological computer models are almost always sloppy in their parameters. Such models use many free values that are hard to measure in living cells. Fitting them together often leaves single values very uncertain. Yet predictions can still be firm. Earlier work on growth factor signalling showed exactly that pattern.

The team examined a set of published systems biology models. Every model showed a sloppy sensitivity spectrum, spread over many orders of magnitude. Even ideal time-series data would often leave many parameters poorly fixed. Direct measurement would need extreme precision to do better. The authors advise modellers to focus on predictions rather than exact parameter values.
europmc-pmc2124971: A medical paper on the nature of the bactericidal substance in leucocytic extract. The white cells' weapon. This article preserves that immunology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2125271: A medical paper on the distribution of immune bodies in antipneumococcus serum. The antibodies, mapped. This article preserves that immunology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2125371: Rabbits with swollen joints helped explain human arthritis in this experimental study. The researchers traced the disease's origins in the animals. The joint inflammation's roots, investigated. The article preserves that rheumatology research. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2125471: A medical paper on the prophylaxis of Weil's disease, spirochaetosis icterohaemorrhagica. The leptospirosis prevention. This article preserves that research. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2128471: A medical paper on growth-inhibitory substances in pneumococcus cultures. The germ's own poison. This article preserves that bacteriology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2131471: A medical paper on reciprocal effects of concomitant infections, the influence of vaccinia. The double infection. This article preserves that virology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2131571: A medical paper on the relation of the bacteriostatic action of certain dyes to oxidation-reduction. The dyed halt. This article preserves that bacteriology. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it.
europmc-pmc2140371: A biology paper on influence of the concentration of electrolytes on physical properties. The salty physics. This article preserves that biophysics. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2394471:
Koukourakis and colleagues, with the Tumour and Angiogenesis Research Group, studied a sugar-burning enzyme in lung cancer in 2003. The enzyme, LDH-5, converts pyruvate to lactate, the hallmark step of oxygen-free energy production in cells. Tumors low on oxygen switch it on through the HIF system, the cell's oxygen alarm.

They built a staining test for LDH-5 and applied it to non-small-cell lung cancers, the common form. High LDH-5 tracked closely with the alarm proteins HIF1 alpha and HIF2 alpha in the same tumors. Patients whose tumors carried high LDH-5 had a poor prognosis. Tumors high in both LDH-5 and a HIF protein behaved especially aggressively. Blood LDH levels, though related, did not reliably mirror the tumor's own level. The authors said the stain gives easy prognostic information from stored tumor samples.
europmc-pmc2409471:
Ross and colleagues asked whether weight loss worsens chemotherapy results in lung cancers in 2004. They used records collected from 1994 to 2001 for three diseases treated with chemotherapy: small-cell lung cancer, advanced non-small-cell lung cancer, and mesothelioma, a cancer of the lung lining. The groups held 290, 418, and 72 patients.

Weight loss was common: 59% of small-cell patients, 58% of non-small-cell patients, and 76% of mesothelioma patients reported it. Those patients more often failed to finish three treatment cycles and had fewer symptom improvements. In non-small-cell cancer they also suffered more anaemia, a drop in red blood cells. After adjustment, weight loss independently predicted shorter survival in all three diseases. The risk of death ran 1.5 times higher in small-cell cancer and 1.92 times higher in mesothelioma for weight-losing patients.
europmc-pmc2507771:
Matus, Aquea, and Arce-Johnson catalogued a family of gene switches in grapevine in this 2008 genome study. The switches are MYB transcription factors, proteins that turn other genes on or off. In plants they steer traits from flower colour to drought tolerance, and several were suspected of shaping wine quality.

The team found and classified 108 members of the grape R2R3 MYB subfamily, comparing their structure with matching genes in Arabidopsis, a model plant. Grape had extra copies in groups tied to skin cell fate and to anthocyanins, the pigments behind red grape colour. One cluster on chromosome 2 held the known grape colour locus. Eight candidate genes matched tannin-related genes, which affect the bitter bite of wine.
europmc-pmc2602971:
Leimu and Fischer meta-analysed reciprocal transplant experiments in 2008 to test how general local adaptation is in plants. Local adaptation means home populations outperform foreign ones in their own habitat, and it matters for evolution and conservation. The team pooled published experiments, comparing local against foreign plants at each site and checking strict cases where each population won at home.

Local plants did perform significantly better at their home sites, winning in 71.0 percent of sites studied. But the strict pattern held in only 45.3 percent of the 1,032 population pairs. Population size was decisive: adaptation was common in populations above 1,000 flowering plants and very rare below that size. Life history, habitat variation, and geographic scale made no difference. The authors warn small populations may struggle to adapt to changing environments.
europmc-pmc2694971:
Stankiewicz and a large team hunted in 2009 the cause of a rare, fatal lung disorder of newborns, alveolar capillary dysplasia. Affected babies' lung air sacs lack proper capillaries, and the lung veins sit in the wrong place; most also have other birth defects. Scanning patients' genomes with fine arrays, the team found six overlapping deletions on chromosome 16, all covering a cluster of FOX genes.

Inside the cluster sat FOXF1, and four unrelated patients carried disabling mutations in that single gene. Two more deletions sat upstream of the gene, close enough to disturb its control switches. The deletions often broke inside repeated DNA elements with matching short stretches, betraying a copy-error mechanism of formation. Which neighbor genes were lost changed the pattern of extra defects: heart defects and gut blockages tracked with wider deletions, bowel rotation problems with point mutations.
europmc-pmc2722371:
Shio and co-authors identified in 2009 how hemozoin switches on the NLRP3 inflammasome. Hemozoin is the crystal malaria parasites make when digesting blood. The inflammasome is an immune alarm that matures the fever signal interleukin-1 beta. The crystal is dumped into blood when infected red cells burst, and phagocytes, eater cells, swallow it at once. The sensing path behind its strong inflammatory effect was unknown.

In knockout mice lacking alarm parts, crystal-driven interleukin release and swelling collapsed, which proves the alarm is required. Two tyrosine kinases, enzymes named Lyn and Syk, proved critical for switching the alarm on. Mice lacking the alarm or the fever signal survived a mouse malaria infection better, which ties the pathway to disease harm.
europmc-pmc2732471:
Bronzwaer and co-authors, for the European Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance System, tested in 2002 whether drug use across Europe tracks with drug resistance in one germ. The germ is Streptococcus pneumoniae, a major cause of pneumonia and meningitis. It was chosen as an indicator, since its penicillin resistance was rising in many lands. Data came from a Europe-wide system set up in 1998.

They compared resistance in invasive isolates from 1998 and 1999 with outpatient drug sales from 1997. Resistance correlated with sales of beta-lactam drugs and of macrolides across countries. Lands with higher sales tended to hold more resistant strains. The result supports restraint in drug use as a lever against resistance.
europmc-pmc2736171:
Kotla and co-authors reviewed in 2009 how lenalidomide, a drug derived from thalidomide, acts against blood cancers and related disorders. Chemical changes to thalidomide raised its potency and removed its sedative and nerve side effects. The drug is approved in the United States for myelodysplastic syndromes with a specific chromosome loss and for multiple myeloma, a bone marrow cancer.

Lenalidomide reshapes both cellular and humoral immunity, the antibody arm, and also blocks new blood vessel growth that feeds tumors. Newer work shows effects on cell signal pathways that may explain its selective strength in certain myelodysplastic subtypes. Its exact molecular targets were still not well known, and its wide activity hints at several sites of action.
europmc-pmc2747671:
Boks and co-authors studied in 2009 how DNA methylation, a chemical tag on DNA, relates to age, sex, and genotype in twins and healthy controls. Methylation helps control gene activity and may mediate genetic and environmental effects on traits and disease. They used a commercial array on blood DNA from forty-six twin pairs and ninety-six controls to test many tag sites at once.

Most sites showed no meaningful differences, partly due to tissue and site choice. Still, replicable links of methylation with age and with sex emerged at specific sites. Some genetic variants strongly shifted methylation nearby, a cis effect, and weakly shifted distant sites, a trans effect. The results show array studies of methylation are feasible and that individual sites behave very differently.
europmc-pmc2799471:
Braun and co-authors asked in 2009 whether contact with bisphenol A before birth shapes how toddlers behave. Rodent work had hinted that early BPA exposure raises aggression and blurs sex-linked behavior gaps. The team followed two hundred forty-nine mothers and children in Cincinnati, Ohio, measuring BPA in urine three times during pregnancy.

At age two, children took a standard behavior rating that scores acting-out and inward-turning problems. Higher prenatal BPA tracked with higher acting-out scores, and the link held only in girls. Samples from around week sixteen of pregnancy tied most strongly to later scores. The authors read the pattern as a suggestion, not proof, that early BPA exposure matters.
europmc-pmc2854771:
Samberg, Oldenburg, and Monteiro-Riviere tested silver nanoparticles for skin safety in 2010, as the germ-killing particles spread through creams, clothing, and baby products. They compared eight particle types, differing in size, washing, and carbon coating, on human skin cells in dishes and on pig skin dosed daily for two weeks.

Only the unwashed particles harmed: they cut cell survival in a dose-dependent way and provoked four inflammatory signals. Washed or carbon-coated particles caused no significant cell loss at any dose tested. On living skin there was no visible irritation, though microscopes found mild focal inflammation and particles resting in the outer skin layers. The authors conclude the danger lies in leftover coating chemicals, not the silver itself.
europmc-pmc2858671:
Brains and computer chips face the same packing problem, and Bassett and co-authors tested in 2010 whether both solve it the same way. Both are networks that must fit complex wiring into real physical space. Chip designers know a scaling law called Rent's rule, which links the number of parts to the number of links between them.

Applying that law to brain scans, Bassett found that human brain networks follow Rent's rule, as does the nerve network of a tiny worm. Both networks are also built in layers of modules, like chips. Their wiring favors low cost but does not cut cost to the bone, trading some extra wire for richer links. The brain measure also explained how gray and white matter scale across many mammal species.
europmc-pmc2864571:
Weinberg and co-authors reported in 2010 a haul of one hundred four candidate structured RNAs found by comparing genomes across microbes. Structured RNAs are RNA strands that fold into shapes and do jobs without becoming proteins, such as sensing chemicals or controlling genes. The team searched bacteria, archaea, and mixed environmental samples for DNA stretches whose changes preserve a folded shape.

Many candidates turned out to be riboswitches, RNA sensors that bind small molecules and switch genes, including types never seen before. Others sit near genes for secretion, motility, and stress defense, which hints at their roles. Each candidate is a concrete lead for lab testing, and the list widened the known RNA world well beyond proteins and the classic RNA machines.
europmc-pmc2866471:
El Hadrami, Adam, El Hadrami, and Daayf reviewed in 2010 how chitosan, a compound made from crustacean shells and fungal walls, can protect crops. Chitin and its derivative chitosan slow fungi directly and show activity against bacteria, viruses, and other pests. Plant tissues also read fragments of these compounds as alarm signals from invading microbes.

Once alarmed, plants build chemical weapons called phytoalexins, make defense proteins, and lay down lignin and callose to wall off attack sites. The compounds can also lock up minerals so germs cannot feed on them. The review gathers field and lab uses, from seed coatings to sprays. It explains each mode of action during plant and pathogen encounters. The case backs chitosan as a softer alternative to harsh farm chemicals.
europmc-pmc2967471:
Zaehle, Rach, and Herrmann delivered weak alternating currents to the scalps of healthy volunteers in a 2010 experiment, aiming to boost each person's natural alpha brain rhythm. Similar direct current methods were established, but proof that alternating current truly engages rhythms was missing.

Current tuned to each volunteer's own alpha rate, applied over the back of the head, raised alpha power in the recorded brain signals, while sham stimulation did not. A computer network of spiking cells showed how lingering changes at synapses could extend such effects past the stimulation period. The result gives direct evidence for rhythm entrainment.
europmc-pmc3039971:
Pacwa-Płociniczak and coauthors reviewed in 2011 how microbe made soaps can clean polluted soil and water. These natural detergents, called biosurfactants, are released by bacteria and fungi and can loosen oily and metal pollutants from surfaces. Growing public concern over pollution has pushed interest in gentler cleanup methods than digging, burning, or harsh chemicals.

Different microbe soaps suit different jobs, which makes the group attractive for many cleanup tasks. The review gathers recent progress on using them, and the microbes that make them, against hydrocarbon spills and heavy metal contamination. Lab and field results show they can raise how much pollutant microbes can reach and break down. The authors present them as a practical, lower harm option for industry and land recovery.
europmc-pmc3043071:
Dhejne and colleagues followed in 2011 every person in Sweden who had surgical sex reassignment between 1973 and 2003, tracking long term health outcomes. The study covered more than three hundred people, each matched with ten general population controls of the same birth year. Records were checked for deaths, suicide attempts, hospital care for mental illness, and criminal convictions.

After reassignment, the group still faced higher risks than controls on most measures. Death rates were higher, driven largely by suicide, and suicide attempts and inpatient psychiatric care were also more common. Results looked similar whether controls were matched by birth sex or by reassigned sex. One subgroup showed higher conviction rates than its birth sex controls. The authors stress that surgery eases gender distress but is not enough on its own, and they call for stronger medical and psychiatric care afterward.
europmc-pmc3061871:
Ringnér, Fredlund, Häkkinen, Borg, and Staaf launched in 2011 a free online tool for probing gene activity in breast cancer, called GOBO. Gene activity signatures promise better forecasts and treatment choices for patients, but breast cancer is so varied that signatures must be checked in large, well sorted sample sets. Their tool opens a dataset of well over eighteen hundred tumors plus a cell line panel to anyone with a browser.

Users can check how strongly any gene is active in tumor subgroups, find genes that rise and fall together, and test whether single genes or whole signatures track patient outcomes. Results come back as ready figures without any local data handling. The design makes it easy to add new datasets and new query types later. The authors aim to speed the validation step that promising signatures usually fail.
europmc-pmc3163271:
Maria Feoktistova and colleagues described a cell-death platform that forms when guardian proteins go missing in a 2011 paper in Molecular Cell. A family of inhibitor proteins quietly restrains death pathways inside cells, but how was enigmatic. Removing them, the team found, lets a huge protein complex assemble on its own in the cell interior.

The complex gathers a core sensor protein, adaptor and executioner enzymes, and two forms of a regulator protein with opposite effects. The long form blocks assembly; the short form promotes it. Once built, the platform can trigger either tidy self-destruction or a bursting death route, depending on enzyme activity levels. The authors name it the ripoptosome and argue it shapes how receptor signals end during inflammation.
europmc-pmc3236671:
Richard Gildea and colleagues presented iotbx.cif, a software toolbox for working with crystallographic data files, in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Applied Crystallography. The CIF format is the standard way to deposit and archive small-molecule crystal structures, and it also underpins the chemical dictionaries that macromolecular crystallography relies on. Programs that read and write the format correctly need solid foundations.

The toolbox gives developers a comprehensive set of tools for building applications that use CIF, handling its syntax and its official dictionaries. The authors place it in context: the format grew from small-molecule work into a backbone for resources such as the Protein Data Bank's chemical component dictionary and standard monomer libraries. Their aim is to make reliable CIF support easy to add to crystallographic software.
europmc-pmc3281871:
Erich Studerus and colleagues pooled two dozen controlled experiments to predict who responds to the psychedelic psilocybin in which way, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Response to hallucinogens is famously shaped by mindset and setting as well as dose, but the relative weight of those factors was unmeasured. The pooled data covered hundreds of administrations to healthy volunteers and twenty-four candidate predictors.

Dose was the strongest predictor of every response measured, but personal and situational factors mattered significantly. Volunteers high in the absorption trait, emotionally aroused and active before dosing, and untroubled in recent weeks were likeliest to have pleasant, mystical-type experiences. Emotional excitability, younger age, and a brain-scanning setting predicted unpleasant or anxious reactions. The analysis confirms, with numbers, the field's folk wisdom about set and setting.
europmc-pmc3308971:
Noto, Goto, Tsujimoto, and Noda combined studies on whether the diabetes drug metformin also lowers cancer risk, reporting in 2012. Metformin is the standard first drug for type 2 diabetes, and lab work hints it may slow tumor growth by calming high insulin levels. Earlier summaries rested on few studies, so the team searched five major databases for newer evidence.

Across the studies, diabetic patients taking metformin had clearly lower rates of dying from cancer and of developing cancer at all. Lower risks appeared for cancers of the colon, liver, and lung as well. The authors caution that most evidence came from studies that observe rather than assign treatment, so long trials that randomly assign the drug are still needed to prove the benefit.
europmc-pmc3365071:
Alvar and the World Health Organization leishmaniasis team produced updated global estimates for a neglected parasitic disease spread by sandflies. National experts supplied case data and treatment information, and the group reviewed the literature for 98 countries and three territories to correct for the heavy underreporting typical of this disease.

They estimated a few hundred thousand visceral cases and around a million cutaneous cases each year. Over ninety percent of visceral disease falls in just six countries: India and Bangladesh in Asia, Sudan, South Sudan, and Ethiopia in Africa, and Brazil. Deaths were tentatively put at twenty to forty thousand annually. The authors intend the figures to guide control strategies and advocacy.
europmc-pmc3394171:
Antonopoulos and colleagues reviewed in 2012 whether cholesterol drugs called statins also fight artery inflammation, not just lipids. In lab and animal work, statins calm inflamed vessel walls, improve nitric oxide supply, and ease oxidative strain. The review traces the molecular routes behind those effects.

Large trials support statins for preventing coronary disease, helped by this anti-inflammatory action. One landmark trial found benefit in people without heart disease whose inflammation ran high. Yet later trials in heart failure and kidney disease found no clinical gain, and the review weighs that letdown openly. It also discusses statin withdrawal, leaving a balanced picture of promise and limits.
europmc-pmc3408371:
Walpole and colleagues weighed humanity in 2012, estimating the total biomass of the world's adults. Ecologists tally species by mass, but for humans the headcount gets all the attention, even as average bodies grow heavier. The team combined height and body mass data country by country to get the total.

Adult humanity in 2005 came to roughly two hundred eighty-seven million tonnes. About fifteen million tonnes of that was excess flesh from overweight, and a smaller slice from obesity. North America held a third of the world's obesity biomass with only a small share of its people, while Asia showed the reverse. If every country matched American body shapes, they note, Earth would carry the food demands of far more people.
europmc-pmc3410871:
Marsh and a large team isolated a brand-new virus from Australian fruit bats in 2012 and named it Cedar virus. It belongs to the henipavirus genus, whose two known members, Hendra and Nipah, kill people and livestock at grim rates. Bats of the pteropid family carry those viruses naturally.

Cedar virus matches its cousins in genome size and layout, cross-reacts with their proteins, and enters cells through the same doorway molecule. Yet in ferrets and guinea pigs it copied itself and raised antibodies without causing illness. The telling difference sits in one gene that its cousins use to dodge immune alarms: Cedar lacks the usual tricks there. Human cells indeed raised a stronger interferon alarm against it.
europmc-pmc3462671:
Grimshaw and co-authors wrote a 2012 review in Implementation Science on knowledge translation, the work of getting research findings used in real care and policy. They note that proven treatments often never reach patients, which wastes money and leaves people exposed to avoidable harm. Their paper sums up the main ideas and evidence meant to guide that transfer work.

The review is built around five plain questions about what should be shared, with whom, by whom, and how. Grimshaw's group says sound summaries of research should be the usual unit shared. They also urge planners to weigh likely blocks and aids before picking a strategy. Evidence is stronger for work aimed at clinicians and patients than for work aimed at policy makers.
europmc-pmc3484671:
Endelman and Jannink tackled a scaling problem in predicting breeding values from DNA markers, in G3 in 2012. Breeders estimate how related animals or plants are by comparing their marker patterns, but the resulting matrix needs a proper scale to match pedigree tradition. The authors derived a scaling tied to the current group's own inbreeding level, estimated from the markers themselves.

They then asked whether a shrinkage method, which pulls noisy estimates toward safer values, sharpens predictions when few markers are used. Simulations said yes for tested lines with known performance, and no for untested lines. Tests in a commercial pig herd confirmed the gain at middle accuracy levels. Endelman's method can raise genetic gain when cheap, sparse marker sets are all a breeder has.

frus-1861-d171:
From Washington on 20 July 1861, William H. Seward sent orders to Carl Schurz in Madrid. The letter is document 171 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote to Madrid on the eve of Bull Run, in the last hours of the short war mood. His orders to Schurz share the bold tone of that week. The letter stands in the file just before defeat abroad and at home reshaped every plan. News of Bull Run would reach Madrid within days and test Schurz's fresh standing. Fresh standing at a proud court is a frail thing after news of defeat.
frus-1861-d271:
Word from Mr. Brown reached Washington on 11 June 1861, in a letter to William H. Seward. It stands as Document 271 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the opening months of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d71:
A third letter of 17 August 1861 went from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams in London. It is document 71 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Three letters in a day show a Secretary clearing a full desk in one sweep. Some points were small, but small points in London could grow teeth. The run of August letters shows how much of high policy was made of plain, dated paper. The three letters, read as one, give a full map of the London agenda that week. A full map of one week's work shows how wide the London front had grown.
frus-1862-d171:
Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed Charles Francis Adams in London on 27 October 1862, and the letter stands as Document 171 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It came near the end of a busy month of Atlantic mail.

Late October brought word that France wanted Britain and Russia to join it in urging a truce on the warring Americans. Washington opposed any such step, which would treat the South as a power in its own right. Seward's letters of this period, this one among them, kept his London envoy ready for the talks ahead. Cotton hunger in British mill towns kept the war a kitchen-table topic across the North of England.
frus-1862-d271:
Dated 28 April 1862, Document 271 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume among the French papers.

By the time this letter reached Paris, New Orleans was in Union hands and the fact was known in Europe. Seward's mail in the following weeks pressed the lesson that the South was shrinking. Dayton used such letters in his calls at the foreign ministry, where France's leaders still kept their options open on the war. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d371:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward answered Viscount Treilhard on 9 August 1862, a day after Treilhard's first letter in this file. The reply is Document 371 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

A next-day answer marks a channel working in the same city at walking pace, unlike the slow Atlantic mails. Treilhard's letters and Seward's replies alternate through the late summer of 1862. Together they show two offices in Washington dealing promptly, in writing, while the war's outcome hung in doubt after a season of Union defeats. Formal calls between the two men were frequent, and their notes followed up the talks.
frus-1862-d471:
On 20 October 1862 George Perkins Marsh reported from Turin to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 471 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed record.

Marsh wrote a month after Antietam, as the emancipation order's meaning sank in across Europe. In Italy, where the war was read through the lens of national unity, the news strengthened the Union's moral standing. His October report measured that shift for Washington. Marsh's Turin letters, calm and observant, give the reader a southern-European vantage on the war. That vantage lies far from the London and Paris exchanges. Those exchanges dominate most accounts of Civil War diplomacy.
frus-1862-d571:
Henry Shelton Sanford received the year's closing Belgian order from Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 19 November 1862. It is Document 571 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

November 1862 brought France's mediation proposal and the Union's flat refusal, which Seward communicated to every post. Sanford in Brussels, with his court's lines into London, was a useful place to have the refusal understood. The instruction ends a year of unusually brisk dealing between Washington and its Belgian legation. Judged by the file's density, the small post had earned its keep. Information came in and instructions went out. A friendly court stayed friendly through the war's hardest year so far.
frus-1862-d671:
Writing on 23 January 1862, Anson Burlingame sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Burlingame was the American minister to China, in the first year of his mission. The dispatch appears as document 671 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Burlingame wrote as a man who liked China and meant to deal fairly with its court, a stance that later made him famous. His early letters set out what he saw and what he thought the United States should do. This dispatch belongs to that first season, when the new envoy was still learning the ground and telling Washington what he found.
frus-1862-d71:
On 26 May 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 71 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d171:
On 24 April 1863, William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 171 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second of Seward's sheets held its own head of the brief, as the file's pairs always did. With Adams's three letters of the same date, the day's pile in the volume runs to five. This letter is Washington's last word in that pile. It closes the peak day of late April, a small monument to how much of the war was waged in ink.
frus-1863p1-d271:
Frederick W. Seward, the Assistant Secretary of State and the Secretary's son, wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 22 August 1863. His letter is document 271 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

When the Secretary was away or overloaded, his son and deputy signed the department's letters. The London instructions therefore sometimes ran under the younger Seward's hand, though the policy stayed the Secretary's. The chief aim was unchanged: keep Britain from treating the Confederacy as a nation. Orders crossed by steamship, and Adams had to act on them in talks with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary.
frus-1863p1-d371:
Britain's side of the Washington exchange speaks in this note, sent by Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 January 1863. It is document 371 of the 1863 papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Under the formal courtesy sits real tension: a neutral Britain trading with both sides, and a Union government sure that trade kept the South alive. This exchange is where the two views met. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d471:
On 22 April 1863 a formal note passed from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d571:
Under the date 17 June 1863, the record holds a letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d671:
Document 671, dated 20 November 1863, records a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late autumn of 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

Each crossing of the Atlantic took the better part of two weeks, so these letters also show leaders acting on news that was already old. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d71:
This second letter of 3 February 1863 went from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 71 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, paired with the letter printed just before it.

Short, split letters were Seward's way of keeping a brief in order. Adams could act on each sheet as its matter came up in his talks with Lord Russell. This one is the second half of the day's work from Washington. It belongs to the steady stream by which the Union held its ground in Britain through the war's hardest winter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d171: Secretary Hull wrote on October 28, 1943 to both the President and Acting Secretary Stettinius, as he had five days before. The letter is Document 171 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The double address again joined the White House and the department in one reading, in the conference's final days. The record names the three men and the date. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d271: An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers a Cairo dinner party of November 1943 at which President Roosevelt was host. Accounts of the evening appear in the President's Log and in the published works of Elliott Roosevelt, Sherwood, Churchill, and Admiral Leahy. Leahy's guest list differs slightly from the others. It names Lord Leathers where another account names Lord Moran. The editors find no sign that weighty problems were discussed at the dinner, and the note serves to place the event in the conference record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d371:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record a luncheon at Tehran on 30 November 1943, at half past one, where the three leaders took up Turkey and the Straits. Before the meal, Roosevelt read Stalin the Anglo-American staff recommendations, which he and Churchill had approved.

Stalin voiced great satisfaction and promised simultaneous Red Army offensives to match. On Turkey, the leaders agree on the invitation to President Inönü to meet them in Cairo. Churchill says he will offer the Turks only twenty squadrons of aircraft and some anti-aircraft regiments. He will offer no land forces. Hopkins warns that no Rhodes landing may be hinted at. The American side holds there are no landing craft for it. Talk then turns to Russia's wish for warm-water ports and an easier regime at the Dardanelles, which Churchill does not oppose in principle.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d471:
Britain's chiefs of staff answered in writing on December 3, 1943, with a memorandum of their own, printed in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume beside the American paper of the same date. The British chiefs had come to Cairo by way of Tehran, where the three leaders had met for the first time.

A written position let the British commanders state their case fully before the Combined Chiefs of Staff argued it out. The memorandum therefore captures London's military thinking at a hinge point of the war. Read against the American memorandum, it shows two allies who agreed on the enemy but still differed on where and how to strike him.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d571:
Joseph C. Grew, the Acting Secretary of State, wrote to the President on January 19, 1945. Grew, a career diplomat and former ambassador to Japan, was minding the department while Secretary Stettinius traveled. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

January 1945 found Roosevelt about to leave for the Yalta Conference, and the department's business ran through Grew's steady hand. An acting secretary's letter to the President marks the flow of decisions continuing while principals traveled. For readers, the message shows the government at a changing of the guard: Hull gone, Stettinius new, and the next great summit only weeks away.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d71: A second Roosevelt letter to Churchill is dated October 29, 1943, and it is Document 71 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Paired same-day letters from the president match the paired Churchill notes in the same run of papers, a measure of the season's pace. The catalog record names no subject for either. The printed text in the Foreign Relations series is the only guide to what each one carried.
frus-1944-quebec-d171: An editors' note in the Quebec volume records a meeting for which the only source is the President's Log. Churchill joined Roosevelt in the president's map room at the Citadel for a review of the latest war news. The discussion also covered naval problems in the Pacific and the difficulties of supply there. No fuller record of the conversation was found.
frus-1944-quebec-d271:
The Netherlands government sent this statement to Roosevelt through Schoenfeld on September 13, 1944, having no direct code link to Quebec. Foreign Minister van Kleffens asked that it be laid before the conference, since Pacific strategy was on the agenda. The Dutch argued that cutting Japan's communications with her occupied southern area would not by itself compel surrender there.

Japanese forces in Burma, Malaya, the Philippines, and the Indies had food and stocks enough to stay on, the statement warns, and might fight irregularly even after Japan's defeat. Delayed liberation would multiply suffering and doom prisoners and internees. The Dutch urged active liberation aimed first at the most valuable territory: Java, with its food, labor, roads, harbors, and airfields.
frus-1944-quebec-d71:
Under Secretary of State Edward R. Stettinius recorded this second memorandum on September 14, 1944, during the Quebec Conference. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, beside his opening-day paper.

Two Stettinius memoranda in three days show the department following the conference closely from Washington, where news of the Morgenthau Plan's acceptance caused immediate unease. The State Department had its own plans for Germany and for the peace organization. For readers, this paper records the home front of American diplomacy reacting, in real time, to a summit it had not attended.
frus-1945-50-intel-d171:
The title "Central Intelligence Group Directive No. 15" heads a text dated 1 October 1946. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 171 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

A directive is not advice: it is an order that offices below must follow until it is changed or replaced. For a reader, the gain is precision: this is the rule as the ruled were told to obey it. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d271:
Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter addressed a memorandum to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 5 May 1948. It stands as document 271 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d371:
"Central Intelligence Agency Memorandum of Comments on the Dulles Report" bears the date 28 February 1949. It survives in print as document 371 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Three men — Dulles, Jackson, and Correa — were touring the CIA's work for the Council and taking notes for a report.

Reports were the heavy guns of paper work: slower than a memo, but built to end an argument. Senior men read the findings first and the detail as needed. The subject is spelled out in the title. The text gives the CIA's own comments on the Dulles Report, the outside survey of its first years.
frus-1945-50-intel-d71:
The presidential directive on the coordination of foreign intelligence activities, dated 22 January 1946, is the founding paper of the volume's second act. By it, Truman created the National Intelligence Authority and its working arm, the Central Intelligence Group. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The directive made a board of the secretaries of State, War, and Navy, joined by the president's chief of staff. It set a director of central intelligence to serve them. It was a compromise: central in name, departmental in control, and far smaller than Donovan's dream. Yet from this seed grew the system that followed. Readers should read the directive whole: its few pages set terms that the rest of the volume argues over, clause by clause.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d171:
How much Soviet sway in Rumania would Washington accept? “Principal Rumanian Problems” calls that the fundamental question in this briefing book paper. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Under the armistice, the Allied Control Commission works under the general direction of the Soviet High Command. From Bucharest, prominent Rumanians have appealed straight to American officers for a sign of United States policy. The British fear that Soviet moves threaten Rumania's very life as a free state. The paper also charges that Soviet authorities settled some matters alone. Among them was the property of American-owned oil companies, though such questions belonged to all three governments together.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d271:
Green Hackworth, the State Department's legal adviser, sent the war crimes machinery forward on 22 January 1945. His covering note to the Secretary, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, presents two memoranda marked A and B. One has already been signed at the top of the government.

Memorandum A, signed by the Secretary, Secretary Stimson, and the Attorney General, states the problem and suggests a course. Memorandum B casts the same ideas as a draft ready for signature, the first step toward setting the machinery in motion. A copy went to Judge Rosenman. The plan rests on a short-lived international tribunal to try the principal culprits. Lesser offenders would face occupation courts and the national courts of the wronged countries.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d371:
First place in the queue for German reparations goes to those who bore the main burden of the war. So opens the Soviet proposal of February 7, 1945, laying down basic principles for exacting reparations from Germany. Other countries would receive payment only in the second place. The question of German labor as payment was set aside for later debate.

Payment in kind would come in two set forms. The first was removal, in a single payment at the war's end, from Germany's national wealth at home and abroad. Equipment, machine tools, ships, rolling stock, and German investments abroad are all named. The paper is the claim the West would argue over for years.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d471:
Twenty decisions and more are counted in this American list of what the three heads of government settled at Yalta, dated February 11, 1945. The first puts the word "dismemberment" into the German surrender terms. The second names a committee — Eden, Winant, and Gusev — to study dismemberment itself.

Next come the adoption of the American voting plan for the Security Council, and the United Nations conference set for April 25, 1945. America would consult China and France on both points, for all three powers. The list runs on to the permanent seats. As a checklist, it is the conference's balance sheet: what eight days in the Crimea had decided.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d71:
James Dunn, director of the Office of European Affairs, sent this preparation memorandum to Under Secretary Stettinius on 10 November 1944. It is titled “Preparation for Big Three Meeting” and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations. Dunn looks ahead to the argument over the Soviet veto.

On the world organization, Dunn warns that Moscow wants a veto covering peaceful settlement as well as enforcement action. If the Russians stay adamant on the wider claim, he advises postponing any United Nations meeting for the present. A veto limited to enforcement, he argues, the United States could accept, and the American people would receive it well.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d171:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff told General Deane in Moscow what they were ready to discuss with the Russians, in a telegram dated June 27, 1945. The message is document 171 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Military talks between the Americans and the Soviets were expected beside the main conference.

The chiefs will be ready, they say, to swap estimates of the Japanese situation and to discuss plans for the war against Japan, so the two sides can coordinate. They will gladly take up other proper subjects the Russians wish to raise. Deane is told to ask the Soviet General Staff to advise Washington soon which further subjects it wants on the table. The telegram set the terms for the first U.S.-Soviet staff talks of the Potsdam period.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d271:
Acting Secretary Grew forwarded a report on Vienna's mood in a letter dated July 9, 1945. The letter and its enclosure extracts form document 271 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The report came from Ambassador Murphy and rested on the questioning of a member of the Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra who had crossed into the American zone.

The informant described a violent reaction among Viennese against the Soviet troops. The Russians, he reported, were agitating with every propaganda agency at their disposal. An election was expected, probably not until fall, and the Russians were working toward election day night and day. Grew thought the Secretary would want the report before him, and perhaps laid before the President, as the delegation left for Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d371: Grew's cable to Pauley of July 8, 1945, is a holding answer, and it is printed in full. Instead of replying now to the questions raised in Pauley's message of July 5, the Secretary suggests a different course. These issues, he writes, should be discussed and decided when Pauley joins the President at Berlin. The brief note pushed the open reparations fights, France's share among them, up to the heads of government themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d471:
Field Marshal Alexander's rebuke of a British treaty draft is reported in an extract of Kirk's cable from Caserta of July 15, 1945. During his recent London visit, Churchill had asked Alexander to confer with Foreign Office officials on the proposed peace treaty with Italy. With Eden ill, Alexander talked with Sargent. After studying the draft carefully, he gave his verdict.

The draft, Alexander told the Foreign Office, was far too severe, and he could not concur in it. Tripoli, he believed, should now be returned to Italy definitely and without strings. Eritrea and Italian Somaliland should also go back, with certain conditions attached. He added that Italy should be given a small fleet, excellent for her morale.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d571:
The Acting Secretary of State, Joseph Grew, wired Belgrade charge Harold Shantz on June 25, 1945. The secret message is document 571 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It tells Shantz how to answer Tito's claim that civil rule in Venezia Giulia was still pending.

Grew calls that claim hard to grasp in light of article 3 of the Belgrade agreement. Shantz is to press this view on Yugoslav officials in his talks. He is also to keep one thought before them at all times. Good will in the United States for just Yugoslav claims, Grew warns, will rest largely on strict keeping of signed pledges.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d671:
Ambassador Armour in Madrid pushed back against inviting Moscow into the Tangier talks on July 9, 1945. His urgent confidential wire is document 671 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It answers Washington's wire of July 5, printed as document 667.

Armour agrees Moscow should not be given the sense that the western powers act alone. But he cannot see how an active Soviet role is justified while small statute powers are kept out. Those states, he argues, have an inescapable interest in any change at Tangier. They ran the zone's administration with others before Spain seized it. Their interest grows if great powers with little direct stake settle the zone's fate in their absence. Armour also reads Washington's wire to mean Russians would join the interim occupation itself, a step he questions.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d71:
President Truman answered Churchill's plan for a royal visit to Berlin in a telegram extract dated June 16, 1945. The extract is document 71 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had proposed that King George VI spend a day in Berlin during the conference, lunching with the Russians and dining with the other heads of state.

Truman's surviving lines are brief and warm. He says he will be very pleased to agree to any arrangements Churchill makes to carry out the King's wishes during the visit. The rest of the message is not printed. The reply left the plan in British hands and kept the King's role, a social rather than political one, on track for the conference weeks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1071:
Ambassador Lincoln MacVeagh sent this long despatch from Athens to the Secretary of State on July 17, 1945. It transmits a survey of conditions in northern Greece by Third Secretary Leonard Cromie. A second report, on the British Army in Greece, was written by Captain William McNeill, who toured Macedonia and western Thrace with Cromie in June.

Cromie's findings do not back claims of anarchy and wholesale terror in the north. The picture matches the rest of Greece, with sharper republican feeling in the cities. Prison figures do show weak courts and royalist officials who slight the civil rights of leftists. Some Slavophones have fled across the Yugoslav border. The reports credit British officers with working to restore order and fair treatment.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1171:
President Truman wrote straight to Generalissimo Stalin on 20 July 1945. A note between the two leaders was the summit's highest channel. No staff drafted the meaning, however clerks may have typed the words; the principals spoke for themselves.

Mid-conference, such a message could praise, press, warn, or smooth a rough point between sessions. Each word in it was weighed in both camps. This exchange is leader-level dealing in a single note. It shows the personal track that ran beside the formal talks, and on which some of Potsdam's hardest points were truly settled.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1271:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 22 July 1945. It is the third of their papers in this stretch of the volume. The British staff's run of notes kept London's team supplied with the soldiers' view through the summit's turn into its second week.

Staff papers of this kind weighed forces and fronts in plain terms. They told the envoys what the services could do, and what they could not. This memorandum does that work at its date. In sequence, the British notes show a staff machine matching the American one paper for paper, across the same crowded days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1371:
Admiral William Leahy, the president's chief of staff, set down a memorandum on 24 July 1945. Leahy stood closer to Truman day by day than almost any other officer in Washington or Potsdam. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Leahy's papers carry weight because he heard everything and said little in public. A memorandum from his hand records how a question looked from the president's own doorway. Readers tracing the summit's inner workings watch for Leahy entries the way they watch for the president's. Rarely long, often placed at turns in the story. This one belongs to the busy days just before the conference issued its call to Japan.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-71:
Churchill's own note stands in for a missing United States record in volume two of the Potsdam papers. No U.S. record of this conversation has been found, the editors say. The note by Churchill is reprinted from Ehrman's official history, Grand Strategy.

Churchill's note reports what Byrnes told him that morning, apparently July 23, 1945. Byrnes had cabled to T. V. Soong, the Chinese negotiator in Moscow. He advised Soong not to give way on any point to the Russians. Soong should instead return to Moscow and keep negotiating, pending further developments. Churchill drew a blunt conclusion from the news, and the note quotes it in full. It is quite clear, he wrote, that the United States does not at present desire Russian participation in the war against Japan. The editors cite the cable itself later in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d771:
Document 771 is a Soviet proposal tabled on July 30, 1945, two days before the close. Soviet endgame texts held the lines Moscow valued most. This one entered the numbered record of the second Potsdam volume. It stands beside American and British drafts of the same final days.

A late Soviet proposal lets readers test the final bargain. What the protocol granted and refused can be read off such texts. The document shows Moscow still pressing as the clock ran down. It also shows the discipline of the Soviet team: positions stated in writing, defended to the end. The paper is a key witness to the closing trades.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d871:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson sent this memorandum to the President on July 22, 1945, during the Potsdam Conference. He titles it the rehabilitation of Europe as a whole. Stimson writes that war has destroyed moral values across the continent, not just property and wealth.

Stimson urges that Germany be given a chance to live and work. Controls, he argues, should go only as far as basic aims require. He also asks for one coordinated plan for all of Europe. American aid, surplus goods, and bank credits should flow through a single agency. He proposes an Economic Council for Europe, chaired by an American, to guide the work.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d971:
Drafting committee members weighed this reparations text at Potsdam in late July 1945. The heading calls it agreed, with reserves noted. Soviet claims would come from the Soviet zone, and Poland's claims from the Soviet share. Western claims would come from the western zones and German external assets, both points reserved by the Soviet delegate.

The USSR would further receive 15 percent of surplus western equipment in trade, and 10 percent more free of charge. The amount must be set within six months, and removals finished within two years of that ruling. A closing line has the Soviet government renounce claims to western securities, external assets, and German gold.
frus-1977-80v11p1-d271: A 1977-1980 FRUS document from the Iran hostage crisis volume. The embassy seizure. This entry preserves that record. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
gao-gaoreports-b-310971: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Colson Services Corporation. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-271: The Joint Strike Fighter needed a safer buying plan in 2005, and GAO's report says a different acquisition strategy could reduce risks. The review rewrites the playbook. The trillion-dollar jet deserved the caution. The strategy had to change. The trillion-dollar jet deserved the caution.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-371: Agent Orange's civilian victims stayed uncounted in 2005, and GAO's report says the toll on non-soldiers was unknown. The review admits the data gap plainly. The hurt deserved the true count badly. The hurt deserved the true count badly. The count was missing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-471: Federal IPv6 transition needed planning in 2005, and GAO's report says agencies had to plan and manage security risks. The findings demand the roadmap. The report warns that the internet's next chapter deserved doing right. The planning had to be done.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-671: The IRS's output gauges needed sharpening in 2005, and GAO's report says fresh methods could tune the math. The findings demand the upgrade. The report warns that the tax agency's output deserved honest measuring. The tax agency's output deserved honest measuring.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-971: A Colombian oil line saw fewer bombings in 2005, and GAO's report says the guard effort cut the strikes, though woes stayed. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the pipeline deserved guarding. The pipeline deserved guarding. The guard effort had to hold.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-171: The Pentagon's asset deployment system had marginal value in 2006, and GAO's report says uncertain joint use and weak expected value warranted review. The findings question the investment. The report warns that the logistics software needed justifying. The value had to be proven.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-271: High-deductible federal health plans got a first-year review in 2006, and GAO's report examines the experience with the new options. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the workers' health gambles needed watching. The experience had to be studied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-471: Undeclared hazardous shipments got new DOT attention in 2006, and GAO's report says the new efforts might reveal more about the hidden cargo. The findings track the start. The report warns that the secret dangerous goods needed daylight. The efforts had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-571: Jumbo-jet airport upgrades cost a fortune in 2006, and GAO's report examines the costs and factors for accommodating the superjumbo. The findings do the math. The report warns that the giant planes needed giant gates. The costs had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-771: Immigration courts' caseload reporting needed work in 2006, and GAO's report says the performance reporting wanted improvement. The findings target the numbers. The report warns that the backlogged courts needed honest scorecards. The reporting had to improve. The courts' numbers had to be honest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1071: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report finding the Export-Import Bank needed to improve how it assessed the economic impact of its financing.
