The bank subsidizes American exports, but GAO questioned whether its impact analyses were rigorous. The report presses for better measurement of whether the bank's deals truly benefit the U.S. economy or mainly benefit the companies receiving them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-371: The bank insurance funds got an audit in 2007, and GAO's report grades the FDIC funds' financial statements for 2006 and 2005. The findings deliver the formal opinion. The report shows the deposit guardian's own books get checked. The insurer's vault got its own inspection.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-671: Moving military families was a logistical tangle in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pentagon needed one coherent plan for its new household-goods system. The findings target the moving-day mess. The report's demand: plan the move like the mission depends on it, because morale does.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-71: GAO's 2007 report revisits the poisoned town of Libby, Montana — and the far-flung sites that took its tainted ore. GAO says the EPA may need to re-grade those sites and must do better at warning the neighbors. The report keeps the heat on one of America's grimmest toxics sagas, where the cleanup's loose ends still threatened lives.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-871: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation: Some Steps Have Been Taken to Improve Contracting, but a More Strategic Approach is Needed. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
german-empire-constitution-1871:
The Constitution of the German Empire took effect in 1871, weeks after the empire was proclaimed at Versailles. Otto von Bismarck, Prussia's chancellor, drafted the charter to bind Germany's princes into one Reich without breaking their thrones. German unity had been won by war; the constitution gave that victory lasting legal form.

The text makes the king of Prussia German emperor by right, and gives the empire power over war, trade, railways, and law. A federal council of state governments faces a Reichstag elected by all adult men, though the chancellor answers to the emperor, not to parliament. Prussia's weight runs through the whole design. The empire's founding statute ruled Germany until the crash of 1918. Its mix of democracy below and authority above defined the Reich that Bismarck built.
goethe-faust-part-2-taylor-1871:
Bayard Taylor completed his metrical Faust with Part Two in 1871. The Osgood first edition gave English readers the first great rendering of the sequel. Goethe had finished the vast second part near the end of his life.

Faust moves through courts, classical myths, and grand schemes of land and sea. Helen of Troy appears, and strange spirits crowd the crowded stage action. The scope is huge, part pageant, part deep thought on man's striving. Faust dies old and blind, still reaching for one good shared work. Taylor's feat let English readers grasp the whole design at last.
govdocs-archive_org-SonsOfLibertyRobertJ:
In September 2005 the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives answered a Freedom of Information request from researcher Ernie Lazar. The release gathers disclosable portions of FBI-originated documents on Robert Jay Mathews and the Sons of Liberty.

Mathews founded The Order, a white-supremacist group whose crime spree ended with his death in 1984, and the files track official interest in him and his circle. Names and passages are withheld where the law allows, as FOIA releases usually are. The library presents the file as a public record, without endorsement, for researchers of the American far right.
govdocs-archive_org-lainedByTheLivSchoup:
Rev. F. X. Schouppe, a French Jesuit, wrote Purgatory Explained by the Lives and Legends of the Saints to teach Catholic doctrine on the afterlife through stories. This copy is the TAN Books pocketbook reprint of 1986, taken from the 1893 Benziger edition.

Schouppe builds his teaching from reported apparitions, visions, and legends of the saints, in which souls in purgatory ask the living for prayers. Each story is followed by the doctrine it illustrates: suffering, prayer, and the bond between the living and the dead. The book was a devotional classic, and the cheap reprint kept it in Catholic homes.
hartmann-erec-haupt-1871:
Hartmann von Aue wrote Erec, the first Arthurian romance in German, in the years around 1200. Moriz Haupt's 1871 edition prints the medieval German text in full, all 10,135 verses of it. The knight Erec stands at the center of the tale.

Erec wins a bride and high honor, then sinks into sloth and lets his name fall. Shamed by his wife's grief, he rides out with her to win his honor back through hard trials. The poem set the pattern for German courtly romance for two full centuries. Haupt's text is the classic school edition of the work.
hunter-natural-history-teeth-1771:
Teeth got their first scientific account in John Hunter's Natural History of the Human Teeth, from 1771. Hunter dissected jaws and teeth at every age of life. He describes how teeth form, grow, and sit in their sockets. Structure comes first, then the diseases that attack it.

Decay, gum trouble, and the ills of teething all receive ordered treatment. His plates show the parts with a clarity earlier books lacked. The work founded scientific dentistry as a field of study. Practitioners gained a base in anatomy rather than craft lore alone. The first edition keeps his terms and figures intact. Modern dentists can still read him with profit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lublinsky-solom:
Solomon Lublinsky, a German journalist and writer, was born at Johannisberg, Prussia, on February 18, 1868. He is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein. He worked for a time as a clerk in a second-hand bookstore at Venice. He then took up journalism at Berlin.

By 1904, the article says, Lublinsky stood among the foremost Jewish writers. Beyond his newspaper work, it lists his Berlin books: a study of Jewish characters in Grillparzer, Hebbel, and Ludwig, and a work on literature and society in the nineteenth century. It also lists the dramas “Multatuli,” “Der Imperator,” and “Hannibal.” A novel, “Gescheitert,” appeared in 1901. The entry is brief, but it fixes the shape of a young career split between journalism, criticism, and the stage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mezei-ernest-10:
Ernest Mezei, born at Satoralja-Ujhely in Hungary in May 1851, was a journalist and member of parliament profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Gabriel Weiss. He studied law and philosophy at Budapest and wrote for the Ellenör while still a student. In 1874 he helped found the opposition daily Egyetértés and stayed on its staff.

Backed by Louis Kossuth, Mezei lost a first run for parliament in 1878 but won the Miskolcz seat in 1881. When the Tisza-Eszlár blood accusation inflamed Hungary, he challenged the minister of justice in the House and spoke hard against the anti-Semites. He also wrote poems, an 1877 book of Italian travels, and a lecture opposing Zionism as a national program.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mirels-meshulla:
Meshullam Zalman ben David Neumark Mirels, born at Vienna about 1620, was a German rabbi whose life followed the expulsions of his age. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. When Vienna expelled its Jews in 1670, he emigrated to Berlin with his son Zeeb Wolf and the wider Mirels family.

In 1678 Mirels became chief rabbi of the triple community of Altona, Hamburg, and Wandsbeck, and held the post until his death in 1706. He lived to see a fifth generation of descendants spread through Poland and Lithuania. His daughter Sarah married Ẓebi Ashkenazi, the Ḥakam Ẓebi, and was mother of Jacob Emden; of his writing, one responsum survives in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monuments-in-th:
Monuments in their bearing on biblical exegesis argues a revolution in evidence, in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board published in 1906. For centuries the Old Testament's authenticity had to be argued from inside its own pages. Now the nations around Israel have risen from the dead with archives of their own.

Egypt and Babylonia, the article shows, had schools, libraries, and literature long before Abraham; under Hammurabi, Babylon was reediting its classics while Egypt read the Proverbs of Ptah-hotep. The monuments give the biblical books a contemporary literature to be tested against — as much external witness for Moses' age, the writers claim, as for Pericles' Athens. Archaeology here becomes a tool of exegesis.
joseph-of-arimathie-skeat-1871:
Joseph of Arimathie is an alliterative Middle English poem about Joseph of Arimathea and the Holy Grail. W. W. Skeat, a leading scholar of old English texts, edited it in 1871. The poem gives the Grail an English origin story.

In the Bible, Joseph buries Christ and then fades from the tale. Here he carries the holy blood across the sea to Britain. There he founds a new church in the west and becomes a missionary hero. The poem mixes prayer, travel, and marvel in driving verse. It shows how eager medieval England was to claim a sacred past of its own.
kenrick-lecture-perpetual-motion-1771: William Kenrick, an English writer and critic, gave this public talk on perpetual motion in 1771. Such talks drew crowds in the coffee house age of London. Kenrick spoke at the height of the craze for wheels that turn for ever. He took the famed claims of his day one by one and showed why each must fail. His case rests on the plain laws of weight, force, and loss in all machines. Short and sharp, the talk is a neat case of a debunk from the craze's own time.
legge-chinese-classics-vol-4-part-2-1871:
James Legge published Volume 4, Part 2 of The Chinese Classics in 1871, completing his She King, the Book of Poetry. Legge was a Scottish missionary and scholar in Hong Kong. The She King, or Classic of Poetry, is one of the five classics of China, a set of songs many ascribed to Confucius's editing.

Part 2 carries the odes onward, with Chinese text, translation, and long notes on words, customs, and history. The songs cover love, war, farming, and court life in early China. Legge's version was the first full English translation of the Classic of Poetry. His notes made the poems usable by readers with no Chinese, and they stayed standard for generations.
maine-village-communities-1871:
Henry Maine, the legal historian who wrote Ancient Law, gave six lectures on village communities that appeared in 1871. He compares villages in India, Russia, and England as the oldest unit of law and property. The book extends his comparative method to land itself.

Maine argues that land was first held by groups, not by single owners, and that private property grew slowly from the kin group. Indian villages under British rule give him living evidence for Europe's past. His famous line, that law moves from status to contract, guides the lectures. Few books have shaped legal history and anthropology together as this one did.
marx-civil-war-france-1871:
Marx wrote The Civil War in France in English in 1871, as Paris burned. The address went to the General Council of the International, the workers' body he helped lead. Its subject is the Paris Commune, the brief workers' government of that spring. Marx hails the Commune as a new form of rule.

He describes how the Communards governed, fought, and fell to the Versailles army. The Commune, he argues, was the first dictatorship of the proletariat in history. That reading founded the Marxist account of the event. The prose burns with the nearness of the fighting. It remains his most famous piece of current history.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o: This Saint-Simon volume covers the Spanish succession crisis. A French Bourbon takes the Spanish throne amid general war. The whole balance of Europe shifts. Great affairs of state seen through a courtier's watchful eyes.
metallographia-or-an-history-of-metals-w: Metallographia, or An History of Metals, 1671. The metals' history. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
milton-paradise-regained-1671:
John Milton published Paradise Regained in 1671, a brief epic in four books. It answers Paradise Lost with a tale of trial, not fall. The subject is Christ in the wilderness, tempted by Satan after his baptism.

Satan offers bread, wealth, glory, and kingdoms to the fasting Christ. Each offer is calm, firm proof of a mind that cannot be moved. Milton keeps the tone spare, grave, and stripped of ornament. The end sends Satan fallen and Christ fed by angels in peace. Readers prize its restraint, the still and thoughtful twin of the far grander epic.
milton-samson-agonistes-1671:
John Milton published Samson Agonistes in 1671, in the same book as Paradise Regained. The text here comes from H. C. Beeching's Oxford edition of 1900. Milton shaped it as a Greek-style tragedy meant for reading, not the stage.

Samson, blind and jailed in Gaza, is mocked by Philistine lords. His wife Dalila and his father Manoa visit him in his shame. A feast summons him to perform, and he pulls the temple down. Foe and hero die in one vast ruin of stone and dust. Milton, blind himself, gave Samson's grief a stark personal force.
mivart-on-the-genesis-of-species-1871:
St. George Jackson Mivart, a Catholic biologist and skilled anatomist, published On the Genesis of Species in 1871. Once close to Darwin's circle, he turned critic of natural selection. His attack came from inside biology, not from theology alone.

Mivart argues that selection cannot explain the first stages of new structures. He points to convergence and to sudden changes in the record. Darwin answered him in the sixth edition of the Origin. Their friendship never recovered. The book remains the sharpest scientific challenge Darwin faced from a former ally. The argument forced evolution's defenders to sharpen their own case in reply.
morte-arthure-alliterative-brock-1871:
The alliterative Morte Arthure is a Middle English poem by an unknown author, retold in the pounding verse style of the north. E. Brock edited it in 1871. Its Arthur is a war leader first and a courtly king second.

Arthur marches to war against Rome itself, after the emperor demands tribute from Britain. He wins battle after battle and is close to taking an empire. Then word comes that Mordred, left in charge at home, has seized the throne and the queen. Arthur turns back to a ruin he cannot prevent. The poem gives England an epic, grim Arthur with no magic to save him.
nightingale-lying-in-institutions-1871:
Introductory Notes on Lying-in Institutions, from 1871, turns Florence Nightingale's methods on childbirth care. Lying-in institutions were hospitals where women gave birth. Nightingale studied their death rates with her usual care for figures. Too many mothers, she found, died from fever after delivery in such places.

The book asks how maternity wards should be built, staffed, and run. Midwifery training receives close treatment, since skill at the bedside decides outcomes. Her mortality statistics were pioneering for the study of childbirth. The Gutenberg text omits the old publisher's catalogue at the end. Readers meet her reform method applied to mothers. The stakes could not be plainer.
openalex-w2011734771: Do electrons and muons behave identically? The LHCb collaboration's 2014 test of lepton universality compared B+ → K+ μ+μ− and B+ → K+ e+e− decay rates. The ratio put the Standard Model's even-handedness on trial.
openalex-w2022905671: The Americas are mixed — and DNA markers can map it. A 2012 study built a panel of ancestry markers to study admixture throughout the Americas. The marker set untangled Native American, European, and African roots.
openalex-w2130606571: Beck's Risk Society — reviewed. A 2009 review discusses Ulrich Beck's early work on risk perception, in German first. The review sits in a series on classic risk books — a classic, revisited for new readers today.
openalex-w2156568771: In 2005, the hottest ocean waters on record swept the tropical Atlantic and Caribbean, and coral reefs paid the price. This 2010 PLoS ONE study documents the crisis: record thermal stress triggered mass bleaching, where corals expel the algae that feed them, followed by widespread death. The paper lays out how severe the damage was, an urgent warning about warming seas threatening reefs worldwide.
openalex-w2267285071: Coffee's most devastating pest — the coffee berry borer, which can slash yields by up to 80% — has a surprising trick for surviving caffeine, the plant's natural insecticide: gut bacteria. This 2015 Nature Communications paper shows the borer's microbiota detoxify caffeine, letting the beetle thrive inside coffee beans. The finding opens a new front in fighting a pest that caffeine was supposed to stop.
openalex-w2553825371: Climate change doesn't hit everyone equally — and gender shapes who adapts and who suffers. This 2016 AMBIO paper reviews 41 studies on climate adaptation through an intersectionality lens, examining how gender is framed. The findings push the field beyond simple male-female dichotomies toward the intersecting inequalities that really determine vulnerability.
openalex-w2613371971: Rheumatic heart disease scars the hearts of Pacific Islanders at shocking rates. This 2017 Nature Communications genome-wide association study of 2,852 people across eight Oceanian countries links risk to a common immunoglobulin heavy chain allele. The finding connects the immune system's antibody genes to a disease of poverty and strep infections.
openalex-w2782974471: Rice feeds half the world, and its wild relatives hold genetic treasures. This 2018 Nature Genetics paper sequences 13 domesticated and wild rice relatives across the Oryza genus — a model for evolution over thousands to 15 million years. The genomes reveal conservation, turnover, and innovation: which genes stayed, which were lost, and which were invented anew.
openalex-w2904384071: Most viruses known to science have never been grown — they exist only as sequences. This 2018 Nature Biotechnology paper extends the MIxS reporting standard with MIUViG: minimum information about an uncultivated virus genome. Developed with the Genomic Standards Consortium, it ensures sequence-only viruses are described rigorously.
openalex-w2997096971: A tumor's neighborhood shapes its behavior — and brain metastases live in a very different neighborhood than the primary tumor. This 2020 Journal of Translational Medicine review compares the tumor microenvironment in melanoma, lung, and breast cancers at their origin versus in the brain. The differences help explain why brain metastases behave so badly.
openalex-w4413899071: Some magnets hold two warring halves in balance at one special heat. This theory paper studies the hum frequency of such magnets near that balance point, where the spin dance gets wild. The authors worked out how the pitch shifts. A magnet study aimed at faster future electronics.
openalex-w7148630071: Fermented shrimp paste yielded four brand-new fatty acids. This paper reports gambaoic acids A through C and a methyl ester from a Bacillus bacterium in shrimp jeotgal. The authors worked out the chemical structures. A natural-products study of novel chemistry hiding in fermented food.
openalex-w7204249771: Garrafadas, traditional Brazilian herbal tonics, carry folk wisdom in a bottle, but what is actually inside? This study ran chemical and microbiological tests on industrial and handmade versions sold commercially. The authors check what the brews contain and whether they are safe. A fascinating meeting of traditional knowledge and lab analysis.
openalex-w7206206171: Police forces need someone to manage ties with other institutions, and in Alagoas that job grew up informally. This article traces how an advisory role took shape and proposes turning it into a formal Directorate of Institutional Relations. The author maps the unit's duties, finds the gaps in its legal footing, and drafts the guidelines for the upgrade. A precise piece of institutional design for a state military police.
openalex-w7206216571: When a boss bullies a subordinate in the military, the chain of command makes it worse. This article studies the rule book of the Alagoas military police and proposes making workplace bullying its own named offense with a clear legal definition. The author maps the gaps in the current rules and drafts the fix. A precise piece of legal reform aimed at shielding officers from abuse by higher ranks.
phrenology-and-how-to-use-it-in-analyzin: Phrenology, and How to Use It in Analyzing Character, 1871. The character analysis. This book preserves that work. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
plos-pbio-0020171:
Alexander Kohlmaier, Fabio Savarese, Monika Lachner, and their team studied X chromosome shutdown in PLOS Biology in 2004. Female cells carry two X chromosomes but use only one. A gene called Xist starts the shutdown, and chemical marks on histones spread the silent state.

The authors found that Xist leaves a kind of memory on the chromosome. That memory guides where the silencing marks land as shutdown proceeds. The idea of a stored mark helps explain how a brief signal creates a lasting state. X inactivation is a model for all long term gene silencing, so its rules inform work on development and disease far beyond this one chromosome.
plos-pbio-0020271:
Mark D. Schroeder, Michael Pearce, John Fak, and co-workers mapped gene control in the fly embryo in PLOS Biology in 2004. A network of segmentation genes cuts the early embryo into repeating bands, the first step toward body segments. Switches that turn these genes on and off set the band edges.

The team charted those switches across the genome and tied them to the genes they control. A full wiring chart shows how a handful of signals create a precise pattern from a smooth start. That precision from loose beginnings is a core wonder of development. The fly network remains one of the best worked examples of it, used to teach and to test new ideas.
plos-pone-0000071:
Nicola Franscini, Ahmed El Gedaily, Ulrich Mahlfeld, and their team tested milk for prion protein in PLOS ONE in 2006. Prions cause BSE in cattle and related brain diseases. The normal form of the prion protein sits in many tissues, and the question was whether it appears in milk from healthy animals.

Finding the normal protein in milk does not mean milk spreads disease; the harmful folded form is the danger. Still, knowing where the normal form occurs guides safety testing. Dairy products reach nearly everyone, so even small risks deserve careful checks. The study gives food safety science a firm fact to build on, replacing guesswork about one common food.
plos-pone-0000171:
Angeline Rose Babel, James Bruce, and John A. T. Young published this virology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies the envelope glycoprotein of subgroup B avian sarcoma and leukosis virus, a bird virus. Two parts of that outer protein, the hr1 region and the fusion peptide, are examined for their role in fusing membranes at low pH.

A virus must merge its envelope with a cell to get inside, and acidity is the trigger here. The authors pinpoint how the two regions shape that fusion step. The details matter for understanding retrovirus entry in general, including how better-studied human viruses breach cells.
plos-pone-0000271:
Tim van Opijnen, Anthony de Ronde, Maarten C. Boerlijst, and colleagues published this HIV evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Its finding is in the title: how HIV-1 adapts depends on the host-cell environment it grows in. The same virus, placed in different cell types, evolves along different paths.

That dependence matters because HIV lives in several kinds of cells in the body. A drug or immune pressure that works in one cell type may select different escape routes in another. The paper warns that lab studies in a single cell line can misread how the virus will evolve in a patient.
plos-pone-0000371:
Taketoshi Kiya, Takekazu Kunieda, and Takeo Kubo studied the honeybee brain in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Forager bees, the workers that leave the hive to gather food, behave very differently from bees that stay inside. The team asked whether a specific group of brain cells works harder in foragers.

The cells sit in the mushroom body, a brain region tied to learning and memory in insects. The authors report increased neural activity in one subtype of these cells in forager brains. Linking a cell group to a bee's job in the colony helps explain how brains support the division of labor in social insects.
plos-pone-0000471:
Gul Shad Ali and colleagues described a new splicing factor that steers plant development, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Splicing is the editing of a gene's message, cutting out some sections and joining others, which lets one gene make several proteins. The team characterized a novel factor that regulates this editing in plants.

Developmental processes from flowering to root growth depend on the right message edits at the right time. A new regulator of splicing adds a control knob biologists did not know plants had. Studies in model plants often transfer to crops, where controlling development can mean better yield or hardiness.
plos-pone-0000571:
Christian E. Badr and colleagues built a sensitive test for a cell's internal shipping stress, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. The secretory pathway moves proteins out of the cell, and the endoplasmic reticulum, where it starts, suffers stress when overloaded. Their highly sensitive assay monitors both the pathway and ER stress.

ER stress is implicated in diabetes, neurodegeneration, and viral infection, so a better gauge has wide use. Sensitivity matters because early, mild stress is when intervention could help most. Assay papers are the plumbing of science: unglamorous, but everything downstream depends on their quality.
plos-pone-0000671:
Koushirou Suga, David Mark Welch, Yukari Tanaka and colleagues catalogued gene tags from a tiny water animal in PLOS ONE in 2007. Rotifers are among the most common non-arthropod animals, and the easiest to work with in their ancient animal group, the Gnathifera. Brachionus plicatilis was becoming a model for ecotoxicology and aquatic ecology.

The team analyzed expressed sequence tags, short reads from active genes, from this rotifer. It reproduces in cycles of parthenogenesis, where females produce offspring without fertilization. A tag catalogue gives researchers handles on its genes for pollution testing and ecology. It also supports studies of its unusual reproductive cycle, which alternates asexual phases with sexual ones.
plos-pone-0000771:
Yixuan Ku, Shinji Ohara, Liping Wang and colleagues traced touch-and-vision links between two brain areas, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their earlier work used event-related potentials recorded from the scalp. One scalp signal, called N140, is evoked by touch vibration in working memory tasks. It grew stronger when subjects expected a visual stimulus that had been paired with the touch. Expectation alone changed the touch response.

Using independent component analysis of the recordings, the team implicated the prefrontal cortex and somatosensory cortex in this crossmodal association. Crossmodal means across senses. The findings help explain how the brain binds touch to sight in memory, a binding everyday life relies on constantly.
plos-pone-0000871:
Ernest Greene studied how the retina handles very brief shape cues, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Shape can be probed by flashing dots along an outline one after another. Gaps of less than a thousandth of a second between dots can already hurt recognition, which raises a puzzle about where the loss happens.

Greene asks whether the eye itself keeps the signal in order, or whether later brain stages do that work. The question goes to how vision turns a stream of flashes into a steady form. It also matters for displays and tests that rely on rapid images. The study keeps the focus on the first stage of seeing.
plos-pone-0000971:
Marie-Christine Desy and Hugo Theoret measured how watching a hand action stirs the viewer's motor cortex, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Watching hand actions raises activity in the observer's own movement system, a response tied to mirror neurons. The brain seems to rehearse what it sees.

The pair asked whether physical similarity between the viewer and the observed hand changes that response. If the mirror system cares about likeness, its firing should shift with how closely the hand matches one's own. Answers shape theories of imitation and empathy. They also matter for rehab methods that use action watching to retrain movement.
plos-pone-0001071:
Elena Gonzalez-Rey, Ruben Martinez-Romero, Francisco O'Valle and colleagues tested a DNA repair enzyme blocker against arthritis, in PLOS ONE in 2007. PARP-1 is an enzyme that helps repair DNA and keep the genome intact. It also drives inflammation forward, and blocking it has eased inflammatory responses in other settings.

The team report a therapeutic effect of a PARP-1 inhibitor on experimental arthritis, by downregulating inflammation and the Th1 immune response. One target touching both joint inflammation and the immune pattern behind it is attractive. Arthritis drugs often trade benefit for broad immune suppression, so any narrower route deserves the test this paper gives.
plos-pone-0001171:
Mosquito bites do more than deliver viruses; the insect's saliva changes the skin it enters. Bradley Schneider and colleagues asked whether past contact with uninfected mosquitoes affects later West Nile virus infection, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. West Nile virus is inoculated in vector saliva into the skin and circulation of its hosts.

The authors report that prior exposure to uninfected mosquitoes enhanced mortality in naturally transmitted West Nile virus infection. The result is counterintuitive, since exposure might be expected to protect. It suggests that immune memory of mosquito saliva can worsen a later viral infection, a factor vaccine designers may need to consider.
plos-pone-0001271:
Clostridium botulinum makes the botulinum neurotoxins, among the most potent poisons known, causing long-lasting and potentially fatal intoxication. Theresa Smith and colleagues analyzed the genes for the toxin complex in several strains, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Toxin variants are grouped into types by their amino acid differences.

The authors report where several toxin gene clusters sit in the A1-A4 and B1 strains examined. Clusters including BoNT/A3, /Ba4, and /B1 are located within plasmids, the small DNA circles bacteria trade between themselves. Mobile toxin genes raise questions about how new toxin types arise and spread.
plos-pone-0001371:
Anne Charlotte Grüner and co-authors published a 2007 PLOS ONE study on malaria shots. Most shots aim to build a strong response to one key part of a germ. That plan has worked well for germs and viruses, but not yet for the parasites that cause malaria. The team tested what drives full, sterile defense in their model.

The authors found that this full defense did not rest on the response to the main surface protein of the parasite. That was a surprise, since that protein had been a top shot target for years. The result pushes shot makers to look past one protein. It suggests broad defense may need a wider set of targets.
plos-pone-0001471:
Cheikh Sokhna and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on guarding children from malaria in Senegal. In the Sahel, most malaria deaths hit children aged one to four in a short wet season. An past trial of seasonal preventive drugs cut cases by a large share. This trial tested four drug plans head to head.

The team weighed how well each plan worked, how safe each was, and how each shaped drug resistance. Seasonal dosing is cheap and timed to risk, so the best plan matters a lot. Results here guide national plans for child malaria in the whole region. They also warn how fast resistance can blunt a good plan.
plos-pone-0001571:
Matthew Coussens and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a protein and sperm making in mice. The protein, Sirt1, trims tags from other proteins and helps run sugar use, cell survival, and energy work. Its role in male fertility was not set. The team studied mice that lack the protein.

Mice without Sirt1 made far fewer sperm, and their germ cells worked poorly. That ties a broad cell regulator to a sharp fertility role. The finding may bear on male infertility with no clear cause. It also warns that drugs aimed at this protein family must watch fertility effects.
plos-pone-0001671:
Zeena E. Nackerdien, Alexander Keynan, Bonnie L. Bassler, and their co-authors studied how bacteria talk to each other in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Vibrio harveyi is a sea bacterium that glows. Bacteria use quorum sensing, a chemical census, to act as a group once enough of them are present. Because glowing tracks quorum sensing, these bacteria are a favorite system for studying it.

The glow, though, is not a clean marker: glowing itself costs energy and feeds back on growth. The authors measured how quorum sensing changes growth rates in ways the glow marker cannot fully explain. The full text gives the growth curves and the marker checks. The caution matters for the many labs that read bacterial group behavior from light alone.
plos-pone-0001771:
Kamakshi Sureka and co-authors studied how some bacteria in a uniform population survive stress, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Genetically identical microbes behave differently from one another, and that variety lets a subset persist when conditions turn harsh. In mycobacteria, the group that includes the tuberculosis germ, nutrient and oxygen starvation switch on a stress pathway.

The team shows that positive feedback and noise activate Rel, the regulator of the stringent response, in part of the population. The full text gives the single-cell data and the circuit model. A bet-hedging circuit like this helps explain how TB germs can ride out antibiotics and immune attack inside the body.
plos-pone-0001871:
David Gisselsson and co-authors tackled a puzzle about cancer cell division in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In healthy cells, two poles pull the sets of chromosomes apart in a neat, even split. Cancer cells at times divide toward three or more poles at once, which scrambles the sets they pass on.

The team asked how such cells slip past the spindle check, a guard that should halt a flawed split. They also asked how near-random the split of chromosomes then becomes. Their work frames these wild divisions as a source of new gene mixes inside tumors. Readers gain a sharper view of how cancers gain the variety that helps them grow and spread.
plos-pone-0001971:
Sahra Abdulle and co-authors compared HIV subtypes inside the fluid around the brain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. HIV-1 comes in many genetic subtypes spread across the world. The virus can enter the brain and spinal fluid, where the immune system reacts in its own closed space.

The team measured viral load in cerebrospinal fluid and signs of immune activation inside the spinal sac, in people infected with unlike subtypes. If subtypes differ in the brain, care and prognosis may need to differ too. The study adds brain data to a field long focused on blood alone.
plos-pone-0002071:
Ajay Wanchu and co-authors tested simple blood markers for tuberculosis in a TB-endemic country, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Spotting TB is harder in people who also carry HIV, and simple biomarkers that work in both groups were needed. Two proteins from the TB bacterium, malate synthase and MPT51, had stood out as strong immune targets in patients.

The team evaluated how sensitive tests for these markers are, in frank TB and in incipient disease, where infection is just taking hold. A cheap marker that catches early cases could change care where TB and HIV overlap most.
plos-pone-0002171:
William Lanier, Ahmed Moustafa, Debashish Bhattacharya, and co-authors read the gene messages of a tiny green alga, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ostreococcus lucimarinus is a pico-eukaryote, a cell with a nucleus barely the size of a bacterium. Its genome, at 13.2 million letters, is among the most compact known in eukaryotes, with genes packed tightly together.

Oddly for so tight a genome, many of its genes still contain introns, the spacer pieces cut out before a gene is used. The team used EST sequences, short reads of active genes, to survey them. They found an excess of introns in the genes the alga uses most.
plos-pone-0002271:
Mark Witton and Darren Naish reappraised the giant flying reptiles called azhdarchid pterosaurs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Azhdarchids were among the most widespread and successful pterosaur groups, with long, shallow beaks and long necks built from stretched, tube-shaped vertebrae. Some stood as tall as giraffes. How they lived and fed, though, stayed controversial.

The authors reviewed the group's functional morphology, what its body plan was built to do, and its paleoecology. They argue against the popular image of these giants skimming water like seabirds. Their reading paints azhdarchids as ground-foraging stalkers of small prey, a very different life for the largest flying animals ever.
plos-pone-0002371:
Polonelli led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Luciano Polonelli, José Pontón, Natalia Elguezabal, among others. Its subject is antibody Complementarity-Determining Regions (CDRs) Can Display Differential Antimicrobial, Antiviral and Antitumor Activities. Complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) are immunoglobulin (Ig) hypervariable domains that determine specific antibody (Ab) binding.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002471:
Scardigli and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Raffaella Scardigli, Cesare Gargioli, Daniela Tosoni, among others. Its subject is binding of sFRP-3 to EGF in the Extra-Cellular Space Affects Proliferation, Differentiation and Morphogenetic Events Regulated by the Two Molecules. sFRP-3 is a soluble antagonist of Wnts, widely expressed in developing embryos.

The Wnt gene family comprises cysteine-rich secreted ligands that regulate cell proliferation, differentiation, organogenesis and oncogenesis of different organisms ranging from worms to mammals. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002571:
Burz joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are David S. Burz, Alexander Shekhtman, among others. Its subject is in-Cell Biochemistry Using NMR Spectroscopy. Biochemistry and structural biology are undergoing a dramatic revolution.

Until now, mostly in vitro techniques have been used to study subtle. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002671:
A 2008 study by Jean Peccoud and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up targeted development of registries of biological parts. The catalog record names Jean Peccoud first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The design and construction of novel biological systems by combining basic building blocks represents a dominant paradigm in synthetic biology. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002771:
Michael C. Otterstatter and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on does pathogen spillover from commercially reared bumble bees threaten wild pollinators?. Authorship is credited in the record to Michael C. Otterstatter and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The conservation of insect pollinators is drawing attention because of reported declines in bee species and the ‘ecosystem services’ they provide. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002871:
Sara E. Heisel, Yuanji Zhang, Edwards Allen and co-authors reported in PLOS ONE in 2008 on small RNAs taken from rice grain. Small RNAs are short molecules, about 20 to 24 units long, that help guide growth in plants and animals. The team compared RNA from mature grain with RNA from young seedlings.

To map the groups they used pyrosequencing, a fast DNA reading method, plus a clustering program to find where the RNAs sit in the genome. The paper describes which small RNA groups appear unique to grain. Plant scientists can use that map to study how rice seeds form and store food.
plos-pone-0002971:
Yone Jung Yoon, Hisashi Kominami, Thomas Trimarchi and co-authors blocked electrical activity in the chick spinal cord in 2008. Spontaneous activity in the cord's networks guides how neurons specialize and how nerve-muscle structures are built during development. The team examined what chronic loss of that activity does.

They used retroviral infection to add Kir2.1 channels, which quiet electrical activity, to developing cells. That disrupted the electrical differentiation of motoneurons, the nerve cells that drive muscles. Published in PLOS ONE, the study shows activity is not a by-product but a teacher in spinal development. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003071:
Satsuki Fukushima, Steven Coppen, Joon Lee and co-authors compared delivery routes for myoblast therapy in rat heart failure in 2008. Injecting skeletal myoblasts into heart muscle had shown promise for post-infarction chronic heart failure. Weak benefit and ventricular arrhythmias were the standing concerns.

The team tested choice of cell-delivery route for the transplant. Route decides how many cells stay in the heart and where they lodge. Published in PLOS ONE, delivery is often the difference between a therapy that works in principle and one that works in practice, making this comparison valuable. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003171:
Yongping Wang, Yun E. Wang, M. Grazia Cotticelli and colleagues describe a new RNA interference library in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. RNA interference blocks gene activity through small non-coding RNAs. Most libraries target single genes through standard pathways. The body's own microRNAs, however, often target many genes at once and can act through other routes.

The authors build a random shRNA-encoding library for phenotypic selection and hit optimization. Readers get a tool that searches by outcome first, then finds the active sequences. Such screens can reveal gene effects that one-by-one testing would miss, including effects spread across several targets.
plos-pone-0003271:
Tiziana Musso, Sara Scutera, William Vermi and colleagues study a signal that makes Langerhans cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Langerhans cells are a well characterized subset of dendritic cells located in the epidermis of skin and mucosae. In the body they originate from resident and blood-borne precursors in the presence of keratinocyte-derived TGF-beta. In vitro, they can be generated from monocytes.

The title reports that activin A induces Langerhans cell differentiation in vitro and in human skin explants. Readers get another route to produce a key skin immune cell. Lab-grown Langerhans cells help study allergy, infection, and skin immune responses.
plos-pone-0003371:
Jennifer E. Bruin and her team studied nicotine exposure in rats for this 2008 paper. Pregnant women who smoke are often advised to use nicotine replacement products instead. The authors wanted to know what pure nicotine itself does to a growing baby. They gave nicotine to rat mothers before and after birth, then tracked the pups.

The exposed pups showed growing damage inside their pancreas cells over time. The harm centered on mitochondria, the small parts that make energy for the cell. Insulin-making beta cells in the pancreas also worked less well. The findings raise doubts about treating nicotine as fully safe in pregnancy.
plos-pone-0003471:
A. K. Srikrishnan and co-authors audited HIV testing growth in Chennai, India, in this 2008 study. They focused on private labs offering voluntary counseling and testing. Surveys captured services and users in 2001 and again in 2006. The question was whether growth matched the real need.

Five years of expansion changed who came for testing and what labs offered. The authors weighed that growth against the epidemic's demands. Gaps showed where diagnostic effort still fell short. The audit gives planners a check on whether services reach the right people. Private labs carry much of India's testing load, so their growth matters.
plos-pone-0003571:
Fiona J. McCallum and co-authors studied how malaria-fighting antibodies are gained in this 2008 paper. Antibodies that inhibit blood-stage Plasmodium falciparum may drive acquired immunity. They may also power vaccine-induced protection. Yet how people acquire them was not well understood.

The team tested dialysed serum and purified immunoglobulin from subjects. Those samples were checked for growth inhibition of the parasite. Charting acquisition shows how exposure builds the protective arsenal. Vaccines aiming to shortcut years of infection need that timeline. Blood-stage attack is what makes malaria fever, so blocking it is the core goal of most vaccine work in the field. Each sample set from exposed people adds one more piece to that long and slow puzzle of immunity.
plos-pone-0003671:
Hemant Kulkarni, Vincent C. Marconi, Brian K. Agan, and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Two gene variants shape how the virus interacts with the body. CCL3L1 comes in different copy numbers, and CCR5 is a doorway HIV uses to enter cells.

The team asked how these genotypes relate to the epidemic spread of HIV-1. They also tested what the variants mean for judging how well vaccines work. Work of this kind shows that a person's gene copy count can ripple outward, from one infection to the course of a whole epidemic.
plos-pone-0003771:
Josefin Skogsberg, Andrea Dicker, Mikael Rydén, and colleagues published this metabolism study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Fat tissue sends fatty acids to the liver, where they shape the making of ApoB-carrying lipoproteins. Whether a signal also travels back from liver to fat was unknown. The team investigated that reverse arm.

They found ApoB100-LDL, the so-called bad cholesterol particle, acts as a metabolic signal to peripheral fat. It inhibits lipolysis, the release of fatty acids from fat cells. The reverse message completes a two-way conversation between the liver and adipose tissue about energy stores.
plos-pone-0003871:
Ira Verena Röder, Yvonne Petersen, Kyeong Rok Choi, and co-authors studied a motor protein in living animals in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns myosin Va, which moves small cargo sacs inside cells. People who lack working myosin Va can have movement disorders. Mice that lack it show a severe form called dilute lethal.

The team asked what myosin Va does at the junction where nerves meet muscle. They looked at how that junction changes shape and adapts over time. The study links the transport protein to the lasting flexibility of the nerve-muscle contact. That flexibility helps muscles keep working as signals change.
plos-pone-0003971:
Brendon O. Watson, Jason N. MacLean, and Rafael Yuste studied cortex activity states in 2008. Cortical neurons flip between a ready UP state and a quiet DOWN state. UP states match bursts of firing across many neurons. Such bursts may carry information processing in the cortex.

Their PLOS ONE article asks whether UP states shield ongoing activity. They tested how thalamic inputs affect cortex during those states. Activity already under way proved protected from incoming thalamic signals. That shielding could let the cortex finish its own patterns without interruption. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004071:
Dennis vanEngelsdorp, Jerry Hayes, Robyn M. Underwood, and co-authors surveyed U.S. honey bee losses in 2008. Honey bees are essential to modern farm pollination. A new ailment, Colony Collapse Disorder, empties hives of bees. Earlier decline estimates lacked full counts of colony losses.

Their survey covered fall 2007 through spring 2008 across the United States. Beekeepers reported losses from their operations for that season. A national count grounds debate about the scale of collapse. It also sets a baseline for tracking the disorder over time. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004171:
De-Kuan Chang and colleagues published this cancer drug study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer worldwide. Standard chemotherapy lacks tumour specificity, so doses are limited by harm to healthy tissue.

The team tested a novel peptide, a short protein fragment, designed to guide liposomal drugs, medicines packed in fat bubbles, toward tumours. In mouse models of human lung cancer, they measured whether the peptide made the packaged drugs work better. A guidance system like this could raise the dose that reaches a tumour while sparing the rest of the body.
plos-pone-0004271:
Dominik Wodarz and Natalia Komarova published this modelling paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Oncolytic viruses infect cancer cells and kill them while leaving healthy cells largely intact. Because they spread through a tumour, they are an attractive therapy, and clinical trials have shown promising results.

The authors work toward predictive computational models of this therapy. Their paper sets out the basis for validating such models against experiments and for choosing between competing models. Good models could predict which tumours a virus can clear before a patient is ever treated. Yet results vary, and prediction remains hard.
plos-pone-0004371:
Anke Popp and colleagues published this brain development study in PLOS ONE in 2009. GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain and is synthesised by glutamic acid decarboxylase, or GAD. GAD exists in two adult isoforms, GAD65 and GAD67. During embryonic brain development, at least two additional transcripts exist, called I-80 and I-86.

The team tracked how adult and embryonic GAD transcripts are regulated across space and time during postnatal development in the rat brain. The pattern shows when each form of the GABA-making enzyme is in charge as the brain matures. Postnatal development is the period after birth, when the brain is still wiring itself.
plos-pone-0004471:
One gene switch turns on the parts of a tiny proton pump in ear, kidney, and male reproductive tissue. Hilmar Vidarsson, Rickard Westergren, Mikael Heglind, and co-authors report on it in PLOS ONE in 2009. The pump, called the vacuolar H+-ATPase, moves protons across cell membranes. Special cells in the inner ear, the kidney, and the epididymis depend on it to keep their fluids at the right acidity.

The switch is Foxi1, a forkhead transcription factor, a protein that controls other genes. The team calls it a master regulator of the pump's subunits in these tissues. When such a master switch fails, hearing, kidney balance, and fertility can all suffer. Naming the switch gives doctors a gene to check when those problems run in a family.
plos-pone-0004571:
Where a retrovirus lands in the human genome is guided by the proteins that switch genes on, show Barbara Felice, Claudia Cattoglio, Davide Cittaro, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gamma-retroviruses and lentiviruses do not integrate at random. They favor active chromatin, promoters, and regulatory regions, the genome's busy districts.

Vectors borrowed from gamma-retroviruses for gene therapy often land near genes that control growth, a safety worry. The team shows transcription factor binding sites are genetic determinants of where integration happens. In other words, the landing pattern is written into the DNA sequence itself. Knowing the rules could let engineers steer therapeutic viruses away from dangerous neighborhoods, a key step for safer gene therapy.
plos-pone-0004671:
Karin Berger and colleagues studied a protein called PDE3B in mouse liver cells for PLOS ONE in 2009. PDE3B helps control signals sent by two small messengers inside cells. It also plays a part in fat breakdown and in how the body handles insulin and blood sugar.

The team asked where PDE3B sits inside liver cells and why that place matters. They found it in small pockets of the cell surface and in smooth inner membranes. Knowing the exact site helps link the protein to control of sugar and fat use. That link matters for work on diabetes and liver health.
plos-pone-0004771:
Rosaura Esteve-Puig and colleagues showed that growth factors and a cancer gene can uncouple a key energy sensor, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Grasping the chemical steps behind melanoma growth is critical for better therapy, the authors note. A kinase called LKB1 switches on a sensor that reins in growth and triggers cell death under energy stress.

A mutant gene common in melanoma was among the factors tested. The team showed such signals can cut the link between LKB1 and its sensor. A cut link may let tumor cells grow despite low energy. Restoring it could be a therapy angle.
plos-pone-0004871:
Thibaud Damy and colleagues linked glutathione deficiency in cardiac patients to working status and structural abnormalities, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tripeptide glutathione is essential to cell survival, and deficiency in cardiac and systemic glutathione relates to heart failure progression and remodeling in animal models. Accordingly, cardiac and blood glutathione were studied in patients across working classes and degrees of structural change.

Lower antioxidant reserves track worse hearts clinically. Deficiency may be cause and consequence together. Supplementation trials need careful patient selection. Oxidative stress remains central in cardiology. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004971:
Plants fight viruses with RNA silencing. The defense chops viral RNA into tiny pieces. Those pieces, called siRNAs, then guide the attack. Xiaopeng Qi, Forrest Sheng Bao and Zhixin Xie mapped part of this system. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used the lab plant Arabidopsis thaliana.

Making several classes of siRNAs requires enzymes called RNA-dependent RNA polymerases. The team deep-sequenced small RNAs to pin down their roles. They found which family members build the virus-derived siRNAs. The result maps a key step in plant immunity. It may help breeders strengthen crops against viral disease.
plos-pone-0005071:
The Alzheimer's-linked protein APP can bind an adaptor called FE65. Together they can regulate gene expression. Yuji Kajiwara and colleagues mapped FE65's partners in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used yeast two-hybrid studies. Their focus was genes involved in nuclear signaling. One partner stood out: a protein named Teashirt.

FE65 binds Teashirt, and the pair inhibits expression of caspase-4. Caspase-4 is a death enzyme found only in primates. The chain links Alzheimer's machinery to a primate-specific switch. It maps a new gene-control route for the APP complex. Such routes may influence how neurons respond to damage. The finding adds depth to a crowded field.
plos-pone-0005171:
Bluetongue is a disease of sheep, cattle, and other cud-chewing animals, spread by insects and caused by a virus. Studying how it harms the body and testing vaccines is hard without a small lab animal that gets sick. Calvo-Pinilla and colleagues addressed that gap in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team showed that adult mice lacking the alpha and beta interferon receptor can be infected with bluetongue virus. That gives labs a working mouse model for the disease. With it, researchers can probe how the virus spreads in the body and screen vaccine ideas before trials in farm animals.
plos-pone-0005271:
Making ethanol from plant fiber needs microbes that can digest tough biomass. The bacterium Clostridium thermocellum is a leading candidate, armed with a large enzyme complex for chewing cellulose. Raman and colleagues fed it treated switchgrass and reported the changes in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Using quantitative proteomics, the team tracked how the microbe's cellulosome changes with different plant carbohydrates. The protein shifts reveal how the bacterium adapts its toolkit to each feed. Knowing the adaptation helps engineers design microbes and processes for cheaper biofuel. Plant stalks and husks are cheap and rich in fiber, but they are hard to break down. A germ that shifts its tools to fit each plant part could cut the cost of fuel made from farm waste in a big way.
plos-pone-0005371:
Low oxygen harms the body in two patterns: steady lack, or repeated dips like those in sleep apnea and asthma. Azad and colleagues used fruit flies to compare tolerance to both patterns in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Constant hypoxia and intermittent hypoxia triggered distinct tolerance mechanisms in Drosophila. The two stresses are not interchangeable, and defenses against one do not simply cover the other. That split matters for treating human conditions where oxygen dips come in bursts. Fruit flies share most of their genes with us, and they can be raised by the thousands in a week. So a split in how they cope with low air is a fast first clue for sleep and lung care.
plos-pone-0005471:
Arnaud Parcellier and co-authors studied a protein that shapes mitochondria, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Mitochondria supply energy to cells and take part in many signals. They form moving networks of tubes that join and split as the cell's needs change.

The team studied a protein called CTMP, found in mitochondria and sometimes released from them. They showed that it helps control how the networks split and join. That control affects how cells handle energy and stress, and it may matter in diseases where mitochondria fail, such as some nerve and muscle disorders.
plos-pone-0005571:
Amanda Denuc and co-authors studied how an enzyme that removes tags is itself controlled, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Cells tag proteins with a small marker called ubiquitin to change their fate. Enzymes that remove the tag are just as important, but how they are controlled is poorly known.

The team studied one such enzyme, USP25, which has a muscle-specific form. They found domains that bind the tag and set the enzyme's own tagged state. That self-control shapes which targets the enzyme can reach and act on. Self-tagging is a neat way for such enzymes to set their own working level inside the cell.
plos-pone-0005671:
Hong-Yan Sui and co-authors tested a gene-silencing tool against flu in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They built small RNA pieces aimed at the M2 gene of influenza A, a virus that can copy itself inside infected cells. Silencing one key gene can block the whole chain of copying.

A known risk is that the virus mutates and escapes the RNA aimed at it. The team used a lentiviral carrier with a short hairpin design to deliver the silencer. They report strong and lasting blocks on viral growth in their tests. The approach points toward flu drugs that target set viral genes.
plos-pone-0005771:
Arun Kamath and co-authors tested a liposome-based TB vaccine in 2009 that aimed at the right immune cells. The search for better tuberculosis vaccines needs formulas that rouse strong T cell defenses. Their formula, CAF01, mixes fat bubbles with a synthetic piece of the TB germ's coat.

The mix targets dendritic cells, the sentries that start T cell responses, with unusual precision. It roused strong, multi-skilled T cells in both adult and newborn models. Newborn protection matters where TB strikes early in life. The study marks CAF01 as a platform worth carrying toward human trials.
plos-pone-0005871:
Mitra Hooshmand and co-authors asked in 2009 how much recovery after stem cell transplant for spinal cord injury comes from the host's own repair. Human stem cells grown as neurospheres can renew themselves and form several nerve cell types. The group had seen injured mice walk better after receiving them.

The team correlated how well the cells engrafted with how much function returned, and probed host-mediated repair mechanisms. If the host does much of the healing, therapies could aim to amplify that response. Untangling graft effects from host effects is essential before human use. The analysis moves the field toward honest mechanisms.
plos-pone-0005971:
HIV rarely passes from mother to child in the first months of pregnancy, despite a placenta that germs can cross. Romain Marlin, Marie-Thérèse Nugeyre, Claire de Truchis and colleagues asked in 2009 which cells in the womb lining the virus can infect at that stage. Their PLOS ONE study focuses on the uterine mucosa in early pregnancy.

The cells that present foreign matter to the immune system turn out to be targets for the R5 form of HIV-1, the team reports. Naming the entry cells maps where mother-to-child spread could begin. That map guides efforts to block the virus at the womb, a step toward cutting one of the saddest routes of HIV infection.
plos-pone-0006071:
The outer surface of a germ is where vaccines and drugs must aim. Marija Pinne and David Haake mapped that surface for a water-borne pathogen in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper takes a combined approach to finding surface-exposed, membrane-spanning proteins of Leptospira interrogans, the spiral germ behind leptospirosis in people and animals worldwide.

A sound surface catalog tells vaccine makers which proteins the immune system can actually reach. The germ spreads through fresh water and settles in the kidneys of host animals, so its surface is its handshake with every host. The paper's full approach, rather than a single test, sets a standard for surface hunts in other germs.
plos-pone-0006171:
Coilin is the marker protein of the Cajal body, a small structure inside the cell nucleus. Michael Walker, Liping Tian, and Gregory Matera studied mice that lack coilin in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The Cajal body helps build small particles that cells use to process their messages, and it is found in both plants and animals.

Mice without coilin showed lower survival, lower fertility, and fewer offspring, as the title reports. The work shows that a protein tied to one tiny nuclear structure can shape the health of a whole animal. It also raises fresh questions about what the Cajal body does across a lifetime. Cell biologists get a useful animal model for those questions.
plos-pone-0006271:
Safer estrogen drugs would target only one of the hormone's two receptors. Sreenivasan Paruthiyil and colleagues compared drugs that selectively activate estrogen receptor beta in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Several synthetic and natural compounds claim that selectivity, but their gene effects may differ.

Regulation of genes depended on both the drug class and the cell type, the team reports. The same compound can thus act differently in different tissues. That caution matters for designing hormone therapies with fewer risks. It also shows why cell context must be part of early drug testing.
plos-pone-0006371:
An inflammatory enzyme rises in gut lining cells in both bowel disease and colon cancer. Oliver Jay Broom and colleagues traced its control in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Collagen I triggers fresh synthesis of the enzyme COX-2 in intestinal epithelial cells, and the surface protein CD47 regulates that response.

CD47 also affects how the gut cells migrate, the team reports. Migration and inflammation together shape healing and tumor spread. Linking a scaffolding signal to COX-2 control names new intervention points. The pathway may serve both bowel disease and cancer research.
plos-pone-0006471:
Joanna Wimpenny, Alex Weir, Lisa Clayton, and colleagues watched New Caledonian crows use tools in sequence for PLOS ONE in 2009. Using a tool on a non-food object, for example to make another tool, is seen as a hallmark of human intelligence. It may have been a crucial step in human evolution. Crows that do similar things offer a rare window on how such minds work.

The study examines the mental processes behind sequential tool use in the crows. Planning, memory, and understanding of cause all come into play. Birds evolved this skill apart from primates, so the comparison is telling. It shows complex tool behavior does not need a human-like brain plan.
plos-pone-0006571:
Francesca Santoni de Sio and Didier Trono studied resting immune cells and HIV in PLOS ONE in 2009. CD4 positive T lymphocytes are the primary targets of HIV-1. When fully quiescent, resting, these cells cannot be infected, due to a post-entry block that prevents completion of reverse transcription. APOBEC3G, a cellular antiviral protein, was a candidate explanation.

The authors tested cells depleted of APOBEC3G. Their title reports resting CD4 T cells remain refractory to HIV-1 infection even without it. So another block must explain the resistance. Knowing resting cells resist infection helps explain how HIV hides and persists in them.
plos-pone-0006671:
Ben Lopman and co-authors studied norovirus in England and Wales for PLOS ONE in 2009. Norovirus is the most common known cause of infectious diarrhoea in developed countries. It appears in single cases and in larger outbreaks. Its cases rise sharply in winter, and the virus itself keeps changing over time.

The team applied time-series analysis to laboratory surveillance records. They weighed three kinds of influence on the pattern of cases. Host factors, weather, and changes in the virus all played a part. Their findings help explain why the winter surge arrives when it does. That understanding can support better forecasting of norovirus seasons and outbreaks.
plos-pone-0006771:
William T. Wojtach, Kyongje Sung, and Dale Purves offered an empirical account of a motion illusion in PLOS ONE in 2009. Perceived speed and direction often match neither physics nor retinal images. That mismatch is a central puzzle of motion perception. The speed-distance effect is one such puzzle. Objects can look faster or slower depending on judged distance.

The authors investigated sources of variation behind the effect. Their explanation rests on accumulated experience with real-world motion statistics. In short, the visual system reports the most probable cause. Probability learned from experience shapes what people see. The account unifies several motion illusions under one learning principle.
plos-pone-0006871:
Shih-Min A. Huang and colleagues ran a genome-wide screen for brakes on insulin signaling in PLOS ONE in 2009. Type 2 diabetes combines insulin resistance with insulin-producing cell failure. Treatments aim at both causes. Several negative regulators of insulin signaling were already known. Drug discovery efforts target some of them.

Their functional screen searched the genome for more such regulators. A screen tests genes one by one for measurable effects. Newly revealed brakes are fresh drug target candidates. Releasing a brake could restore insulin sensitivity. The study widens the target list beyond the few regulators known before.
plos-pone-0006971:
Archana Shenoy and Robert Blelloch analyzed a gene control circuit in PLOS ONE in 2009. A protein pair called the Microprocessor cuts raw microRNA strands into their working form. The pair contains Dgcr8 and the enzyme Drosha. It also keeps its own levels in check by cutting hairpin loops in the Dgcr8 message itself.

Their genome-wide analysis asked how widespread that self-cutting is. The evidence suggested this message-breaking route is specialized for Dgcr8 auto-regulation. In other words, the system mainly throttles itself. Self-control like this keeps microRNA output steady, which cells need for normal growth.
plos-pone-0007071:
Russell Dinnage studied plant communities in an old field system in PLOS ONE in 2009. When farmland is abandoned, its plant community changes fast. Plowing and other disturbances restart that succession. The mix of species shifts as the field ages. Dinnage asked how disturbance reshapes the family tree of the community.

He tracked the phylogenetic makeup and structure of the plants over time. Relatedness patterns reveal which forces are sorting the species. Close relatives may share traits that help or hurt after disturbance. Reading succession through the family tree gives ecologists a deeper test than species lists alone.
plos-pone-0007171:
Manqi Deng and Rong Li published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how mouse eggs divide after fertilization. Their work looks at a step called polar body extrusion. In this step an egg sheds a small cell so its own set of chromosomes is cut in half.

The authors focus on eggs made by injecting sperm directly, a method called ICSI. They report that sperm chromatin can trigger this shedding in the wrong place when egg activation is delayed. Readers interested in fertility treatment get a close look at how timing and position signals can go wrong inside an egg.
plos-pone-0007271:
Tiffany J. Morris, Mark Vickers, Peter Gluckman, and colleagues studied undernourished pregnancies in rats in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Prenatal nutrition is linked to metabolic and cardiovascular disease later in life. That process is called developmental programming, where early conditions shift the body's long-term trajectory in lasting ways.

The authors profile gene activity in offspring of undernourished mothers. They look for changes that could explain later differences in metabolic traits. Their results connect gestational undernourishment to altered gene programs. The work helps explain why poor nutrition before birth can echo into adult disease.
plos-pone-0007371:
Hironori Asai, Shunsuke Iwamori, Kentaro Kawai, and colleagues traced cell lineages in a nitrogen-fixing bacterium in 2009. Anabaena forms chains of cells, some of which become heterocysts that capture nitrogen. Heterocyst pattern formation is one of the simplest known patterns in cell differentiation, with specialized cells spaced along each filament.

Most earlier studies used statistics on collected cells. The authors instead follow individual cell lineages over time and space. They track expression of the hetR gene during pattern formation. Their lineage view shows how the pattern builds cell by cell.
plos-pone-0007471:
Sybille Krauß and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on GLI3, a transcription factor controlled by the Sonic Hedgehog signal. Mutations in GLI3 cause malformation syndromes such as Greig cephalopolysyndactyly and Pallister-Hall syndrome. These conditions affect the skull, limbs, and other structures. Many of the harmful changes are single point mutations. The team asked what those small changes do to the protein.

They found the mutations misregulate where GLI3 sits inside the cell. Sent to the wrong compartments, the protein cannot do its normal job of controlling genes. That misrouting explains how a tiny spelling change grows into major malformations. The study links a molecular traffic problem to human birth defects. It also suggests that a protein's address can matter as much as its structure.
plos-pone-0007571:
Sergio Simonetta and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on daily rhythms in the roundworm C. elegans. Circadian rhythms are driven by internal clocks and tuned by light and darkness. The worm is a workhorse of developmental and genetic research. Its clock, though, was barely described. The team measured the timing of the worms' locomotor activity across the day-night cycle.

They characterized when the animals move and when they rest, and how those rhythms align with environmental cues. Establishing the pattern is the first step for any clock research. A simple animal with a working clock offers cheap, fast genetics for chronobiology. The study makes that case with baseline data. Later work on clock genes in the worm builds on timing maps like this one.
plos-pone-0007671:
Benjamin Johnson and colleagues published a case study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on children who died of influenza A in the United Kingdom. In the winter of 2003 and 2004, a drifted H3N2 strain, resembling one first seen in Fujian, spread widely. Its circulation came with an unusually high number of laboratory-confirmed flu deaths in children. The team reviewed those fatal cases to document what happened. Details of each case were gathered from the season's records.

The review documents how a routine winter virus turned deadly for the young that year. Antigenic drift had moved the virus away from the vaccine's target. Case series like this teach clinicians which presentations end worst. They also inform vaccine strain choices and public warnings in drift years. Childhood flu deaths are rare enough to study one by one. The study makes that grim accounting useful.
plos-pone-0007771:
Saskia Heeringa and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It reports a new mutation that causes a kidney disease in children. The disease, FSGS, scars the kidney's filters and can end in kidney failure. The gene involved is TRPC6, which codes for a calcium channel.

Seven TRPC6 mutations were already known to cause the adult inherited form. This new one causes the childhood form instead. Finding it extends genetic testing to younger patients. It also confirms that calcium entry through this channel is vital for the kidney's delicate filter cells.
plos-pone-0007871:
Quique Bassat and co-authors published a trial in PLOS ONE in 2009. It compares two combination therapies for malaria in African children. Artemisinin combination therapies were the preferred treatment for uncomplicated malaria. One fixed-dose option, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, looked promising but had limited data in African children.

The randomised trial tested it against artemether-lumefantrine, a standard rival. The design was a non-inferiority trial, asking whether the new pairing is no worse. Both safety and efficacy were measured in the children. Solid trial data like this shapes malaria treatment policy across Africa. It also helps clinics choose which drug to stock first.
plos-pone-0007971:
Laura Cerchia and colleagues used a selection method to tell brain tumors apart in PLOS ONE in 2009. The method, differential SELEX, breeds short DNA strands that stick to one cell type but not another. Their test cells were glioma lines, cancers of the brain's support tissue.

Strands bred this way could mark the fine gaps between close tumor types. Sorting tumors with care matters, because the right treatment plan hinges on the exact type. Such strands, called aptamers, may one day guide both tests and drugs aimed at the tumor alone.
plos-pone-0008071:
Mariena van der Plas and colleagues found that maggot spit can retrain immune cells toward repair in PLOS ONE in 2009. Maggots of a blowfly species are used to clean chronic wounds that will not heal. Their secretions were already known to calm inflammation in human blood cells.

Exposed to the secretions, young immune cells grew into a type that builds blood vessels rather than one that attacks. That shift is just what a stuck wound needs to move from fight to repair. The work explains a folk cure in modern terms and may inspire wound drugs that copy the maggot's trick.
plos-pone-0008171:
Nicolas Dard and colleagues watched the angle of cell division in early mouse embryos in PLOS ONE in 2009. Between the eight-cell and sixteen-cell stages, uneven divisions give the embryo its earliest pair of distinct cell lines. In many species the spindle, the gear that pulls chromosomes apart, is carefully aimed to do this.

Mouse embryos seemed to break that rule, with spindle angles looking loose. The team measured the angles through the transition to test how loose they truly are. The answer shapes how we think the first fate split in our own kind is guided.
plos-pone-0008271:
Michelle Sexton and colleagues tested imaging probes on brain tumor cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The translocator protein, TSPO, rises in glial cells during disease and injury. Probes that bind TSPO can reveal tumors and inflammation on scans. Two near-infrared probes, NIR-conPK and NIR-6T, bind this protein family with high affinity. The team checked them on astrocytoma and microglial cells.

Binding suggested a protein related to TSPO was present in those cells. Better probes could improve imaging of brain tumors. They could also help track inflammation in the living brain. The work evaluates candidates for future scans.
plos-pone-0008371:
Amanda M. Cooksey and colleagues searched for stress performance markers in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Attrition from aviation training is a serious cost for the United States Navy. Each late-stage training failure costs taxpayers more than a million dollars in their account. It also reduces the fleet's operational readiness. Predicting who thrives under psychological stress would help selection.

The team sought blood biomarkers and physiological processes that distinguish superior performers. Biology might flag resilience that interviews miss. Better selection could cut costly late failures. The study serves military training and stress science alike.
plos-pone-0008471:
Brendon Parsons and co-authors compare RNA tools in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. RNA interference, or RNAi, can shut off single genes. Scientists use it to find new regulators in cell pathways. In simple animals, the process is direct and strong. In mammal cells, labs use pools of small RNAs or single duplexes. Each approach has costs and risks of off-target effects.

The team compare pools with many single duplexes in the same test. They measure how well each approach finds true hits. They also weigh noise and false results. Their findings help labs pick a screening method that fits their goals.
plos-pone-0008571:
Shan Gao and co-authors explain green tide growth in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Ulva prolifera is a common green seaweed. It is a main causative species of green tides that hit Qingdao in 2008. Those tides harmed preparations for the Beijing Olympic sailing competition. More than thirty percent of the sailing area was covered at the peak.
