The team investigate the proliferation strategy behind such explosive growth.

They find the seaweed forms sporangia by fragmentation. Fragments break off and each can release spores that seed new growth. That strategy multiplies the seaweed at exceptional speed. Knowing it helps predict and manage future green tides.
plos-pone-0008671:
Kristian Otkjaer, Helmut Holtmann, Tue Wenzel Kragstrup, and their co-authors published a cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was IL-24, a signaling protein linked to immune defense and to holding back tumor growth. Cells build IL-24 from a messenger RNA copy, and that copy breaks down fast.

The team traced control of that breakdown to p38 MAPK, an enzyme inside cells. When p38 MAPK is active, it steadies the tail end of the IL-24 message, a stretch called the 3 prime UTR. A steadier message lasts longer, so the cell can make more IL-24 from it. Readers learn one exact way cells tune how long an immune signal stays switched on.
plos-pone-0008771:
Yi-Chun Loraine Tung, Eduard Ayuso, Xiaoye Shan, and colleagues tweaked an obesity gene inside rat brains. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Variants near the human FTO gene are the strongest common genetic link to obesity. Carriers tend to eat more and feel hungrier. The gene's brain site of action was the open question. The hypothalamus, the brain's appetite center, was the natural suspect.

Raising or lowering Fto in the rat hypothalamus changed food intake. Local changes in this one region shifted eating behavior. That result pins part of the obesity effect on appetite circuits. It directs drug thinking toward the brain.
plos-pone-0008871:
Joost le Feber, Jan Stegenga, and Wim Rutten tried to teach dish-grown brain networks with slow electric pulses. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rat cortical neurons grown on electrode grids form living networks. Such networks change their connections, a form of plasticity. An earlier protocol claimed to train networks toward a target response. Reproducing and refining that claim was the team's aim.

Slow electrical stimuli were applied while network responses were recorded. The team assessed whether activity shifted in the intended learned direction. Dish networks offer a stripped-down model of learning rules. Clear results, positive or negative, guide the whole cultured-network field.
plos-pone-0008971:
Rafael Medina-Navarro and co-authors argued that proteins themselves fight chemical rust in the body, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Oxidants are reactive molecules that damage living tissue over time. Proteins are their most common target, simply because proteins are everywhere in cells. Yet proteins such as albumin also seem to soak up oxidants and protect other molecules.

The paper links a protein's shape to how well it can act as a shield. Folded structures expose different surfaces, and those surfaces decide the reaction. Viewing proteins as defenders, not just victims, changes how stress damage is framed. It could guide design of protein-based protectors for medicine and food.
plos-pone-0009071:
Siu-Hong Chan and co-authors worked out what a stomach bacterium's DNA scissors need to run, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Helicobacter pylori infects the stomach and raises gastric cancer risk. It is also rich in restriction enzymes, tools that cut DNA at set spots. One of them, HpyAV, was new to science.

The team made and purified the enzyme in the lab. They then tested which helper chemicals, or cofactors, it requires. Some restriction enzymes need metal ions or energy molecules to cut. Pinning down HpyAV's needs adds a tool to the molecular biology kit.
plos-pone-0009171:
Panagiotis Alexiou and co-authors launched a web server that guesses microRNA jobs from gene data, in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs are small molecules that tune the activity of many genes at once. When they go wrong, development and health can suffer in many ways. Gene studies produce long lists of changed genes, but not the drivers behind them.

The DIANA-mirExTra server takes a researcher's gene data as its input. It works backward to the microRNAs most likely driving the changes seen. Anyone can run it in a web browser, with no special software needed. Tools like this connect raw gene lists to testable biology very fast.
plos-pone-0009271:
Simon Tobin, Nicolas Bisson, and Simon Grondin published this timing study in PLOS ONE in 2010. People judge time differently when watching the clock versus remembering afterward. Most lab studies used short intervals and artificial tasks. This study took a more natural route with long durations.

The team studied gamers playing video games in a natural setting. Players judged how long sessions lasted, both while playing and from memory. Comparing the two kinds of judgment in a real activity tests timing theories fairly. The ecological approach shows whether lab findings survive contact with everyday life.
plos-pone-0009371:
Elisabeta Vergu, Henri Busson, and Pauline Ezanno published this epidemic modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most epidemic models assume people stay infectious for an exponentially distributed time. That assumption is convenient but rarely realistic. In a single population, it was already known to distort predictions.

The authors tested the assumption in a metapopulation model, where linked towns host one epidemic. They varied the distribution of the infectious period while keeping its average fixed. The shape of that distribution changed how the epidemic spread between towns. Modelers who ignore it may misjudge both timing and reach of an outbreak.
plos-pone-0009471:
Harald Biessmann and colleagues studied smell in the malaria mosquito in PLOS ONE in 2010. Female Anopheles gambiae mosquitoes find people by scent and spread malaria when they bite. Proteins in their antennae first catch scent molecules from the air. One such protein is named AgamOBP1. The team tested what scent it binds best.

The protein proved to be the mosquito's detector for indole, a scent given off by humans. Blocking that detector could blunt the insect's hunt for people. The work pinpoints a single link in a chain that ends in a bite. It offers a target for new ways to keep mosquitoes away.
plos-pone-0009571:
Masahiko Morita, Shigemitsu Morokami, and Hiromi Morita studied how the brain joins object traits in PLOS ONE in 2010. The visual system handles shape, color, and motion in separate brain areas. Yet we see one whole object, not loose traits. The puzzle of how traits are bound is a classic one. The team tested memory and recognition using pairs of traits.

Their results show how pairs of attributes are stored and recalled together. That pairing seems to be a basic unit of visual memory. The work gives a clean handle on the binding problem. It shows the brain files objects as small bundles of traits, not as single pictures.
plos-pone-0009671:
Guy Caljon and co-authors identified a blood thinning protein in tsetse fly saliva in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tsetse flies feed on blood and spread sleeping sickness. To keep blood flowing while they feed, their saliva blocks clotting. The team isolated a salivary protein that stops human platelets from clumping. Platelet clumping is an early step in forming a clot.

The protein acts in two ways at once against platelet aggregation. A natural double action blocker is a prized lead for drug design. New clot preventing drugs are still needed for heart disease and stroke. The study shows how a pest's feeding trick can point medicine toward fresh chemistry.
plos-pone-0009871:
Some people in malaria regions resist severe illness better than others. Charlotte Joos and colleagues looked for a blood test signal that matches that protection. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Clinical protection from falciparum malaria correlated with neutrophil respiratory bursts. Neutrophils are front-line white blood cells, and a respiratory burst is their chemical attack on germs. The bursts were triggered by merozoites, the parasite stage that invades red blood cells. The merozoites were opsonized, coated with human serum antibodies that mark targets. A correlate like this can guide vaccine trials.
plos-pone-0009971:
Mood and blood sugar travel together more often than chance explains. Vanessa Bouwman and colleagues measured that link in everyday Dutch adults. Their study, part of the New Hoorn Study, appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The New Hoorn Study follows adults in the town of Hoorn.

Depression and anxiety were weighed against glucose metabolism, how the body handles sugar. The sample was the general population, not clinic patients. Links in the general public matter because most cases never reach specialists. The results help doctors watch mood and metabolism as one picture.
plos-pone-0010071:
Morgan Langille and Jonathan Eisen proposed a new way to share science data in 2010. Their PLOS ONE article introduced BioTorrents, a file sharing service built for researchers. Datasets keep growing, and calls for open access keep rising. Standard transfer methods scale poorly, so big files can take very long to move.

BioTorrents borrows peer-to-peer sharing, where many computers each send part of a file. That design can move large datasets faster and with less strain on one server. The service aimed to make open science data practical to share at modern scale.
plos-pone-0010171:
The authors were Cristina Lanni, Lavinia Nardinocchi, Rosa Puca, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study linked an Alzheimer's protein to a cell survival kinase. The kinase, HIPK2, helps keep the guard protein p53 working normally. Healthy p53 decides whether a DNA-damaged cell lives, repairs itself, or dies, so its control matters greatly.

The team reported that beta amyloid, the protein that builds up in Alzheimer's, targets HIPK2. That attack leads to misfolded p53 and inappropriate cell survival. The chain offers one explanation for how amyloid quietly corrupts brain cell decisions.
plos-pone-0010271:
Daniele Fanelli asked whether publish-or-perish pressure bends science itself in a 2010 study. Academic competition forces scientists to produce publishable results at almost any cost. Papers reporting negative results are less likely to be published and cited. That reward system, Fanelli reasoned, might inflate positive findings unevenly across places with different career pressures.

Using data from United States states, he tested for empirical support. His PLOS ONE analysis linked stronger publish pressure to stronger bias in results. The finding matters for how universities judge researchers without corrupting the record. The paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010371:
Charlotte Labalette and colleagues asked whether a protein called FHL2 feeds gut tumors, in PLOS ONE in 2010. FHL2 moves between cell anchor points and the nucleus, passing signals as it goes. It had been found active in several human cancers. But proof that it actually helps tumors grow was thin. The team used mice carrying a mutation that makes intestinal tumors likely.

When those mice also lacked FHL2, they developed fewer gut tumors. Removing one protein slowed a cancer-prone system. That is stronger evidence than merely finding the protein in tumors. It marks FHL2 as a possible drug target in colon cancer. The study also shows how mouse genetics can test a suspect gene's guilt.
plos-pone-0010471:
Maurizio Chiriva-Internati and colleagues tested a vaccine against ovarian cancer in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. Their target was a protein called Sp17, normally found in sperm. Ovarian tumors make this protein at all stages, including after spread. That makes it an attractive flag for the immune system to attack. The team vaccinated mice and challenged them with the cancer.

The vaccine produced long-lasting protection in the mouse model. Durable defense is the hardest part of cancer vaccination to achieve. Ovarian cancer is often caught late, so a protective vaccine would be precious. Mouse protection is only an early step, with human trials far ahead. Still, the target choice and lasting effect make this study notable.
plos-pone-0010571:
Bakhtier Vasiev, Ariel Balter and Mark Chaplain modeled how the primitive streak forms in the chick embryo in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gastrulation builds the body plan of all higher animals. In it, thousands of cells divide, specialize, and migrate in coordination. In chick embryos, the process opens with a structure called the primitive streak. Through it, cells move to form the body's layers. The team built a mathematical model of its formation.

A good model must reproduce the streak's shape and timing from simple cell rules. Testing such rules in a model saves years of trial in embryos. Chick embryos are a classic, accessible system for this stage. The study blends math with developmental biology productively. It helps explain how order emerges from many moving cells.
plos-pone-0010671:
Bobette Dickerson and colleagues mapped northern fur seal populations with DNA, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fur seals breed on islands across the North Pacific. Adults return to the same island, even the same beach section, year after year.

The team read two kinds of DNA markers from seals across the range. Strong site loyalty had indeed split the seals into distinct genetic groups. Some groups differed sharply despite breeding fairly close together. Wildlife managers treat such groups separately for good reason: losing one beach's seals would erase unique genetic variety that wandering cannot quickly replace.
plos-pone-0010771:
Richard Berry and Michael Ibbotson built a full three-dimensional model of the honeybee neck, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A bee holds its head steady while its body banks and turns in flight. That steadiness takes a neck full of small muscles and joints, arranged in a space smaller than a pinhead.

Thin sections of the head-neck system were imaged, aligned, and rebuilt on a computer. The atlas names and places each muscle and moving part. Neuroscientists can now match nerve recordings to exact muscles. Engineers designing tiny flying robots face the same steering problem, and the bee's solution is now drawn in full.
plos-pone-0010871:
Pim Bongaerts, Cynthia Riginos, Tyrone Ridgway and co-authors published this coral study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Coral reefs hold huge variety, yet how new coral species arise there is poorly understood. The team studied a common brooding coral on the Great Barrier Reef and the algae that live inside it, which supply much of its food.

They sampled the coral across three neighboring habitats spanning a depth range of about thirty meters, at three reef locations. Genetic markers for both the coral and its algae showed lineages sorted by habitat rather than by place. Host and symbiont gene pools stayed distinct side by side, as if each habitat favored its own pairing. Bongaerts and colleagues present rare evidence that ecological differences can split reef populations, a possible first step toward new species.
plos-pone-0010971:
Harald Kellner and Micheline Vandenbol published this forest soil study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fungi are the main recyclers of tough plant material in forests, breaking down lignin, cellulose, and insect chitin, yet most soil surveys count fungal species rather than measuring what they are doing. The authors instead listened for working fungal genes.

They collected RNA, the working copies of genes, from the organic layer of a sugar maple forest in eastern North America. Plots had received either normal rainfall nitrogen or extra nitrogen fertilizer for years, which changed how much organic matter piled up. Kellner and Vandenbol amplified fungal gene transcripts for the enzymes that digest wood and chitin. Their approach measures decomposition in action, helping predict how nitrogen pollution will change forest carbon storage.
plos-pone-0011071:
Kellie Burnside, Annalisa Lembo, Melissa de los Reyes and co-authors published this staph study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Staphylococcus aureus injures tissue with toxins called hemolysins, which burst red blood cells. Screening a library of mutants with random gene disruptions, the authors searched for the switches that control how much toxin the bacterium makes.

Disruptions in seventy-two genes raised or lowered hemolysin output. Cutting a phosphatase called Stp1 reduced toxin production and lowered the toxin gene's activity, while cutting its partner kinase, Stk1, did the opposite and reshaped hundreds of other genes. Burnside and colleagues map a push-pull control pair at the center of staph virulence regulation. Targeting such switches could disarm the bacterium without killing it, an antivirulence strategy meant to slow resistance.
plos-pone-0011171:
Tsai, Chung, Zou and colleagues showed how tumors disarm a guard in PLOS ONE in 2010. A protein called FOXO3 normally helps suppress tumors. In a mouse tumor model, another protein tagged FOXO3 for destruction using the cell's waste labeling system, removing the guard from duty.

With the guard degraded, its tumor blocking function was lost. That reveals one way cancers clear obstacles to growth from inside the cell. Drugs that stop the tagging or save the guard could restore its protection. The study names both the tagger and the process as targets worth pursuing.
plos-pone-0011271:
Pal, Dolai, Yadav and colleagues studied a tropical parasite in PLOS ONE in 2010. The parasite causes leishmaniasis, spread by sand flies. At its infective stage, it must survive the oxidative burst of the immune cells that swallow it. An enzyme that destroys peroxides helps it withstand that attack.

That enzyme controlled how virulent the infective stage proved to be. Disarming it would leave the parasite exposed to the body's own defenses. It is thus a clear drug target for a neglected disease. The study ties one stress defense directly to the parasite's power to cause illness.
plos-pone-0011371:
Ge Li and co-authors traced in 2010 how an HIV protein borrows the cell's disposal machinery to help the virus copy itself. The viral protein Vpr has several jobs during infection, and one partner it needs is a human protein that normally guides damaged material to the cell's shredder, the proteasome. The team mapped how that partnership works.

They showed that Vpr reaches the proteasome through this human partner, and that the contact supports viral replication. Breaking the chain weakened the virus's ability to copy itself in their system. The finding exposes a borrowed crutch that HIV leans on. Drugs that block the handoff between viral and human protein could add a new angle of attack, distinct from current drugs that target the virus's own enzymes.
plos-pone-0011471:
Elizabeth Wilbanks and Marc Facciotti benchmarked in 2010 the computer programs that find protein binding peaks in genome data. A method called ChIP-seq locates where proteins grip DNA across the genome, but its raw data are noisy, and peak-calling programs disagree about where the true peaks are. Biologists needed to know which programs to trust, and for what kinds of binding.

The authors ran competing algorithms on data with known answers and scored their accuracy in a systematic head-to-head test. Performance varied with the shape of the binding signal, so no single program won everywhere. The benchmark gives labs a practical guide: match the caller to the protein and the question. For a technique used in thousands of studies, that guidance quietly improves the reliability of a large share of modern genetics.
plos-pone-0011571:
Isabelle Hesling and co-authors scanned the brains in 2010 of people with high-functioning autism as they listened to the melody of speech. Prosody, the tune, rhythm, and stress of language, carries emotion and intent that the words alone do not. People on the autism spectrum often miss those cues, and the team used fMRI to watch how their brains integrate prosodic information during listening.

This preliminary study maps where the neural handling of speech melody differs, pointing to circuits that fail to bind tune to meaning. A brain map of a specific social difficulty is more useful than a general claim about autism and language. It suggests therapies could train prosody directly, with the scan pattern as a measure of progress. Small and preliminary as it is, the study gives a diffuse complaint, missing the tone, a defined address in the brain.
plos-pone-0011671:
Stéphanie Devignot and co-authors profiled gene activity in severe dengue patients, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dengue shock syndrome is the life-threatening form of this mosquito-borne viral illness. Clinicians struggle to predict which patients will crash and to treat them in time, and the host responses driving the crash were poorly charted.

Using prospective patient samples, the team read genome-wide expression patterns tied to shock. Their profile highlights the innate immune system, the body's fast first defence, as a key player in severe disease. Those early immune signals may help doctors spot danger sooner and design better treatments.
plos-pone-0011771:
Bin Xia and co-authors found a nuclear protein moonlighting in cell movement, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein mDpy-30 is part of a complex that tags histones, the spools of DNA, inside the nucleus. A subset of it also sits at the trans-Golgi network, the cell's shipping hub, recruited by a local partner protein.

The team showed mDpy-30 and its interacting proteins modulate how cells adhere and migrate. A gene-packaging protein steering stickiness and travel was unexpected. The finding reveals how DNA-wrapping machinery can also direct the way whole cells move and cling.
plos-pone-0011971:
Chun-hui Chang, Joshua Berke, and Stephen Maren recorded in 2010 single neurons in rat brains as fear memories were unlearned at different times. Extinction training minutes after fear learning suppresses fear only briefly; by the next day the fear fully returns. Delayed extinction lasts better, and a division of the medial prefrontal cortex is thought to store that lasting calm.

Recording individual cells during immediate versus delayed extinction shows how prefrontal activity differs between the two schedules. The contrast helps explain why timing decides whether unlearning sticks. That question reaches beyond rats: exposure therapy for human fear and trauma also depends on when and how the brain is asked to relearn safety.
plos-pone-0012071:
Mathias Hegele and Herbert Heuer studied in 2010 how extra information changes the way younger and older adults adjust their movements. When the visual world is rotated, people adapt their reaching, and aging changes that process. Earlier work suggested age differences lie mainly in strategy: older adults rely differently on conscious corrections and explicit knowledge.

By varying the augmented information given during adaptation, the team tested how guidance interacts with age. Knowing whether added information helps, hinders, or simply shifts strategy matters for rehabilitation and for training older workers on new tools. Movement learning does not end at retirement, and instruction design should match how older brains adapt.
plos-pone-0012171:
Lucia Zacchi, Wade Schulz, and Dana Davis studied two gene-silencing enzymes in a fungal pathogen, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Candida albicans lives harmlessly in many people but can turn dangerous, and its ability to switch shape helps it infect tissue. Chemical tags on its DNA packaging proteins control traits like drug resistance and shape switching, and the enzymes studied here remove those tags.

Surprisingly, the two enzymes pushed shape change in opposite directions, one favoring a form the other opposed. That tug-of-war gives the fungus a dial for balancing its forms. Since these enzymes differ from human ones in key ways, they remain candidate targets for new antifungal drugs.
plos-pone-0012271:
Jonathan Houseley and David Tollervey showed that a supposed gene oddity can be a lab artifact, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trans-splicing joins two separately made RNA messages into one, a routine trick in simple organisms but long thought absent from animals like us. Computer searches of sequence databases had recently suggested it might be widespread in mammals after all, a claim with big implications if true.

The authors demonstrate that the enzyme used to copy RNA in the lab can itself stitch messages together, manufacturing the evidence. That single caution can dissolve a whole literature built on database artifacts. It is a model of how a careful methods check protects biology from chasing ghosts.
plos-pone-0012371:
Wei Bao, Fangfang Song, Xiangyang Li and colleagues measured a stress-response protein in the blood of people with type 2 diabetes, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The protein, heme oxygenase-1, protects cells from damage, and its blood levels rise in several long-term diseases. No one had checked whether it also rises in type 2 diabetes, a very common condition.

The team compared more than five hundred newly diagnosed patients with healthy controls and found clearly higher levels in the diabetes group. A raised level does not prove the protein causes diabetes; it may be the body's defense switching on. Still, the finding marks a possible blood sign for tracking the disease and its strain on the body.
plos-pone-0012471:
Heidi Chial, Peter Lenart and Yong Chen watched two cell trafficking proteins interact live on membranes, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. APPL1 and APPL2 help run Rab5, a manager of early cargo sorting inside cells, and they bind many receptors and signals. A curved region called the BAR domain lets such proteins hug membranes and meet partners.

Using FRET microscopy, which lights up when two tagged proteins come very close, the team directly saw APPL proteins interact through their BAR domains on cell membranes. Direct viewing beats indirect inference for fleeting contacts. The observations clarify how cargo sorting stations assemble, a process that fails in several diseases.
plos-pone-0012571:
Darren Plett, Gehan Safwat, Matthew Gilliham and colleagues engineered salt-tolerant rice, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Salt ruins farmland worldwide, and rice is especially salt-sensitive. A sodium transporter gene, AtHKT1;1, had already improved salt tolerance in the model plant Arabidopsis when switched on only in certain root cells, keeping sodium out of the shoots.

Moving the same cell-specific trick into rice improved its salinity tolerance too. Targeting one tissue beats flooding the whole plant with the transporter, which can backfire. The result is a practical recipe for breeding or engineering rice that yields on salty land, a growing need as irrigation salinizes fields.
plos-pone-0012671:
Tsvetanova, Klass, Salzman and co-authors searched the whole yeast proteome for proteins that bind RNA. RNA-protein links sit at the heart of how cells control genes after they are copied. Their 2010 study worked in baker's yeast, where the full set of proteins can be tested at once.

The search turned up RNA-binding proteins nobody had expected to do that job. Each surprise widens the map of gene control and hints at hidden roles for known proteins. A fuller map helps explain how yeast, and by extension other cells, fine-tune their genes.
plos-pone-0012771:
Renshaw, Montero-Melendez, Dalli and co-authors mapped the genes switched on when a calming signal engages its receptor. Inflammation must end cleanly, and pro-resolution signals guide that ending. One such signal, annexin A1, acts through a receptor called ALX.

Their 2010 study listed the downstream genes that this pairing turns on. Those genes form a program for winding inflammation down rather than letting it fade or flare. Drugs that copy this program could treat chronic inflammation without shutting the whole immune system down.  Gene lists from one receptor can be tested drug by drug.
plos-pone-0321671:
Diana Sofia Rosales-Gurmendi and her team built time-to-ill tools for a hard call in brain care. Some folk with mild mind loss slide to Alzheimer's, and some do not. The team used facts from five hundred sixty-four such folk in a big US study. Brain scans, mind tests, spine fluid marks, and a gene risk mark all fed the tools.

The best tool used all four streams of facts. It caught most true slides and cried wolf on few. Mind test scores weighed most, then fluid and scan marks. The team says clear tools that mix streams can flag high-risk folk in good time.
plos-pone-0331271:
Deiby T Culhe and colleagues measured two local goat types, Landim and Pafúri, kept at a research station in southern Mozambique. Their 2026 PLOS One study recorded body shape and size in about one hundred forty animals, hoping to spot clear differences that could guide breeding and conservation.

All Pafúri goats had a curved forehead profile, while Landim goats split between curved and flat. Landim animals tended toward longer horns, taller shoulders, and longer bodies, and Pafúri toward slightly wider chests. None of the gaps cleared the bar for statistical proof, though. The authors read the two herds as close cousins shaped by similar conditions.
plos-pone-0334571:
Clara Pujol-Fuentes and colleagues set out the protocol for a proof-of-concept trial comparing two treatments for stiff legs after stroke: botulinum toxin injections and dry needling. Spasticity, where muscles lock in contraction, limits walking and quality of life. Toxin injections are standard but can cause side effects, and nobody has compared the two treatments head to head at the level of the spinal cord.

Ninety patients in Canada, Belgium, and Spain, within a year of a first stroke, will receive either one toxin session or twelve weekly needling sessions, with assessors kept unaware of assignments. The trial checks feasibility and safety while exploring effects on muscle, function, quality of life, and cost. This paper is the plan, published before recruitment results.
plos-pone-0337671:
Emmanuel Otukpa and coauthors published a protocol in PLOS ONE for a scoping review on designing digital health tools with, rather than merely for, users in low-resource settings. Technically sound health apps fail at striking rates in poor settings, often because designers ignored users' environment, literacy, and beliefs. Participatory design methods promise fixes, but nobody has mapped their use across digital health, or the results.

The review will gather studies from 2015 onward that applied user-centered design or its cousins, human-centered design, co-design, and co-creation, to digital health innovations in constrained settings. It will chart which technologies and disease areas dominate, how deeply users were involved, and reported outcomes such as usability, satisfaction, adoption, and scalability. The authors distinguish genuine co-design, where users are partners, from lighter consultation. Their map should show funders and developers where participation is real and where it is decoration.
plos-pone-0338171:
Mohammad Saydul Aman leads a team of six testing a blood marker that might warn of complications after liver surgery, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The prospective study followed forty-two patients having part of the liver removed at a Bangladeshi center through 2021 and 2022. Blood was drawn on the first, third, and seventh days after surgery for procalcitonin, a marker that rises with serious infection, alongside standard white cell counts and C reactive protein.

Patients who developed complications, just over half the group, showed clearly higher procalcitonin on every measured day. The two standard markers, by contrast, did not separate the groups at all. A first day procalcitonin reading gave moderate power to flag trouble, balancing sensitivity and specificity at the best cutoff the authors found. In a setting with limited monitoring resources, one early blood test with real signal is a practical lead.
plos-pone-0340571:
Amanuale Zayede and colleagues pooled African studies of food handlers carrying antibiotic-resistant gut bacteria in their stool. These organisms can ride silently from hands to food. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis ran to a registered protocol. It gathered nine studies covering more than four thousand food handlers, published between 2012 and 2023. Each study was appraised with a standard quality tool.

About one food handler in four carried the resistant bacteria. That pooled figure hides wild variation between studies. These organisms shrug off frontline antibiotics. Their presence in people who prepare public food is a standing transmission risk. The authors argue for routine screening, hygiene enforcement, and surveillance in the food sector. Carriage should not be discovered only when outbreaks strike.
plos-pone-0342371:
Zainab Said Al-Hashimy and colleagues surveyed four hundred and twenty-four nurses working for Oman's health ministry about what they know and believe concerning antibiotics and drug resistance. Nurses give much of the hands-on care around these medicines, so their understanding shapes how safely the drugs are used. The survey was adapted from a standard European questionnaire on the topic.

Almost all nurses knew that overusing antibiotics causes harm, and most knew the drugs do not work on viruses, though fewer connected them correctly to the common cold. About three in five knew of Oman's national action plan on resistance. Many asked for more training on which drug fits which illness. The authors call for stronger teaching so nurses can act as frontline defenders against resistance.
plos-pone-0342871:
Twikirize and colleagues measured a common stomach infection among patients in Kampala, Uganda, in a 2026 study. The germ lives in the stomach and can drive ulcers and long-term pain, yet local data for people with gut symptoms were thin. More than three hundred fifty patients at the national referral hospital gave stool samples and answered questions about home life and past care.

Nearly nine in ten patients tested positive, a very high share. Infection was more likely in people supporting many dependents, in those treated for the same germ before, and in those with family history of the infection or ulcers. The authors suggest routine testing, or carefully guided treatment, deserves a place in local care.
plos-pone-0344971:
Usman Ali and colleagues benchmarked machine learning methods for forecasting wind power across four sites in different countries. Grid operators need these predictions to balance supply. The team cleaned outliers from each dataset, then compared gradient boosting, random forest, and support vector machines with three kernel styles, judging them on accuracy and average error.

Gradient boosting aced every site. Random forest matched it in three places but fell apart at the fourth, with errors ballooning. Among support vector variants, the simplest linear version quietly excelled everywhere, while fancier kernels lagged. The authors recommend the two winners as dependable choices across varied wind climates.
plos-pone-0346471:
Qiong Hong led a team of five authors fusing two kinds of images into one, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Infrared images reveal heat signatures but lack fine detail; visible images have detail but fail in darkness. Their network, DHAFGan, blends the two using dense connections and hybrid attention inside a generative adversarial design.

Hong's network aims for clean blends that keep heat cues and surface detail together. Fused images serve surveillance, night driving, and search and rescue, where missing a warm body in a dark scene can be fatal. Generative adversarial training pushes the output toward natural-looking results that human watchers can read quickly. The study adds a tested architecture to a competitive corner of image processing.
plos-pone-0346971:
Jessica-Lynn A. Walsh and colleagues explored natural supports, the everyday web of neighbours, volunteers, and local champions who look out for one another, in an urban Canadian community. Working with a community partnership, they interviewed local champions about what helps residents connect and what gets in the way, then built a grounded theory from the answers.

Their theory describes communities moving from disconnected to naturally supportive when three ingredients combine: connectors who link people, local assets to build on, and concrete action. Scarce meeting space and trouble keeping volunteers were the main obstacles. The authors urge planners to invest deliberately in these connective tissues of neighbourhood life.
plos-pone-0347871:
Elena Vieth and Lisa von Stockhausen ran two strict trials on breath work and bias. Some claim that calm breath drills sharpen mind control. Sharp control should help folk hold back snap, biased calls. Each trial set breath drills next to muscle rest drills and plain audio plays. Timed screen tasks then gauged biased acts.

The drills did the flip of the claim. Breath work made bias weigh more in snap calls. It did so by heightening the clash when a case broke the mold. Muscle rest drills, in turn, eased biased calls. The team says forces past mind control are at play here.
plos-pone-0348071:
Peiran Chen and a large team used records from more than seventy-two thousand Chinese mothers to ask how blood haemoglobin during pregnancy relates to giving birth too early. Too little haemoglobin means anaemia; too much can signal other trouble, and earlier studies disagreed. The team separated early births that start on their own from those induced by doctors, and followed haemoglobin patterns across all three trimesters.

The overall early birth rate sat near seven percent. Against a standard cut-off late in pregnancy, the risk curve bent into an L shape for spontaneous early birth, falling as haemoglobin rose from low levels. A U shape appeared for other comparisons, warning at both extremes. The authors say timing and subtype matter: a single haemoglobin reading, read without its trimester or the kind of early birth feared, can mislead antenatal care.
plos-pone-0348171:
Jinrong Zhao and colleagues studied the microbes living inside the roots of Arnebia euchroma, a medicinal plant prized for red pigments that fight inflammation. The team compared plants aged one to four years grown in one Chinese county, cataloguing the fungi and bacteria within the tissue and measuring eight pigment-related compounds in the same roots.

Hundreds of microbial species turned up, and the diversity of both fungi and bacteria peaked at a particular growth stage rather than rising steadily. Linking the inner microbial community to pigment levels tests whether helpful microbes boost the plant's medicine. For growers, knowing the best harvest age, and possibly which microbes to encourage, could raise the quality of this traditional remedy.
plos-pone-0348271:
Yaru Yang and co-workers simulate a wind turbine with two rotors instead of one, linked through a special gearbox. Twin rotors could pull more power from the wind, but their behavior under stress needs checking. Their 2026 study runs fluid and structure computer models for the new design and a matching single-rotor turbine across varied wind conditions.

The twin-rotor design cleared its wake faster, letting air recover sooner behind it. Peak stress in its blades over time also dropped by a large share. Those gains came despite a more complex build. The results give designers firmer ground for tuning control and structure before such turbines face real weather at sea or on land.
plos-pone-0348371:
Sharper screens show faces in finer detail, and Koji Mizukoshi and colleagues asked whether that detail changes how attractive a face looks. Their 2026 PLOS One study photographed one hundred eighty Japanese women with an 8K camera and showed the portraits on an 8K display.

Each face appeared twice: once at full resolution and once pixelated down, with viewers rating both on a six-point scale without knowing the trick. High-resolution versions earned slightly higher attractiveness ratings. The effect was small but consistent in the statistical model. As displays push toward the limit of human vision, the authors note, image quality itself becomes part of beauty judgment.
plos-pone-0348571:
Dong-Jun Lee, Tae-Ho Lee, and Taesoo Kwon presented AgrOmicSo in 2026, a friendly front end for heavy genome data analysis. Sequencing analysis needs big servers, but their command line interfaces shut out many biologists who think in menus, not code.

The software splits into a local graphical client and a server engine holding tools for quality checks, mapping, variant calling, and annotation. Three variant calling methods are built in. One step mode runs whole pipelines for batches; step by step mode exposes each stage. Lowering the interface barrier may matter as much to farm genomics as any single algorithm.
plos-pone-0348871:
Rana Ahmed, Motaz Amer, and Lina Ismail redesigned how yarn tension is controlled on winding machines at an Egyptian cotton producer. The work links a factory detail to the huge water footprint of dyeing cloth. Uneven tension causes defects and forces dyehouses to use more water and chemicals to fix uneven colour. Their controller, driven by a digital signal chip, reacts to events as they happen and holds tension steady across fine, medium, and thick yarns.

Trials showed tension swings shrank sharply, yarn defects fell by about a third, and machines ran more than a quarter faster without quality loss. The striking result sat downstream: dyeing water use dropped by roughly two thirds, chemical demand fell with it, and energy use eased by about a fifth. The authors pitch the method to producers in countries where water and money are both scarce.
plos-pone-0348971:
Angela Nana Esi Ackon, Hubert Amu, and Martin Amogre Ayanore asked insured patients with high blood pressure in Ghana why they still pay out of pocket. Ghana's national insurance scheme is meant to shield patients from such costs, yet nearly four hundred patients at a referral hospital in Hohoe described paying anyway during twenty twenty-two. Almost everyone reported some payment, and almost all of it happened at the pharmacy counter for drugs.

About three in ten struggled to find the money. Difficulty tracked with having borrowed for health costs before, with payments so burdensome that they changed hospital attendance, and with keeping an alternative way of treating the condition on the side. The authors warn that insurance on paper is not protection in practice, and that the gap threatens global goals for controlling chronic disease.
plos-pone-0349171:
Hanning Xu and co-authors sifted huge gene datasets for the markers that make liver cancer tied to hepatitis B behave like stem cells, able to regrow and resist treatment. Combining single-cell and bulk data, they scored cell groups for stem-like character and followed cells along a simulated timeline to find the group where that character concentrates.

Attention landed on an unexpected quarter, a subset of the blood-vessel lining cells inside tumours. Cross-checking datasets yielded fifty-two shared genes, and a machine learning pass elevated two of them into a diagnostic pair that performed well in independent patient groups. High levels of one and low levels of the other spelled poorer survival, and both tied into cell stress and growth pathways. The authors offer the pair as candidate biomarkers needing wet-lab confirmation.
plos-pone-0349371:
Xiaoyu Huang and colleagues traced how losing estrogen after menopause weakens the pelvic floor muscles that hold women's organs in place. In rats whose ovaries were removed, both fast and slow muscle fibres in the pelvic floor shrank, and a key estrogen sensor faded with them. Muscle precursor cells deprived of estrogen grew poorly, divided less, formed fibres badly, and died more often, while their energy factories faltered.

The team mapped the chain: less estrogen sensor meant less of a glucose gate protein and its traffic controller, so the gate never reached the cell surface and sugar entry failed. Switching the sensor back on, or forcing extra gate protein, rescued the cells. The authors name this pathway as a possible drug target for pelvic floor disorders.
plos-pone-0349471:
Avi Kumar Badhon led a team of six authors reporting a new plant disease in Bangladesh, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. They found the fungus Corynespora cassiicola infecting chia plants, the first time this pairing has been recorded in the country. Chia is a growing crop, so an early warning has real value for farmers.

Badhon and his colleagues confirmed the fungus and tested how well selected fungicides work against it. Knowing which products still control the pathogen lets growers act before the disease spreads to nearby fields. Reports of first occurrence may look minor, but they are how plant health systems catch new threats while control is still cheap and possible.
plos-pone-0349571:
Anja Karlstaedt and co-authors profiled the heart metabolism of Egyptian fruit bats in 2026. Flight is hugely demanding, and bat hearts sustain it without the damage such loads cause in other mammals, a puzzle with medical interest.

Bat and mouse heart tissue were compared by two chemical profiling methods, then a computer model of heart metabolism estimated pathway activity. Bat hearts held little stored sugar fuel and leaned on fat burning, with strong activity in energy making pathways and low breakdown of amino acids. The pattern suggests bats rewire heart fuel use for flight, a contrast that may inspire heart research.
plos-pone-0349671:
Arun Kumar and colleagues propose a method to tame signal peaks in a wireless technique planned for future mobile networks. The technique stacks several users' signals at different power levels on the same channel, which boosts capacity but creates spiky waveforms that strain amplifiers and garble decoding. Older smoothing methods treat the whole signal the same way and miss how users interfere with each other.

Their method first models the combined waveform as a graph, capturing how signal parts connect, then reshapes peaks in a way guided by that structure. The goal is lower peaks without wrecking the delicate power differences that let receivers separate users. Cleaner signals mean more efficient transmitters and fewer errors in crowded networks.
plos-pone-0349871:
Sultan Almuntashiri and colleagues reanalysed public gene and outcome data from one hundred and forty four intensive care patients with sepsis from lung infection. Twenty patients picked up a new infection inside intensive care. Death within twenty eight days and admission blood gene patterns were compared between those who did and did not gain a second infection, split by where pneumonia began.

Patients whose pneumonia began in the community and who gained a second infection died at far higher rates, near forty six versus eighteen percent, on the edge of statistical certainty. Their blood showed lowered activity of a key immune receptor gene. Early immune dulling may flag who needs extra infection guarding, pending larger proof.
plos-pone-0350071:
Guoqiang Sun and co-authors built a forecasting model for power generation and load in 2026. Grid operators must predict demand closely to keep supply steady, yet power data has long patterns that simple recurrent networks lose, and big attention models cost too much.

Their model stacks gated memory layers with attention placed inside the stack, letting it stress the time steps that matter without ballooning in size. On three real energy data sets it beat ten rival models, cutting errors sharply against plain recurrent networks. It matched leading attention models on accuracy while training faster, a practical gain for daily grid planning.
plos-pone-0350271:
Brenna Ellison and co-authors surveyed American consumers in 2026 about government rules for ultra-processed foods. Six possible policies were tested, from defining the category to taxing it, as debate over such foods heats up.

Nearly a thousand adults answered. Information policies, a clear definition and dietary guidance, won the most support, while a tax won the least. Views split by beliefs about the foods, self rated knowledge, and personal traits. The pattern tells policymakers that the public will accept being informed and protected in schools long before it accepts paying more at the till.
plos-pone-0350571: Chang and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on hard-to-treat cervical cancer. The cancer had come back or spread to other parts of the body. The team tested the safety and effect of pairing immune checkpoint inhibitors with a class of drugs called TKIs. All patients carried a gene change named PIK3CA. Pairing drug types is a common hope when single drugs stop working.
plos-pone-0350671:
Dongwook Kim and colleagues reviewed emergency patients whose only complaint was spinning or dizziness, with no other clear stroke signs. A hidden stroke in the back of the brain can still be the cause, so doctors checked brain scans for fresh damage. Records covered four straight years at one emergency service, sorted by blood thinning and clot preventing drug use.

Patients fell into groups taking no such drugs, taking platelet drugs like aspirin, or taking stronger blood thinners. Finer sorting split aspirin alone, a second platelet drug alone, and both together. The study weighs whether prior drug use links with more or fewer hidden strokes once other illnesses are taken into account. For front line care, even isolated dizziness deserves careful stroke checks.
plos-pone-0350771:
Jan Turra and colleagues measure what a charcoal filter does to stress hormones during a specialized liver cancer treatment that floods the liver with chemotherapy while shielding the rest of the body. Blood from the liver is cleaned outside the body before returning, and patients often become unstable during the process. In fifteen procedures, blood was sampled at set points before and after the filter to track hormone levels and doses given.

The filter stripped out nearly all of one key stress hormone, noradrenaline, even as doctors kept infusing it at high doses to hold blood pressure. Two sister hormones passed through barely touched. After the circuit stopped, hormone levels rebounded sharply. Turra and colleagues say teams must plan dosing around this hidden drain.
plos-pone-0350971:
Yunnuo Zhu and colleagues used a long running United States military cohort to test whether how service members rate their own health forecasts later readiness. More than fifty thousand active duty members answered health and habit surveys, then were tracked three to five years later for care use, lost work days, weight, satisfaction, and staying in service.

Self rated physical and mental health predicted all five readiness outcomes, even after habits like smoking and poor sleep were counted. Members in the top band for physical health kept healthier weight, lost fewer days, used less care, and stayed longer. Low scores warned of the reverse. A short survey, the work suggests, can flag readiness risk early.
plos-pone-0351171:
Max Carlos Ramírez-Soto and four colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It follows pneumonia in Peru through health records. The authors compare how often pneumonia occurred, how often it sent people to hospital, and how often it killed. The comparison spans the years before COVID-19 and the pandemic years.

During the pandemic, masks, distancing, and overwhelmed hospitals all changed how pneumonia appeared in statistics. Separating real change from disrupted counting is the hard part of such comparisons. Health authorities in Peru, and researchers of pandemic side effects on other diseases, are the readers who need this careful before-and-during picture.
plos-pone-0351471:
Jinyang Dong and co-authors study a plant called cocklebur across China in this 2026 paper. Cocklebur is both a useful medicinal plant and an aggressive invader, so knowing where it will thrive matters. The team combined computer models of suitable habitat with analysis of the bacteria living around the plant's roots.

Their models show that human activity, elevation, and slope shape where cocklebur grows today, and that warmer future climates could expand its suitable habitat considerably. High-risk zones cluster in provinces such as Yunnan, Guangdong, and Inner Mongolia. Around its roots, bacteria tied to nitrogen cycling dominate, and these microbes seem to help the plant cope with stress and settle into disturbed ground. The authors argue that managing such two-sided species means watching both the climate and the microbes.
plos-pone-0351571:
Yi Chen, Xing Wang, and Wang Shaohua published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on using artificial intelligence to repair images of damaged cultural heritage objects. Their system, called YOLO-WSR, first detects damaged areas in a photograph, then restores them with a diffusion model guided by the object's structure and fine wavelet details. A quality-check module scores each restored image and feeds the result back so the output can be refined again.

On several public datasets, the combined system beat existing approaches at finding damage and produced restorations that scored better on standard image-quality measures. Removing individual parts of the system in turn showed that each piece contributed to the gains. The authors frame the method as practical support for digital preservation work: spotting damage accurately, restoring images automatically, and keeping visual records of fragile heritage objects in usable shape.
plos-pone-0351671:
Hafeez Ahmad and colleagues shrank the brain needed to sort fashion photos into their ten clothing classes, a standard test problem for image software. Top models for the task carry tens of millions of settings and need graphics processors, shutting out cheap devices. Their design pairs a small convolutional network with a lean form of self-attention, keeping under half a million settings in total.

The small model trained on an ordinary processor and sorted the Fashion-MNIST benchmark with accuracy a little above ninety-one percent. The team also added several ways to picture where the model looks when it decides, so users can audit its attention. For shops and apps running on phones or shop-floor hardware, the message is that respectable image sorting no longer requires a data center, and the reasoning can be shown, not just trusted.
plos-pone-0351971:
Anni Byman and colleagues studied five hundred seventeen Finnish primary school children, asking how the social weather of a classroom connects with movement, sitting, and grades. Wrist- and hip-worn motion trackers measured activity during school hours, children rated their peer relations, and grade averages came from school records. The team analyzed girls and boys separately, since their school days can differ.

Among girls, warmer peer relations went with less vigorous in-school activity, and more sitting went with higher grades. Among boys, more vigorous activity went with higher grades. Formal tests could not confirm the boy-girl split, so the authors treat the patterns as leads, not law. Still, the study argues that adding activity to the school day works through friendship and peer norms, not around them.
plos-pone-0352171:
Farah Seedat and seven co-authors set out this 2026 PLOS One protocol. It will check a set of survey tools that map how well migrants fit into a country's health system. The three tools list migrant health data sources, policies, and service provision. Tunisia is the test case. Forty to fifty national experts will each complete one tool matched to their skills.

As a protocol, the paper describes the plan, not results. Experts will rate each item for relevance and clarity. A follow-up survey will judge the tools as a whole. Focus groups will add depth. The team will measure how much the raters agree. They will also study the themes in the group talks. The aim is to confirm the tools capture what they claim. Only then should other countries adopt them.
plos-pone-0352671:
Mwalukunga, Moshi, and Kibusi asked young women students in Tanzania how they prefer to get sexual health information and care in a 2026 study. Early sex, limited contraception, and infection risk affect many students, while cultural and policy limits restrict services. Interviews explored what channels and settings young women would actually trust and use.

Knowing preferences matters because services that feel unsafe or judgmental go unused, whatever their quality. Young women can describe which sources feel private, accurate, and reachable from campus life. Their answers can guide colleges and health programs to offer information in forms students will accept, helping prevent infection and unplanned pregnancy.
plos-pone-0352771:
Aaron Eisen and four colleagues published this 2026 PLOS One study on how hardships faced early in life change the health effects of living near greenery. Their starting idea was that people raised with more stress may react more strongly to their surroundings, for better or worse. They tested this using health records from a group of nursing students.

Greenness around each student's home showed no simple straight-line link to fasting blood sugar. Instead, students with either heavy or light early-life stress had lower blood sugar when they lived in greener areas, while those in the middle showed no link at all. The authors argue that adding green space in poorer neighborhoods could lower diabetes risk for the people most shaped by early stress.
plos-pone-0352871:
Zepeng Chen and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One single-cell study of how colon tumors handle tryptophan, an amino acid whose breakdown can dampen immune attack. Working from single-cell sequencing data, the team scored metabolic activity cell by cell using several algorithms, then applied four machine learning methods to pinpoint the genes most consistently tied to that activity.

Immune cells called macrophages and gut-lining Paneth cells showed the highest tryptophan activity. Two genes, CYP1A1 and its partner regulator AHR, stood out as raised in the cancer and were selected by every algorithm, marking them as consensus findings. The authors propose both as candidate markers and treatment targets, while noting the analysis is computational and awaits experimental tests.
plos-pone-0353071:
Monowar Hossain and Mohammed Aman Ullah build a mathematical model of rotavirus spread in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Rotavirus causes severe diarrhoea that still kills many children under five, mostly in poorer countries. Their model sorts people into susceptible, vaccinated, infected, and recovered groups, using a fractional form of calculus that lets past states keep influencing the present.

They work out when the disease dies out and when it settles in, and derive a vaccination threshold number that separates the two fates. Approximate solutions come from a Laplace-based decomposition technique, checked for stability and accuracy. Models of this kind help officials judge how much vaccination coverage a community needs.
plos-pone-0353171:
Abdul Karim and three colleagues explore how first-year university students experienced learning persuasive essay writing online, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. During the pandemic the university taught its English foundation course through its own platform, with sequenced materials guiding students through outlining, drafting, editing, and revising. Eight students described the experience in interviews and questionnaires, and the team interpreted their accounts using phenomenological analysis.

Students said the step-by-step structure kept them engaged rather than lost. Writing collaboratively and giving each other feedback guided by a rubric stood out as especially meaningful. The authors draw a practical lesson for online teaching: sequence the work clearly, build in peer review, and students will lean into a skill many find intimidating.
plos-pone-0353271:
Kun Zhang and five colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One imaging study on telling harmless lung nodules from cancerous ones without surgery. Their method uses a tracer scan taken at two time points, producing simple uptake ratios for each nodule. Records from more than one hundred thirty patients, most with malignant nodules, were used to build and test machine learning classifiers on those ratios plus clinical variables.

Cancerous nodules took up more tracer early and held onto less of it over time. A blood tumor marker and one retention measure independently predicted malignancy. The best machine learning model separated the groups almost perfectly on its training data, with others close behind. The authors pitch the approach as an interpretable option for hospitals where advanced image analysis is unavailable, though outside validation is still needed.
plos-pone-0353571:
Wen Yu and Robert Langer report this 2026 PLOS One study on turning sandwich composite panels into portable outdoor tabletops that factories can mass-produce. Such panels, a light core bonded between stiff outer skins, are common in aircraft and transport but rare in consumer furniture. The authors built five panel designs that differed in core material, surface finish, edge sealing, and fasteners.

Testing the designs against customer needs and product standards showed that no single property decided success. What mattered was how materials, surface durability, moisture-proof edges, fasteners, and cost worked together. Blind rivets proved a practical fastening choice, and finishes behaved differently depending on the surface beneath them. The authors map out design routes that could bring these panels to the mass market.
plos-pone-0353671: Olorunmoteni and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on teen sleep health in Africa. As a scoping review, it maps patterns of sleep, what drives them, and what outcomes they link to. Teens need much sleep, yet school, work, and screens cut it short. A map of African evidence helps health planners see where research exists and where whole regions are missing.
plos-pone-0353871:
Vinh and Yen, in a 2026 study in Danang, Vietnam, build a phone app that screens high school students for color vision deficiency and then advises them on study and career choices. Weak color vision can quietly steer students away from fields where it matters, and paper tests are slow and rarely linked to guidance. Five hundred twenty-seven students took part.

The app uses a digital version of the classic dot-plate test. It agreed closely with the standard paper test, and it picked out seventeen students with some form of color deficiency, including rare complete color blindness. Students rated the app much the same whether or not they had the deficiency, and the feedback questionnaire held together well. The authors present the tool as a cheap, scalable way for schools, including poor ones, to screen early and counsel honestly about careers where color matters.
plos-pone-0353971:
Lina Wang and colleagues build in 2026 a new way to map disease clusters. Colour maps first show the broad pattern on a map. A flexible scan then tests which clusters are not due to chance. A dot map next shows detail inside the top cluster. That last step adjusts for how people are spread out.

Trials used made up data and real measles cases. The joined method found clusters more truly than single steps did. It also located hot cores inside the clusters. Each stage checks the stage before it. The flow moves from search to proof to fine detail. Health teams could aim control work with more care.
plos-pone-0354271:
Kim and Shin, in a 2026 study, use a decade of national health insurance claims to show how long-term care hospitals in South Korea have become places where many older people die. Patient numbers rose, and deaths involving these hospitals climbed sharply. The authors trace yearly trends and each person's path from entry to death.

New patients arrived in their early eighties, most often women, and people on medical aid or with disabilities were overrepresented. After admission, stays varied hugely: many died within a month, while more than a fifth stayed a year or longer. Most who died did so inside the hospital. The final phase of life often shifted from slow frailty to sudden infection, such as pneumonia or sepsis. The authors argue policy should build in palliative care, advance planning, and staff training to match that role.
plos-pone-0354371:
Houn Kim and co-authors surveyed parent runners to learn whether pushing a stroller changes injury risk. Stroller running keeps new parents active, but its effect on overuse injuries was unstudied. Their 2026 survey recruited parents online and compared two hundred stroller runners with a smaller group who ran without one.

Overuse injuries were reported by about three in ten non-stroller runners, against about two in ten stroller runners. Per distance run, the stroller group's injury rate was less than half the control rate. Injury types looked similar in both groups, with heel pain notably common in each. Kim and colleagues conclude stroller running appears safe and may help parents sustain activity in early parenthood.
plos-pone-0354471:
Deborah Ekusai-Sebatta and co-authors review in 2026 how human gene data are shared in joint research that involves lower income countries. Funders now often require sharing plans, yet sharing raises hard questions about consent, control, and fairness. Their review screened thousands of reports and kept a small set that dealt directly with practice on the ground.

Consent, misuse fears, unequal benefit, stigma, and unclear ownership all appeared as concerns. Mistrust and over strict rules slowed sharing. Trust and consent processes that fit local culture stood out as vital. The authors call for balance between open science and protecting the people whose data are shared.
plos-pone-0354671:
Heba H Mostafa and colleagues tested whether a commercial automated HPV test can find viral DNA floating in the blood of patients with HPV-driven disease. Such a test could be a shortcut for detecting and monitoring these cancers. Their 2026 pilot study ran the test on blood from cervical and throat cancer patients. It then re-tested the same samples with a custom, more sensitive three-primer laboratory assay.

The commercial test caught the virus in advanced cervical cancers and most throat cancers. It missed early disease and precancer entirely. The custom assay proved sharper, finding low viral levels in some early cases. Its sporadic signals in treated, disease-free patients complicate interpretation, though. The work maps both the promise and the current sensitivity ceiling of blood-based HPV monitoring.
plos-pone-0354871:
Sayaka Sato and co-authors test in 2026 whether gender fair wording in French changes how teenagers picture jobs typed as male or female. French uses a masculine form as the default for mixed groups, and paired forms name both genders. Two preregistered experiments asked adolescents to rate jobs described in either form for warmth, skill, and whether they could belong there.

Paired forms did not make views more inclusive among teenagers, unlike earlier adult findings. The job's own gender stereotype drove representation most, especially for girls, and age and gender shaped the effects. Language reform alone may not shift career pictures at this age, the authors suggest.
plos-pone-0354971:
Elizabeth Grylls and colleagues evaluate in 2026 a high performance training programme for sports officials run by a sport institute in Australia's Northern Territory. Five officials and their mentors gave measures before and after, covering confidence, resilience, how demands were judged, preparation, and assertiveness. Written reflections added depth to the numbers, and changes were checked for reliability rather than chance.

Three of the five officials showed reliable gains in confidence and resilience, with varied shifts in narrower skills such as decision making and communication. Interview material backed the positive picture. With such a small group, the authors present the work as insight into how elite officials grow, not proof for all.
plos-pone-0355371: Pointon and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a trial called ACTIVATE, aimed at medical students. The program under test is Thumos, a talking-therapy course based on cognitive-behavioral methods. The trial will assign students at random to judge whether it helps. Medical training is stressful, and a tested program could be offered before distress turns into illness.
plos-pone-0355471:
Cheng-Ru Wu, Ming-Han Chiang, Bao-Hui Huang, Hung-Lung Lin, and Yanran Huang published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies how tourists who meet Zhangjiajie online feel about the place, a Chinese scenic area famous for its towering stone pillars. The tools are text mining of online writing and a combined LDA-FDEMATEL analysis.

Online reviews and posts carry visitors' feelings in their own words, and text mining turns thousands of them into patterns. Understanding what moves online tourists helps scenic areas design for people who experience the place partly through screens. Tourism managers and researchers of digital travel behavior share the audience.
plos-pone-0356071: Fora and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how partners' faces move in step. Facial synchrony means two people's expressions rise and fall together during interaction. The team described this matching across several dimensions at once. They tested whether the patterns can reveal the quality of a relationship. If faces betray how well two people connect, such measures could aid therapy and social research.
plos-pone-0356171:
Li Quan Warrick Tan, James Barkell, and Donna O'Connor map the research on how youth sport coaches learn their craft, in this 2026 scoping review. Coaching children in participation-focused sport, as opposed to elite pathways, has drawn growing interest, yet little is known about how those coaches actually develop. Searching sports and education databases for empirical studies since 2010, the team found just eleven articles that fit, and charted them by focus, setting, and findings.

Most studies tested coach education programs about autonomy-supportive coaching in team sports, and nearly all came from Western countries. Four themes organized the evidence: what enables coach learning, what blocks it, what coaches gain, and what determines whether training changes their practice. Across four public livestock datasets, the model posted strong accuracy scores. It stayed efficient enough for farm deployment. It beat the usual trade-off between precision and speed. For luminal cancers, which feed on hormones, doctors want to know before surgery whether chemotherapy will erase the tumor. Complete disappearance is the outcome most tied to survival. The tool is a scoring chart, a nomogram, built partly on a seventy gene test. The team checked it on fifteen hundred patients treated at a Seoul hospital between 2008 and 2021.

Bibhuti Bhusan Mishra, K. Abhimanyu Kumar Patro, and Sudhakar Das published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE proposing a new way to encrypt several images at once. Most schemes handle either gray or color pictures, not a mix, which limits real-world use. Their method, ECPD-MIE, first joins multiple images of any size into one composite. It then scrambles and diffuses the pixel values using chaotic maps, with keys seeded from a hash of the image itself.

An entropy control step adjusts the diffusion so randomness stays high across both gray levels and color channels. In the authors' tests, encrypted images showed flat histograms, almost no correlation between neighboring pixels, and entropy close to the ideal value. Standard attack measures also looked strong, and the outputs passed national randomness tests. The scheme aims at secure image sharing where mixed gray and color files must travel together under one lock.
