Hudson Tuttle set the faith in a scheme in Arcana of Spiritualism, his hand book of 1871. Tuttle was a farm lad of Ohio who claimed seer gifts from youth. He and his wife built a press and school for the faith. Here he lays out its whole creed: God, souls, spheres past death, and the laws that rule growth from sphere to sphere.

The tone is clear, firm, and fit for class use. Groups in the United States used it as their school text for years. It is the faith set in order by a true hand.
un-ga-res-a-69-71: Telling the world about disarmament is the task of a UN programme backed in Resolution A/69/71, from the Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The work began in 1982 as the World Disarmament Campaign, at the second special session on disarmament. In 1992 it took a new name, the United Nations Disarmament Information Programme, and its trust fund was renamed with it. The Secretary-General is praised for spreading word on arms control as widely as thin funds allow.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/71, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, reviews the United Nations Disarmament Information Programme. It commends the Disarmament Yearbook for 2012 and 2013 and its online editions. It welcomes continued updating of the disarmament website. It invites contributions to the Voluntary Trust Fund that supports the programme. It asks the Secretary-General to report again to the seventy-first session.
un-sc-res-1171:
Sierra Leone reached the Council's table and drew Resolution 1171, adopted on 5 June 1998. The elected government was back in power after the junta fell. Rebels still fought its authority and kept committing atrocities. Broad sanctions from 1997 had outlived their first purpose.

The Council ends the last of those broad bans. In their place it bans arms sales to anyone in Sierra Leone except the government. Government arms may enter only through named entry points, and every shipment must be marked and reported. Leading junta and rebel figures face a travel ban. The measures will end once the government controls the whole country and all rebel forces have disarmed.
un-sc-res-1371:
Macedonia's peace deal won the Council's backing in September 2001. Albanian and Macedonian leaders had signed a Framework Agreement at Skopje on 13 August. On 26 September 2001 the Council supported its full and timely use. The deal aimed to keep Macedonia a multi-ethnic state. The government in Skopje had taken steps toward that goal. European and security bodies were helping with observers.

Violence as a path to political aims was rejected outright. Only peaceful politics, the Council said, could give the country a stable future. It restated Macedonia's sovereignty and borders. It also demanded full use of resolution 1345 from that March. NATO troops were then collecting rebel weapons under the deal's terms.
un-sc-res-1471: Under the number 1471, the Security Council issued this formal resolution, now held as a Wikisource transcription of the UN record. The Council's job is keeping world peace, and resolutions are how it orders, authorizes, or condemns. The text follows the standard shape: cited prior actions and facts first, then the decisions themselves in numbered form.
un-sc-res-1571: Judge Gilbert Guillaume resigned from the International Court of Justice in 2004. His resignation would take effect on 11 February 2005. On 4 November 2004 the Security Council fixed the date to fill the vacancy. The election would take place on 15 February 2005. It would be held at a Council meeting and at a General Assembly meeting. The Assembly was then in its fifty-ninth session. The resolution does nothing beyond setting that date.
un-sc-res-1671:
European troops entered Congo's story through Resolution 1671, adopted in April 2006. Congo was preparing its first free elections in decades, and the UN mission there, MONUC, needed backup. The Council authorized a European Union force to support the mission during the voting period.

The text limits the force's stay to the election window and tasks it with protecting the mission, airports, and civilians in immediate danger. It was a rare case of the EU deploying soldiers under a UN request in Africa. Readers see two organizations sharing one peacekeeping job, with the terms spelled out in advance.
un-sc-res-171:
Resolution 171 deals with fighting between Syria and Israel. The fighting centred on Lake Tiberias and the demilitarized zone. The Council adopted the text on 9 April 1962. It heard both governments. It also read a report from the Chief of Staff of the UN Truce Supervision Organization. A cease-fire was already in place.

The Council deplores the hostile exchanges. They began on 8 March 1962. It tells both governments to obey Article 2 of the Charter. That article bars threats and the use of force. It finds the Israeli attack of 16-17 March broke Resolution 111. That earlier text had condemned Israeli action in breach of the armistice. It did so whether or not the action was retaliation.
un-sc-res-1771:
Sanctions on the Democratic Republic of the Congo are renewed by Resolution 1771 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 10 August 2007. The Congo had newly elected leaders, yet armed groups still held ground in the Kivus and Ituri. Weapons kept flowing in, fed in part by illegal mining.

The text renews the arms embargo until 15 February 2008. Travel bans and asset freezes on named offenders run for the same term. Supplies for the Congolese army and police stay exempt, under strict conditions and notice rules. A group of experts returns to watch compliance, with a written report due by 15 January 2008.
un-sc-res-1871: Resolution 1871 is one of the Security Council's formal decisions, held here in official wording sourced from English Wikisource. The members' text moves in the settled direction, from the world's facts as they state them to the world's duties as they set them. The entry preserves that movement entire, in the form the members voted.
un-sc-res-2071: Resolution 2071, adopted in 2012, is a formal Security Council decision kept here through a Wikisource transcription of the record. The act's authority rests on the fifteen members who voted it, five of them permanent. Their joint findings and instructions are preserved entire in this entry, in the form that governments received and answered to.
un-sc-res-271: Readers meet Resolution 271 here as a Security Council record, catalogued with a date of 1969. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-371:
Egypt's consent kept the Sinai emergency force alive in 1975. Cairo had signaled it might not renew the mandate. A Council appeal went to Egypt on 21 July. Egypt's reply satisfied the members. On 24 July 1975 the Council renewed the United Nations Emergency Force until 24 October. The parties again had to carry out resolution 338 at once.

The Secretary-General owed a report by the end of the term. He could report sooner if events required. The force stood between Egyptian and Israeli armies. A second Sinai disengagement deal was then being negotiated. The short renewal bridged the gap until that deal was signed. It followed the pattern of three-month terms that year.
un-sc-res-671: Resolution 671 of the Security Council reaches readers here as an official record text, catalogued under the year 1990. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades.
un-sc-res-71:
Liechtenstein wanted a place at the world court before it joined the United Nations. States outside the organization can join the court's statute on set terms. On 27 July 1949 the Security Council recommended those terms to the General Assembly. Liechtenstein would become a party when it deposited a signed instrument. The instrument would accept the statute's rules. It would also accept the duties of a United Nations member under the Charter's court article.

The principality had to promise to help pay the court's costs. The Assembly would fix its share from time to time. The short text opened the court's doors to a small state. Liechtenstein used the same path decades later in a famous case on wartime assets.
un-sc-res-971:
Georgia's Abkhazia conflict kept its observer mission in January 1995. On 12 January 1995 the Security Council extended UNOMIG until 15 May 1995. The Secretary-General had reported on the situation days earlier. The Council restated Georgia's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Talks on a political settlement, including Abkhazia's status, needed fresh effort. The Secretary-General had to push those talks forward.

He also owed a report within two months on every side of the question. The parties were called on to cooperate with the mission. UNOMIG's unarmed observers patrolled the ceasefire line from 1993. Their reports were the Council's main window on a frozen conflict. The renewal kept that window open through the spring.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Sierra Leone's sanctions are retargeted from the government to the rebels in Resolution 1171, adopted on 5 June 1998. The elected government was restoring administration after its return, but rebels kept resisting. Resolution 1132 (1997) had imposed prohibitions after the military coup.

The Council terminates the remaining prohibitions imposed by Resolution 1132 (1997). It then rebuilds the arms embargo to protect the restored government. All states must prevent arms sales to Sierra Leone except to the government, through entry points it lists with the Secretary-General. Arms for ECOMOG or UN use are exempt. States must notify the sanctions Committee of arms exports to Sierra Leone, and the government must mark, register, and notify its imports. A travel ban bars members of the former military junta and the Revolutionary United Front as designated by the Committee. The measures end once government control is re-established and non-governmental forces are disarmed and demobilized.

A small war in Macedonia ended with a deal at Lake Ohrid. The pact was signed at Skopje on 13 August 2001. It gave the Albanian minority more rights. In trade, the rebels would lay down their arms. Guns were being stacked as the Council met. Resolution 1371 passed with no dissent on 26 September 2001.

Full weight went to the pact and its swift use. Force as a path to gain was ruled out for good. A world guard force for the men who watched the deal won the Council's nod. The host state had asked for that guard. EU and OSCE work on the ground was cheered. Arms flows through Kosovo had to be choked by KFOR. All hands were told to keep world staff safe.

Another 12 months are granted to UNAMA, the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, on 28 March 2003. The mission had been created a year earlier to support the Bonn Agreement. The Transitional Administration is recognized as Afghanistan's legitimate government pending elections planned by June 2004.

The mandate is renewed from the date of adoption, and the United Nations' central, impartial role in helping Afghans rebuild is stressed. The mission is to keep aiding the Afghan Independent Human Rights Commission in carrying out the Bonn Agreement's human rights promises. All Afghan parties are called on to cooperate with the mission and keep its staff safe, and the Kabul security force is asked to work closely with it.

French judge Gilbert Guillaume announced he would leave the International Court of Justice on 11 February 2005, partway through his term. Resolution 1571, adopted unanimously on 4 November 2004, handles the practical consequence of that resignation: arranging the election of his successor for the time he had left.

Members set the vote for 15 February 2005, four days after the seat fell vacant. As the Court's statute requires, the election would be held at the same time in the Security Council and in the General Assembly, then sitting in its fifty-ninth session. The resolution is brief, factual, and entirely about keeping the bench complete.

Congo's first elections get a European Union force in support, authorized on 25 April 2006. Congolese voters had approved a new constitution in a referendum, and it had entered into force in February 2006. The United Nations mission, MONUC, was giving the electoral commission huge logistical help, but more security backing was judged necessary.

The deployment of Eufor R.D. Congo is authorized for a period ending four months after the first round of the presidential and parliamentary elections. The force would support MONUC, help protect civilians and the airport in Kinshasa, and assist with evacuations if needed. It could take all necessary measures to carry out those tasks, working in close coordination with Congo's government and the United Nations.

An Israeli attack on Syrian positions near Lake Tiberias is condemned on 9 April 1962. Fighting had broken out on 8 March 1962, and Israel struck on the night of 16 to 17 March. A ceasefire had since been arranged by the Chief of Staff of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization.

The hostile exchanges are deplored, and Syria and Israel are called on to keep their Charter duty to avoid force. The Israeli attack is found to be a flagrant violation of the ceasefire and the General Armistice Agreement, whether or not it was meant as retaliation. The Chief of Staff's steps to strengthen the truce observers are backed, and both sides are told to keep armed forces out of the demilitarized zone, as the armistice requires.

Congo's arms embargo is renewed by Resolution 1771, adopted on 10 August 2007. Illicit weapons still flowed into and around the Democratic Republic of the Congo, feeding conflict in the Great Lakes region. Armed groups held on in North and South Kivu and Ituri, and children were still being recruited. Newly elected institutions were in place, and the Group of Experts had filed its final report.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms measures until 15 February 2008. It keeps exemptions for integrated army and police units. It requires advance notice of exempt supplies to the Sanctions Committee. It also renews the transport controls and the financial and travel measures against designated persons. It re-establishes the Group of Experts to 15 February 2008, reporting by 15 January, focused on the Kivus and Ituri. A review of all measures is promised by 15 February 2008.

Western Sahara's mission, MINURSO, is renewed on 30 April 2009, with backing for the small-format talks between the parties. Four rounds of negotiations had been held since 2007 under the Secretary-General's auspices, without a breakthrough. Both sides' 2007 proposals remained the stated starting points, and a new Personal Envoy was taking the process forward.

Morocco and the POLISARIO Front are called on to keep showing political will. They are to continue negotiating in good faith toward a mutually acceptable solution, one providing for the self-determination of Western Sahara's people. The mission's mandate is renewed alongside the talks. Member states are urged to fund confidence-building measures, above all family visits between the territory and the refugee camps, and regular reports are requested.

Mali had split in two during 2012, and armed groups held the north of the country. Some of those groups had links to Al-Qaida in the Islamic Maghreb. A coup in the spring had shaken the state. A transitional government in Bamako was struggling to restore constitutional rule. Resolution 2071, adopted on 12 October 2012, responds to the crisis.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council backed the transitional authorities. It demanded a clear road map toward elections. Malian rebel groups were told to cut all ties with terrorist organizations, or face targeted sanctions. The text demanded an end to abuses in the north. Attacks on civilians and the use of child soldiers were named. Mali and its neighbors had asked for an international force, and the resolution set the stage for planning one.

An arson attack badly damaged the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem on 21 August 1969. The mosque is one of the most revered shrines in Islam. It stood in territory under Israeli military occupation. Speakers before the Council described the worldwide outrage at the attack. Resolution 271 was adopted on 15 September 1969.

The Council said the damage showed why Israel had to stop breaking earlier resolutions. Measures meant to change the status of Jerusalem had to be undone. Israel was condemned for failing to carry out those resolutions. It was told to observe the Geneva Conventions and the law of military occupation. Israel also had to let the Supreme Muslim Council of Jerusalem do its work without hindrance. A report on compliance was requested at the earliest date.

Egypt nearly let the Sinai peace force lapse in July 1975. The force, UNEF, stood between Egyptian and Israeli troops. Its term was about to end. Cairo's foreign minister wrote to the UN on 14 July. The Council's president sent an appeal on 21 July. Egypt agreed to a short stay. Resolution 371 passed on 24 July 1975 by thirteen votes to none.

The force gained just three months, to 24 October 1975. The Council paired the move with its old demand. Both sides had to act on Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. The text voices worry at the tense mood and the lack of peace talks. A report on the whole scene was due when the term closed, or sooner if events turned.

A short new term for the Iran-Iraq observer group was granted on 27 September 1990. The group, called UNIIMOG, watched the cease-fire between the two countries. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 21 September, had recommended the step. The Gulf crisis over Kuwait held the world's attention that autumn. Resolution 671 records the decision.

The Council extended the observer group's mandate for two more months, until 30 November 1990. The short length was deliberate. The Secretary-General was asked to report during November on his further talks with the parties. Those talks concerned the future of UNIIMOG itself. The mission was moving toward a decision on whether it should continue, shrink, or close. That open question explains why the Council renewed it for weeks rather than months or years.

A tiny alpine state sought the world court's law in 1949. Liechtenstein, with a prince as head of state, was no UN member. Court rules still let outsiders join the court's statute. The Assembly would set the terms, on the Council's advice. Resolution 71 passed on 27 July 1949 by nine votes to none. Two Soviet bloc teams held back.

The terms match those given to the Swiss in 1946. The state would file a signed pledge with the chief. It would accept the court's statute in full. It would take on the court duties the Charter sets. It would pay a fair share of court costs, set by the Assembly after talks. Small states gain real weight from such texts: the court door stood open to them too.

Georgia's split land of Abkhazia held a truce in 1995. UN men, UNOMIG, watched the line. A CIS force, led by Russians, kept the peace beside them. Folk who fled the war still could not go home. Talks on Abkhazia's place in Georgia crawled. Resolution 971 passed with no dissent on 12 January 1995.

UNOMIG won a stay to 15 May 1995. The chief's report of 6 January fed the choice. A deep look at the whole file was set for May. Gains on a deal and on home-going would drive that look. The Abkhaz side was told to speed the trek home. Rights of the fled to return in safety were stressed. Cash gifts for aid and mine work were sought from states with means.
zola-fortune-rougons-1871:
Ernest Vizetelly edited this English Fortune of the Rougons, the first Rougon-Macquart volume. His opening essay calls it Zola's first great bid for lasting fame. The grand plan, he explains, was a natural and social history of one family under the Second Empire.

Zola began the writing in the summer of 1869 and needed twenty-five years to finish the set. In the town of Plassans, the coup of 1851 crushes the republic in this opening tale. The scheming Rougons climb to power over fallen idealists. Heredity and history collide here at the root of French fiction's greatest family chronicle.
